front: What is ADH (vasopressin), where is it made, and what controls its release?
back: Arginine vasopressin is a nonapeptide made in the supraoptic and paraventricular hypothalamic nuclei with neurophysin, and released from the posterior pituitary. Its main controls are plasma osmolarity, sensed by hypothalamic osmoreceptors, and effective circulating volume, sensed by stretch receptors in the atria, ventricles and pulmonary veins. Angiotensin II, prostaglandins, histamine and acetylcholine increase release; atrial natriuretic peptide, GABA, alcohol and glucocorticoids decrease it.

front: How does vasopressin increase water permeability through V2 receptors?
back: V2 receptors on the basolateral membrane of collecting duct principal cells raise cAMP through adenylyl cyclase. Protein kinase A then drives aquaporin-2 water-channel vesicles into the apical membrane and slows their retrieval. Sustained stimulation also increases aquaporin-2 synthesis. Water then follows the hypertonic medullary gradient. V2 stimulation also increases urea permeability of the inner medullary collecting duct.

front: V1 receptors: subtypes, signalling and main actions.
back: V1 receptors act through phospholipase C, IP3 and DAG to release intracellular calcium. V1a sits on vascular smooth muscle, causing vasoconstriction, and also on visceral muscle, platelets and liver. V1b is on the anterior pituitary, where it promotes ACTH release. V1 receptors also constrict the vasa recta, which helps keep the medulla hypertonic.

front: Desmopressin: why is it the drug of choice for V2 indications?
back: It is a synthetic V2-selective agonist, about 12 times more antidiuretic than vasopressin, with negligible vasoconstrictor action and slow enzymatic breakdown. Its half-life is 1 to 2 h and its duration of action 8 to 12 h. Intranasal bioavailability is 10 to 20%; oral tablets have only 1 to 2% bioavailability and need a dose 10 to 15 times higher, but they avoid nasal side effects.

front: Why do thiazides reduce urine volume in diabetes insipidus?
back: Sustained electrolyte depletion makes the proximal tubule reabsorb more of the filtrate iso-osmotically. Less salt is reabsorbed in the cortical diluting segment, so a smaller volume of less dilute urine reaches the collecting ducts. Thiazides also lower GFR. They work in both pituitary and nephrogenic DI, but they cannot make urine hypertonic, so they are less effective than vasopressin. Potassium supplements are usually needed. The mechanism is not fully understood.

front: Lithium-induced nephrogenic DI: which drug is preferred and why?
back: Amiloride, because it blocks sodium entry through the epithelial Na+ channel of collecting duct principal cells, which lithium also enters through. Indomethacin can also reduce polyuria by lowering renal prostaglandin synthesis, and it can be combined with a thiazide and amiloride. Other NSAIDs are less active.

front: Tolvaptan: class, indications and key cautions.
back: An oral nonpeptide V2 antagonist that increases free water clearance, used for hyponatraemia in heart failure, cirrhosis or SIADH. The most frequent side effect is thirst and dry mouth; others include fever, GI upset and hyperglycaemia. It is metabolised by CYP3A4, so CYP3A4 inhibitors should be avoided. Half-life is 6 to 8 h, given once daily. Start it in hospital and do not raise serum sodium too fast (no more than about 8 to 10 mEq/L in 24 h), because rapid correction risks osmotic demyelination.

front: Which antitussive is the standard reference drug, and how does it act?
back: Codeine (methylmorphine) is the reference antitussive: more selective for the cough centre than morphine, it suppresses cough for about 6 hours, and naloxone blocks this, showing an opioid-receptor action in the brain. The antitussive dose is lower than the analgesic dose. Constipation is the main drawback; abuse liability is low but real. It depresses breathing at higher doses, so avoid it in asthma, poor respiratory reserve and children. About 10% is O-demethylated to morphine by CYP2D6; ultra-rapid metabolisers get unexpectedly high morphine levels (dangerous via breast milk), while poor metabolisers get little analgesia. Morphine itself is unsuitable because of addiction and respiratory depression.

front: Dextromethorphan: mechanism, advantages over codeine and important interaction
back: A synthetic central antitussive that blocks NMDA receptors and does not act on mu-opioid receptors; the d-isomer is antitussive (the l-isomer is analgesic). It is about as potent as codeine against cough but has no analgesic action, does not impair mucociliary function and hardly constipates, with fewer GI and subjective side effects. Though regarded as non-addicting, it is abused by some. Side effects: dizziness, nausea, drowsiness. It inhibits neuronal serotonin uptake, so it must be avoided with MAO inhibitors (serotonin syndrome). Not advised below 6 years.

front: Noscapine: what kind of antitussive is it, and what is the caution in asthma?
back: A non-narcotic opium alkaloid of the benzoisoquinoline series. Its antitussive potency is close to codeine, but it has no narcotic, analgesic or dependence-producing action; it is especially useful in spasmodic cough. It can release histamine, so it may provoke bronchoconstriction in asthmatics. Headache and nausea occur occasionally.

front: When is an antitussive justified, and why should a productive cough not be suppressed?
back: Justified for dry, non-productive cough, or when cough disturbs sleep or is hazardous (hernia, piles, cardiac disease, after eye surgery). A productive cough clears airway secretions, so suppressing it can retain secretions and is harmful.

front: How does bromhexine act as a mucolytic, and what is its active metabolite?
back: It depolymerises mucopolysaccharide chains directly and also by releasing lysosomal enzymes, which breaks up the fibre network of tenacious sputum. It is derived from vasicine, an alkaloid of Adhatoda vasica. Its metabolite ambroxol has a similar action.

front: Why should inhaled salbutamol not be used on a regular schedule?
back: Inhaled salbutamol acts within minutes and lasts only 2 to 4 hours, so it is a reliever, to be used as required by symptoms rather than on a regular schedule. Regular use can lead to receptor down-regulation and tolerance and may worsen bronchial hyperreactivity; rising use signals that more anti-inflammatory therapy is needed. GINA now advises that every asthmatic, however mild, should get inhaled corticosteroid at least each time a bronchodilator is used, and GG14 notes that ICS-formoterol is now recommended as the rescue bronchodilator of choice because it avoids the dangers of SABA overuse.

front: Compare salmeterol and formoterol as long-acting beta-2 agonists.
back: Both last about 12 hours and are given twice daily for maintenance. Salmeterol is a partial agonist with a slower onset, so it is not used for relief; its long aliphatic side chain is thought to anchor it near the receptor. Formoterol is an almost full agonist with a rapid onset, so combined with an inhaled corticosteroid it can also be used as the reliever. In asthma a LABA must never be used alone, because it does not treat inflammation and may increase the risk of life-threatening and fatal attacks; it is given with an ICS, preferably in one combination inhaler.

front: What are the main mechanisms by which theophylline helps asthma and COPD?
back: Non-selective, weak inhibition of phosphodiesterases (PDE3 and PDE4 matter most), which raises cAMP and relaxes bronchial muscle and damps inflammatory cells. It also blocks adenosine receptors, and adenosine A1 blockade is implicated in toxic arrhythmias and seizures. At low concentrations it may enhance histone deacetylation, which suppresses inflammatory gene transcription.

front: Why does theophylline have a narrow safety margin and non-linear kinetics?
back: The safety margin is narrow: dose-related toxicity begins in the upper part of the therapeutic range (KDT: 5 to 20 µg/mL; GG14 now regards 5 to 15 mg/L as therapeutic, since anti-inflammatory benefit occurs below 10 mg/L). Metabolism, mainly by CYP1A2, is saturable, so at higher doses kinetics change from first to zero order, the half-life lengthens (up to about 60 hours) and plasma levels rise out of proportion to dose. Clearance varies widely between patients (age, smoking, heart failure, liver disease, interacting drugs), so only sustained-release preparations are used, to avoid high peaks.

front: Name drugs that lower and drugs that raise theophylline levels, and the dose response for each.
back: Lower (CYP1A2 inducers): smoking, phenytoin, rifampicin, phenobarbitone; the dose must be increased. Raise (CYP inhibitors): erythromycin, ciprofloxacin, cimetidine, oral contraceptives, allopurinol; the dose is reduced to about two-thirds. Theophylline itself potentiates furosemide, sympathomimetics, digitalis, oral anticoagulants and hypoglycaemics, and reduces the effects of phenytoin and lithium.

front: What is the role of inhaled corticosteroids in asthma, and when do they act?
back: Inhaled corticosteroids suppress bronchial inflammation and hyperreactivity, improve peak flow, reduce the need for rescue beta-2 agonist and prevent acute episodes. They have no role during an acute attack or status asthmaticus. Peak effect is seen after 4 to 7 days (KDT), though maximal effect on airway hyperresponsiveness may take several weeks or months (GG14); benefit persists for a few weeks after stopping. GINA recommends ICS for all asthmatics, however mild, at least on an as-needed basis with each bronchodilator dose. Systemic effects are clinically relevant only above about 600 µg/day (KDT).

front: Omalizumab: what is it, how does it work, and in which patients is it used?
back: A humanised monoclonal antibody against IgE, given subcutaneously every 2 to 4 weeks; the dose is set by the circulating total IgE level. It neutralises free IgE, so little is left to bind the high-affinity receptor (FcεRI) on mast cells, and mediator release on allergen challenge falls; it also lowers FcεRI expression and circulating IgE. Used in severe allergic (extrinsic) asthma, where it reduces exacerbations, including virus-induced ones, and steroid needs. No benefit in non-allergic asthma; very expensive.

front: Montelukast and zafirlukast: mechanism, role and limitations.
back: Competitive antagonists at the cysLT1 receptor, reducing bronchoconstriction, mucus secretion, vascular leakage and eosinophil recruitment. Taken orally. Used as alternative or add-on controllers in mild-to-moderate asthma, particularly aspirin-induced and exercise-induced asthma; they are less effective than even low-dose ICS and are not for acute attacks or COPD. Generally well tolerated, but headache and eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis are reported, and montelukast now carries an FDA black-box warning for serious neuropsychiatric events, including suicidal thoughts.

front: Sodium cromoglycate: mechanism, uses and why it fails in an acute attack.
back: A chromone that stops mast cells degranulating, limiting release of histamine, leukotrienes and PAF. It is not a bronchodilator and does not block constrictor agonists, so it is useless during an attack. Oral absorption is negligible, so it is inhaled, and benefit takes 2 to 4 weeks. Used prophylactically in extrinsic and exercise-induced asthma, and in allergic rhinitis and conjunctivitis.

front: Essay: Bronchial asthma: pathogenesis and the rationale for drug treatment

front: Classify: antitussives
text: Opioid antitussives: {{codeine}} is the standard; {{morphine}} is most effective but unsuitable. Nonopioid central agents: {{noscapine}}, {{dextromethorphan}} and {{chlophedianol}}. Peripheral agent: {{prenoxdiazine}}, which desensitises pulmonary stretch receptors.

front: Classify: beta-2 agonists by duration
text: {{Salbutamol}} is a short-acting selective agonist acting for 2 to 4 hours; {{salmeterol}} is a long-acting agonist given {{twice daily}} with slow onset; {{formoterol}} has a faster onset and acts for about {{12 hours}}; {{indacaterol}} is an ultra-long-acting agent given {{once daily}} in COPD.

front: Classify: antiasthma drugs by class
text: Methylxanthine: {{theophylline}}. Muscarinic antagonist: {{ipratropium}}. Mast cell stabiliser: {{sodium cromoglycate}}. Cysteinyl leukotriene receptor antagonists: {{montelukast}} and {{zafirlukast}}. 5-lipoxygenase inhibitor: {{zileuton}}. Anti-IgE antibody: {{omalizumab}}.

front: Classify: theophylline drug interactions
text: CYP1A2 inducers such as {{smoking}}, {{phenytoin}} and {{rifampicin}} lower theophylline levels, so the dose must rise. Inhibitors such as {{erythromycin}}, {{ciprofloxacin}} and {{cimetidine}} raise levels, so the dose is cut to about {{two-thirds}}.

front: Classify: aerosol particle size and deposition
text: Particles of {{1 to 5 micrometres}} reach the bronchioles; larger particles settle in the {{oropharynx}}; very fine particles are {{exhaled}}. Only about {{10 percent}} of an inhaled dose reaches the site of action. A {{spacer}} lets larger particles settle out, reducing swallowed dose and {{candidiasis}}.

front: Classify: leukotriene and mast cell pharmacology
text: Cysteinyl leukotrienes act on the {{cysLT1}} receptor; {{zileuton}} blocks {{5-lipoxygenase}} but is limited by {{hepatotoxicity}}; cromoglycate {{stabilises}} mast cells and is {{not}} a bronchodilator.

front: Short note: Biologics for severe asthma

points: Severe asthma uncontrolled despite high-dose inhaled therapy
Choice depends on phenotype: allergic (high IgE) or eosinophilic type 2 inflammation (blood eosinophils above 300/µL)
Omalizumab: severe allergic asthma; SC every 2 to 4 weeks, dose by IgE level
Mepolizumab (SC every 4 weeks) and reslizumab (IV every 4 weeks) block circulating IL-5
Benralizumab (SC every 8 weeks) blocks IL-5R and causes eosinophil apoptosis
Dupilumab (SC every 2 weeks) blocks signalling by both IL-4 and IL-13; for eosinophilic or steroid-dependent asthma; also atopic dermatitis and nasal polyposis
Can cause peripheral eosinophilia, usually transient
Tezepelumab blocks the epithelial alarmin TSLP; works in eosinophilic and also non-type 2 asthma; approved from 12 years
Anti-IL-5 drugs cut exacerbations by about half and reduce oral steroid dose by at least 50%

front: Why is ICS-formoterol now preferred over a SABA alone as the reliever in asthma?
back: Formoterol has a rapid onset, so unlike salmeterol it can relieve symptoms, and each reliever dose of the combination also delivers inhaled corticosteroid when symptoms flare. GG14 states that ICS-formoterol is now recommended as the rescue bronchodilator of choice, being more effective and avoiding the dangers of SABA overuse. GINA (cited in Katzung) advises that all asthmatics, however mild, take ICS at least whenever a bronchodilator is used, because even mild asthma carries a risk of life-threatening attacks; other guidelines do not all agree.

front: Roflumilast: mechanism, use and adverse effects
back: An oral PDE4 inhibitor given once daily, converted by CYP3A4 and CYP1A2 to the more active N-oxide metabolite; it exerts an anti-inflammatory action mainly in the lungs rather than direct bronchodilation. Used as add-on therapy in severe COPD (FEV1 below 50%) with chronic bronchitis and frequent exacerbations, reducing exacerbations by about 20% with little effect on symptoms; not approved for asthma. Adverse effects: diarrhoea (commonest), nausea, headache, weight loss and psychiatric disturbances. CYP inhibitors raise and rifampicin lowers its levels; contraindicated in moderate-to-severe liver impairment (Child-Pugh B or C).

front: Short note: Drug therapy of stable COPD

points: Progressive airflow limitation from noxious particles, chiefly cigarette smoke; may progress even after exposure stops
Inflammation is relatively resistant to corticosteroids
LAMAs (tiotropium, glycopyrronium, umeclidinium, aclidinium) are bronchodilators of choice in preference to LABAs alone
Once-daily LABAs (indacaterol, olodaterol, vilanterol); LABA/LAMA combination inhalers improve lung function over either alone
Reserved for frequent exacerbators with blood eosinophils above 300/µL, usually as ICS/LABA/LAMA triple inhalers
Increase pneumonia risk
Roflumilast for severe COPD with chronic bronchitis and exacerbations
Daily azithromycin reduces exacerbations
Theophylline: low-dose trial showed no reduction in exacerbations; limited by toxicity
Managed much as in asthma (bronchodilators, systemic steroids), plus routine antibiotics such as beta-lactams, doxycycline or azithromycin against H. influenzae
A short 1 to 3 week course of oral glucocorticoid may help (KDT)

front: How does a sedative differ from a hypnotic, and where does general anaesthesia fit?
back: A sedative calms and reduces excitement, often with drowsiness but without true sleep, and has a flatter dose-response curve. A hypnotic induces and maintains sleep that resembles normal arousable sleep, with quicker onset, shorter action and a steeper dose-response curve. Sedation, hypnosis and general anaesthesia are increasing grades of CNS depression, and the drugs overlap; a hypnotic given at high dose can produce anaesthesia.

front: Why are benzodiazepines safer than barbiturates?
back: Benzodiazepines are selective modulators rather than global CNS depressants, so their depression has a lower ceiling. Even large overdoses usually leave consciousness and breathing largely intact, whereas barbiturate overdose causes coma and respiratory failure. They also distort sleep architecture less, cause less rebound and dependence, and do not induce hepatic enzymes the way barbiturates do.

front: Describe the normal sleep cycle: its stages and approximate length.
back: Non-REM stages 1 to 4 are followed by REM sleep, and the cycle repeats every 80 to 100 minutes. Stage 2 is the largest share of sleep (about 40 to 50%). Stages 3 and 4 together form slow-wave sleep. REM sleep is about 20 to 30% of sleep, with irregular breathing, fluctuating heart rate, dreaming and full muscle relaxation.

front: How do barbiturates act on the GABA-A receptor, and how does this differ from benzodiazepines?
back: Barbiturates bind a site on the GABA-A chloride channel complex that is separate from the benzodiazepine site. They prolong the time the channel stays open, whereas benzodiazepines increase how often it opens. At high concentrations barbiturates can open the chloride channel directly, which benzodiazepines cannot do. This direct effect helps explain the higher depressant ceiling of barbiturates.

front: What happens to sleep on repeated barbiturate use, and what follows withdrawal?
back: Barbiturates shorten sleep onset and reduce night waking, but they suppress REM and deep (stage 3 and 4) sleep and disrupt the REM-NREM cycle. These sleep effects weaken with nightly use. When the drug is stopped after a few nights, REM sleep rebounds with vivid dreams or nightmares, and normal sleep may take several nights to return. Morning hangover is common.

front: Why do thiopentone and phenobarbitone differ so much in duration of action?
back: Duration depends on lipid solubility, redistribution, metabolism and excretion. Thiopentone enters the brain within seconds and redistributes to fat and muscle, so consciousness returns in minutes, although its eventual half-life is about 9 hours. Phenobarbitone enters the CNS slowly, is partly excreted unchanged in urine, and has a half-life of about 80 to 120 hours. Alkalinising the urine increases its excretion.

front: How is acute barbiturate poisoning managed?
back: Supportive care comes first: a patent airway, assisted ventilation, oxygen, fluids and vasopressors if needed, with dopamine preferred for renal perfusion. Gastric lavage with a charcoal suspension left in the stomach limits absorption. Alkaline diuresis helps mainly for long-acting, renally excreted barbiturates. Haemodialysis or haemoperfusion over activated charcoal removes both long- and short-acting drugs. There is no specific antidote.

front: Classify the drugs acting at the benzodiazepine site: agonist, inverse agonist and antagonist.
back: Agonists such as diazepam increase GABA-induced chloride influx and produce sedation and anxiolysis. Inverse agonists such as DMCM reduce GABA action and are convulsant. Flumazenil is a competitive antagonist that blocks both, so it reverses both sedative and convulsant effects at this site. Picrotoxin blocks the chloride channel directly rather than acting at the benzodiazepine site.

front: Flumazenil: what is its profile and main uses?
back: It is a benzodiazepine analogue with little intrinsic activity of its own. It acts within seconds after IV injection and lasts 1 to 2 hours, with an elimination half-life of about 1 hour, so resedation can occur. It is not given orally. Uses are reversal of benzodiazepine sedation after anaesthesia or procedures, and as an adjunct in benzodiazepine overdose alongside supportive care. It also reverses the hypnotic effect of zolpidem-type drugs.

front: Why are zolpidem, zaleplon and eszopiclone called non-benzodiazepine hypnotics?
back: They are chemically unrelated to benzodiazepines but act at benzodiazepine receptors that contain the alpha-1 subunit, which mediates hypnosis and amnesia. Because they lack meaningful anxiolytic, muscle relaxant and anticonvulsant action, their hypnotic effect is more selective. They have lower abuse potential, and their hypnotic action is reversed by flumazenil.

front: How should a hypnotic be chosen for sleep-onset insomnia versus frequent night waking?
back: For difficulty falling asleep, use a rapidly absorbed, short-acting agent taken late enough to avoid morning sedation. For frequent night waking, a longer-acting agent such as flurazepam or nitrazepam may be used, accepting some daytime sedation. Long-acting drugs and those with active metabolites accumulate on nightly use and cause next-morning impairment. Choose by pharmacokinetic profile, use the lowest effective dose and keep the course short.

front: What are the roles of melatonin and ramelteon in sleep disorders?
back: Melatonin acts on MT1 and MT2 receptors to set the timing of the sleep-wake cycle. Low doses (2 to 10 mg) mainly shift the propensity to sleep, which helps jet lag, shift work and delayed sleep phase syndrome, but it is not a dependable hypnotic. Ramelteon is a selective MT1/MT2 agonist taken about 30 minutes before bed for sleep-onset insomnia. It has no GABA action and no benzodiazepine-type effects, and CYP inhibitors such as fluvoxamine raise its levels.

points: Dizziness, ataxia, disorientation and anterograde amnesia

Complex sleep behaviours (sleepwalking, sleep driving) with no memory of the event
Paradoxical excitement, irritability and nightmares, especially with flurazepam and nitrazepam

Worsen obstructive sleep apnoea: avoid
Additive CNS depression with alcohol and other depressants

Chemically unrelated to benzodiazepines but reversed by flumazenil

Agitation, anxiety, fearfulness, coldness and withdrawal seizures

Alcohol synergises with hypnotic CNS depression

points: Sedation, hypnosis and anaesthesia are grades of CNS depression
Sedatives have flatter dose-response curves; hypnotics act faster and more sharply
Insomnia is the main indication
Barbiturates: historical, now used mainly for epilepsy and anaesthesia
Benzodiazepines: anxiolytic, hypnotic, anticonvulsant and muscle relaxant
Non-benzodiazepine hypnotics: zolpidem, zaleplon, zopiclone, eszopiclone
Melatonin receptor agonist (ramelteon) and orexin receptor antagonist (suvorexant)
Obsolete agents: bromides, chloral hydrate, paraldehyde, glutethimide

Benzodiazepine site increases opening frequency; barbiturate site prolongs opening
High-dose barbiturates open the channel directly

Lower ceiling and wider safety margin for benzodiazepines

Rebound effects on withdrawal differ by drug and half-life

Plasma protein binding ranges from about 10% (flurazepam) to 99% (diazepam)
Long-acting agents and those with active metabolites accumulate on nightly use
Biological half-life can far exceed plasma half-life when active metabolites exist
Long-acting: flurazepam (for frequent waking; avoid in elderly), nitrazepam
Short-acting: triazolam (quick onset, poor maintenance), temazepam (sleep onset), alprazolam
Midazolam is not used orally as a hypnotic because of ataxia and abuse risk in the elderly
Psychomotor impairment, amnesia, next-day effects

Weak reinforcers, seldom abused alone

Withdrawal mostly mild; more intense with rapidly eliminated drugs
CYP3A4 inhibitors (ketoconazole, erythromycin) prolong action
Cimetidine, isoniazid and oral contraceptives slow metabolism
Synergy with alcohol and other CNS depressants

front: Essay: Insomnia - pharmacological management

points: Poor subjective sleep quality is the key criterion
Transient (1 to 3 days), short-term (3 to 21 days) and chronic (more than 3 weeks)
Look for causes: stress, bereavement, pain, reflux, COPD, alcohol, sleep apnoea
Sleep hygiene and regular sleep-wake times
Avoid daytime napping, caffeine and alcohol; relaxation and stimulus control
Treat the underlying somatic or psychiatric illness
Match onset and duration to the sleep problem
Next-day impairment depends on dose and kinetics
Short-term use limited to about 2 to 3 weeks
Hypnotics for chronic insomnia are of uncertain value
Intermittent use (for example every third night) may be tried
Slowly eliminated drugs cause less rebound and withdrawal
Benzodiazepines and non-benzodiazepine hypnotics are first choice when needed
Melatonin and ramelteon suit sleep-onset problems and circadian disorders
Suvorexant (dual orexin receptor antagonist) is described as suitable for longer-term use; start at 10 mg and go higher only if well tolerated
Tolerance and loss of effect after a few days in most hypnotics
Hypnotics are contraindicated in obstructive sleep apnoea
Suvorexant: CYP3A4 inhibitors can raise levels and cause next-day effects; watch for daytime somnolence and unusual night-time behaviour

front: Classify: drugs at the GABA-A complex
text: Benzodiazepines increase the {{frequency}} of chloride channel opening, barbiturates increase its {{duration}}, and {{flumazenil}} is the competitive antagonist at the benzodiazepine site.

front: Classify: sleep stages
text: Stage {{2}} forms the largest share of sleep (about {{40 to 50%}}), stages {{3 and 4}} together are called {{slow-wave sleep}}, and {{REM}} sleep takes about {{20 to 30%}} of the night.

front: Classify: benzodiazepine hypnotics by duration
text: Long-acting hypnotic benzodiazepines include {{flurazepam}} and {{nitrazepam}}; short-acting ones include {{triazolam}} and {{temazepam}}, and {{alprazolam}} is a short-acting agent with a short-lived active metabolite.

front: Classify: non-benzodiazepine and orexin-based hypnotics
text: {{Zolpidem}} and {{zaleplon}} act on alpha-1 containing benzodiazepine receptors; {{zopiclone}} has a half-life of about {{5 to 6 hours}}; {{suvorexant}} is a dual {{orexin}} receptor antagonist.

front: Classify: melatonin receptor agents
text: Melatonin acts on {{MT1 and MT2}} receptors; {{ramelteon}} is a selective agonist at these receptors, taken about {{30 minutes}} before bed for {{sleep-onset}} insomnia.

front: What is the typical presentation and EEG pattern of absence seizures?
back: Brief episodes, usually in children, lasting about half a minute. The child stares and freezes with no or only momentary loss of consciousness and no fall. The EEG shows a generalised 3 per second spike-and-wave pattern. Several episodes may occur daily, and seizures often remit in adolescence.

front: How does phenytoin block seizures at the cellular level?
back: It prolongs the inactivated state of voltage-gated sodium channels, which limits high-frequency repetitive firing while leaving normal low-frequency activity largely unchanged. At therapeutic levels it does not alter resting membrane potential or normal synaptic transmission. Its effects on glutamate release and calcium entry need higher concentrations, so their contribution is uncertain.

front: Why does phenytoin plasma level rise disproportionately with small dose increments?
back: Its hepatic hydroxylation (mainly CYP2C9 and 2C19) is capacity limited, so clearance shifts from first-order to zero-order over the therapeutic range. Once levels exceed about 10 mcg/ml, the half-life lengthens from 12 to 24 hours towards about 60 hours. Small dose increases then produce large rises in concentration, so plasma level monitoring guides dosing.

front: List the chronic adverse effects of phenytoin.
back: Gum hypertrophy is the commonest, more common in younger patients, and oral hygiene reduces it. Others are hirsutism, coarsening of facial features, acne, rashes or lupus-like reactions, and rarely neutropenia. Long-term use can cause megaloblastic anaemia through folate malabsorption and osteomalacia through impaired vitamin D activation. Exposure in pregnancy can cause foetal hydantoin syndrome.

front: Which drug is the first choice for trigeminal neuralgia, and why does it work?
back: Carbamazepine. It selectively reduces high-frequency nerve firing that drives the temporal summation of pain impulses, so it has an almost diagnostic effect in these neuralgias, unlike a general analgesic. About 60% of patients respond well. Phenytoin, lamotrigine and baclofen are less effective alternatives, and gabapentin may be tried in non-responders. It is not useful for diabetic or other neuropathic pain.

front: What happens to carbamazepine's half-life with chronic use, and which drugs does it affect?
back: Its half-life falls from 20 to 40 hours at first to about 10 to 20 hours on chronic use, because it induces its own metabolism. It is oxidised to an active 10,11-epoxide and is an inducer of CYP3A4 and 2C9. It lowers levels of valproate, lamotrigine, oral contraceptives and haloperidol, and phenytoin and phenobarbitone induce it in turn. Erythromycin, fluoxetine and isoniazid raise its levels.

front: What are the mechanisms and spectrum of valproate?
back: Valproate is broad spectrum. It prolongs sodium channel inactivation in a frequency-dependent way, weakly reduces the T-type calcium current, raises brain GABA by inhibiting its breakdown and possibly by increasing synthesis, and blocks NMDA-type glutamate receptors. It is the drug of choice for absence, myoclonic and atonic seizures, and a first-line drug for generalised tonic-clonic and partial seizures.

front: What are the serious risks of valproate?
back: Fulminant hepatitis is rare but serious and occurs mainly in children below 3 years, especially those with liver disease, on other antiseizure drugs or on other hepatotoxic drugs; liver function should be monitored. Given in pregnancy it has caused spina bifida and other neural tube defects, so it should be avoided. Concurrent carbamazepine raises the risk of foetal abnormalities. Concurrent clonazepam is contraindicated because absence status may be precipitated.

front: What are the key features of lamotrigine?
back: It is a broad-spectrum drug with a carbamazepine-like profile: it prolongs sodium channel inactivation and may reduce the release of glutamate and aspartate. It is used for partial and generalised tonic-clonic seizures, and also for absence and myoclonic seizures. Valproate doubles its level by inhibiting glucuronidation, so the dose should be halved when valproate is added; lamotrigine in turn lowers valproate levels. A severe rash, especially in children, requires withdrawal.

front: Explain the mechanism and interaction profile of levetiracetam.
back: It binds the synaptic vesicle protein SV2A, which may alter release of glutamate and GABA, and it inhibits N-type calcium channels. It is not oxidised by CYP enzymes and does not induce or inhibit them, so it has no pharmacokinetic interactions. It is mainly excreted unchanged in urine with a half-life of 6 to 8 hours. Side effects are sleepiness, dizziness, weakness and occasional behavioural change. It is not approved below 4 years.

front: What are the mechanism and main uses of gabapentin and pregabalin?
back: They are GABA derivatives that do not act at GABA-A receptors. They modulate calcium channels containing the alpha-2-delta subunit, which may reduce glutamate release, and gabapentin may also enhance GABA release. They are add-on drugs for partial seizures. Gabapentin is first-line for neuralgic pain, such as diabetic neuropathy and postherpetic neuralgia. Gabapentin has no drug interactions and is excreted unchanged in urine, with a half-life of about 6 hours.

front: What is the first-choice drug for status epilepticus, and what is the dose?
back: IV lorazepam, 0.1 mg/kg (about 4 mg in adults), injected at no more than 2 mg/min. It can be repeated once after 10 minutes if needed. It controls seizures in 75 to 90% of cases with a sustained effect of 6 to 12 hours, because it is less lipid soluble and redistributes more slowly than diazepam. Thrombophlebitis is also less likely. The airway, glucose and oxygenation should be secured at the same time.

front: Short note: Status epilepticus management

points: Maintain airway, oxygenation and intubation if needed
Give IV dextrose to correct possible hypoglycaemia
Monitor BP, cardiac rhythm, fluid and electrolytes
Lorazepam 0.1 mg/kg IV at no more than 2 mg/min; repeat once after 10 minutes
Diazepam 0.2 to 0.3 mg/kg IV is the older standard, but its effect fades after about 20 minutes and it damages the vein more
Rectal diazepam is used where IV access is not possible
Fosphenytoin 100 to 150 mg/min IV up to 1000 mg, with ECG monitoring; given whatever the lorazepam response
Phenytoin only when fosphenytoin is unavailable, at 25 to 50 mg/min
Phenobarbitone 50 to 100 mg/min IV up to 10 mg/kg as an alternative
Failure of lorazepam and fosphenytoin within about 40 minutes of onset
Treat with IV midazolam, propofol or thiopentone anaesthesia, with or without curarisation, in intensive care

front: Why can antimicrobials be used against an infection without harming the patient?
back: They act on a target the microbe has but human cells lack, such as the bacterial cell wall, bacterial folate synthesis, or a microbial enzyme with high affinity for the drug. This is selective toxicity.

front: When should surgical prophylaxis be given, and when should it stop?
back: Give it so that effective blood levels are present at incision and during the procedure: oral agents about 1 hour before, i.v. agents just before or after induction. Stop early. Beyond about 4 hours after closure it is justified only for contaminated or dirty wounds, for up to 5 days. Clean surgery in healthy patients usually needs none.

front: Give one narrow-spectrum and one broad-spectrum antibiotic.
back: Narrow: penicillin G or streptomycin. Broad: tetracyclines or chloramphenicol. The line between them is now blurred, so the terms are a matter of degree.

front: Which four antimicrobial groups are most often implicated in hypersensitivity?
back: Penicillins, cephalosporins, sulfonamides and fluoroquinolones. The reactions are unpredictable, not dose related, and range from rash to anaphylaxis.

front: What is meant by a low therapeutic index, and which agents have very low indices?
back: The margin between effective and toxic dose is narrow, so dosing must be individualised and monitored. Polymyxin B and amphotericin B have very low indices, so they are reserved for cases with no alternative. Aminoglycosides, vancomycin, tetracyclines and chloramphenicol have lower margins than penicillins or erythromycin.

front: How do natural resistance and acquired resistance differ?
back: Natural resistance is a trait of a whole species or group, for example gram-negative bacilli and penicillin G, or anaerobes and aminoglycosides; it rarely matters clinically. Acquired resistance develops in a previously sensitive strain after drug exposure and is a major clinical problem.

front: Contrast vertical and horizontal transfer of resistance.
back: Vertical transfer is selection of pre-existing mutants when the drug kills sensitive cells; it is slow and usually low grade, as with a single anti-TB drug. Horizontal transfer moves resistance genes between bacteria by conjugation (plasmids and R factors), transduction by phage, or transformation. It is fast and can spread multidrug resistance at once.

front: Name the three mechanistic types of drug-resistant bacteria.
back: Drug tolerant: the target changes so the drug binds poorly (for example altered RNA polymerase or penicillin-binding proteins). Drug destroying: an enzyme inactivates the drug (beta-lactamases, aminoglycoside-modifying enzymes). Drug impermeable: less drug gets in, through lost porins or active efflux pumps.

front: What is the MBC, and what does a small versus large MBC-to-MIC gap indicate?
back: MBC is the lowest concentration that kills 99.9% of the inoculum; it is judged by subculturing a clear tube into drug-free medium. If the MBC is close to the MIC, the drug is bactericidal. If it is far above the MIC, the drug is bacteriostatic. MBC is not used to choose drugs at the bedside.

front: Which antibiotics show concentration-dependent killing and which show time-dependent killing?
back: Concentration-dependent: aminoglycosides, fluoroquinolones and metronidazole, where the peak to MIC ratio drives effect, so a single large daily dose works better. Time-dependent: beta-lactams, glycopeptides and macrolides, where the time above MIC matters, so divided doses work better.

front: How do sulfonamides stop bacterial growth, and why are human cells spared?
back: Sulfonamides resemble PABA and competitively block dihydropteroate synthase, so the bacterium cannot make folate. Human cells take preformed folate from the diet and are unaffected. Excess PABA reverses the effect.

front: Name three bacterial routes to sulfonamide resistance.
back: Increased PABA production; a folate synthase with low affinity for sulfonamides; or an alternative pathway that uses preformed folate taken up from the medium. Resistance to one sulfonamide usually means resistance to all of them.

front: What causes sulfonamide crystalluria, and how is it prevented?
back: The acetylated metabolite is less soluble than the parent drug, especially in acidic urine, so it can precipitate. Prevent it with high fluid intake and alkalinised urine. It is now infrequent.

front: Why are sulfonamides avoided in neonates, and which patients risk haemolysis?
back: They displace bilirubin from albumin, and the neonatal blood brain barrier is more permeable, so kernicterus can follow. Haemolysis occurs with high doses in G6PD-deficient people.

front: What is the logic of combining trimethoprim with sulfamethoxazole?
back: It is a sequential block of folate synthesis: sulfamethoxazole blocks an early step and trimethoprim blocks bacterial dihydrofolate reductase. Each alone is static, but together they are often cidal. Trimethoprim is far more potent against the bacterial enzyme than the human one.

front: What are the main current uses of cotrimoxazole?
back: Uncomplicated and recurrent urinary tract infection, including prostatitis because trimethoprim concentrates in prostatic fluid; respiratory tract infection; Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (treatment and prophylaxis); chancroid as a second-line option. Its use for typhoid has largely been dropped.

front: Why is cotrimoxazole avoided in pregnancy, and what can happen if it is given near term?
back: Trimethoprim is a folate antagonist with a theoretical teratogenic risk, so it is avoided in pregnancy. Given near term it can cause neonatal haemolysis and methaemoglobinaemia.

front: How do fluoroquinolones kill bacteria, and why do they spare the host?
back: They inhibit DNA gyrase (the main target in gram-negative bacteria) and topoisomerase IV (main target in gram-positive bacteria), so the bacterium cannot relax and separate DNA and dies. Human cells rely on topoisomerase II, which binds these drugs poorly.

front: How do beta-lactams kill bacteria?
back: They acylate the transpeptidases (penicillin-binding proteins) that cross-link peptidoglycan, so the cell wall cannot be properly built. Growing cells become wall-deficient, swell osmotically and lyse, helped by autolysins. Human cells make no peptidoglycan, which explains their low toxicity.

front: What are the three main ways bacteria resist penicillins?
back: Beta-lactamase (penicillinase) that opens the lactam ring; altered penicillin-binding proteins, as in MRSA (PBP2a) and resistant pneumococci; and reduced entry through porins in gram-negative bacteria.

front: Why is penicillin G given parenterally, and what limits its duration?
back: Gastric acid destroys it, so less than a third of an oral dose is absorbed. Renal tubular secretion clears it rapidly; the adult half-life is about 30 minutes. Probenecid blocks tubular secretion and prolongs levels.

front: What are the serious toxic effects of high-dose penicillin G?
back: It is among the least toxic antibiotics, but very large i.v. doses (above about 20 MU) can cause confusion, twitching, convulsions and coma, especially with renal failure. High doses also impair platelet function. Intrathecal use is not recommended. Accidental i.v. procaine penicillin causes CNS stimulation.

front: Name three infections for which penicillin G is still the drug of choice.
back: Syphilis (all stages, with benzathine for latent and late disease), leptospirosis, and streptococcal infection such as pharyngitis, with benzathine for rheumatic fever prophylaxis. Penicillin G is also the choice for diphtheria carriers and some rare infections.

front: How do procaine and benzathine penicillin G differ?
back: Both are insoluble depot salts given deep i.m., never i.v. Procaine penicillin gives lower plasma levels that are sustained for 12 to 24 hours, with procaine-related toxicity. Benzathine releases penicillin very slowly, giving low but prophylactically useful levels for up to about 4 weeks.

front: How common is penicillin hypersensitivity, and how severe can it be?
back: About 1 to 10% of patients react. Penicillin G is the most commonly implicated drug. Procaine penicillin causes the most reactions since procaine is itself allergenic. Rash, urticaria and fever are common; anaphylaxis is rare (about 1 to 4 per 10,000) but can be fatal.

front: After an immediate-type penicillin reaction, what other drugs should be avoided?
back: Other penicillins, because cross-sensitivity is partial. Cephalosporins are also generally avoided after an immediate reaction. If the earlier reaction was only a rash, a penicillin may be given cautiously. Hyposensitisation is used only when no alternative exists.

front: Why is a negative penicillin skin test not reassuring, and which test is safer?
back: A negative intradermal test does not exclude delayed hypersensitivity, and penicillin skin testing can itself trigger fatal anaphylaxis. Benzylpenicilloyl-polylysine is the safer test. Penicillin antibodies alone do not mean allergy, since almost everyone treated makes them.

front: How does clavulanic acid work, and which enzymes does it block?
back: It is a suicide inhibitor: it binds beta-lactamase and is destroyed in the process, so the enzyme is inactivated. It blocks class II to V enzymes but not class I cephalosporinase. It has little antibacterial activity of its own and is combined with amoxicillin as co-amoxiclav.

front: Why does piperacillin with tazobactam fail against some Pseudomonas?
back: Tazobactam does not inhibit the inducible chromosomal beta-lactamase of Pseudomonas and other Enterobacteriaceae, and it cannot reverse loss of drug permeability. Clavulanate and sulbactam share this limitation.

front: What defines fourth-generation cephalosporins, and name two.
back: They keep high potency against Enterobacteriaceae with a third-generation-like spectrum, but resist hydrolysis by inducible chromosomal beta-lactamases. Examples: cefepime and cefpirome.

front: What distinguishes fifth-generation cephalosporins?
back: They are active against MRSA and penicillin-resistant pneumococci because they bind altered penicillin-binding proteins (such as PBP2a). Examples: ceftaroline fosamil and ceftobiprole medocaril. They are still vulnerable to some extended-spectrum beta-lactamases.

front: What is aztreonam, and why is it useful in penicillin allergy?
back: A monobactam with a narrow spectrum: it covers gram-negative enteric bacilli, H. influenzae and Pseudomonas, but not gram-positive cocci or anaerobes. It lacks cross-allergy with penicillins and cephalosporins, except ceftazidime, which shares a side chain with it.

text: Imipenem is given with {{cilastatin}} to block {{dehydropeptidase I}} in the renal tubule, and it causes {{seizures}} more often than meropenem. {{Aztreonam}}, a monobactam, is generally safe in penicillin allergy; the exception to cross-sensitivity is {{ceftazidime}}.

front: How do tetracyclines stop bacterial growth, and why are they selectively toxic to bacteria?
back: They are mainly bacteriostatic. They bind the 30S ribosomal subunit and stop aminoacyl-tRNA from reaching the acceptor site, so the peptide chain cannot grow. Susceptible bacteria concentrate them by an energy-dependent active transport system that host cells lack, and host ribosomes are less sensitive.

front: Classify the tetracyclines in clinical use.
text: Clinically relevant tetracyclines are {{tetracycline}}, {{oxytetracycline}}, {{demeclocycline}}, {{doxycycline}} and {{minocycline}}; the glycylcycline {{tigecycline}} is a newer synthetic subclass member.

front: Why is doxycycline preferred over the older tetracyclines?
back: It is almost completely absorbed whether or not food is present. Older agents need an empty stomach, and calcium, iron, milk, antacids and sucralfate bind them. Doxycycline is excreted mainly in faeces, so it can be used in renal failure, and the usual dose is 100 mg once or twice daily. Enzyme inducers such as phenobarbitone, carbamazepine and phenytoin shorten its half-life.

front: What distinguishes minocycline from the other tetracyclines?
back: It is the most lipid-soluble and most potent member, and it accumulates in body fat. It is mainly metabolised, not excreted by the kidney. Its distinctive toxicity is vestibular (ataxia, vertigo, nystagmus), which settles after stopping. It remains active against some meningococci and has useful activity against M. leprae.

front: Which sexually transmitted and atypical infections are first-line for tetracyclines?
text: {{Chlamydial}} urethritis and cervicitis (doxycycline for 7 days); {{lymphogranuloma venereum}}; {{granuloma inguinale}} (about 3 weeks); {{Mycoplasma}} pneumonia and {{psittacosis}}; cholera as an {{adjunct}} that reduces stool volume.

front: Which rickettsial, zoonotic and other serious infections are first-line tetracycline targets?
back: Rickettsial diseases (typhus, Rocky Mountain spotted fever, Q fever) respond dramatically. Brucellosis: doxycycline plus rifampicin for 6 weeks, with gentamicin added in acute cases. Plague (bubonic and pneumonic) and relapsing fever also respond, and tetracyclines are favoured for mass treatment in an epidemic, although streptomycin acts faster.

front: Tigecycline: what is special about it, and where is it not used?
back: A glycylcycline derived from minocycline that is active against many tetracycline-resistant Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria, including MRSA and VRE, because the usual tetracycline efflux pumps and ribosomal protection do not work against it. It is given only by slow i.v. infusion and is approved for severe community-acquired pneumonia, complicated skin infections and complicated intra-abdominal infections. Not used for hospital-acquired or ventilator pneumonia (higher mortality), for urinary infection, or in children and pregnancy. Pseudomonas and Proteus are inherently resistant.

front: How does chloramphenicol act, and how does its spectrum differ from tetracyclines?
back: It binds the 50S ribosome near the acceptor site and blocks peptide bond formation, while aminoacyl-tRNA binding to the 30S unit is unaffected. It is mainly bacteriostatic. Compared with tetracyclines it is more active against H. influenzae, N. meningitidis, B. pertussis and B. fragilis, and less active against gram-positive cocci and spirochaetes.

front: Chloramphenicol: classify its bone marrow toxicity.
text: Dose-related marrow suppression is {{predictable}} and usually {{reversible}}; the idiosyncratic aplastic anaemia is rare (about 1 in {{40,000}}), often fatal, probably genetic, and survivors may later develop {{leukaemia}}.

front: What is grey baby syndrome, and when does it occur?
back: A toxic reaction to chloramphenicol given at high doses (about 100 mg/kg), mainly prophylactically to premature or newborn infants. Their liver cannot conjugate the drug and their kidney cannot clear it well. Features: feeding refusal, vomiting, hypotonia, hypothermia, abdominal distension, irregular breathing and ashen grey cyanosis, progressing to circulatory collapse and death. Blood lactate rises. Chloramphenicol should be avoided in neonates.

front: What are the important drug interactions of chloramphenicol?
back: It inhibits hepatic metabolism of warfarin, phenytoin and cyclophosphamide, raising their levels. Enzyme inducers (phenobarbitone, phenytoin, rifampicin) speed up chloramphenicol metabolism, so therapeutic failure can occur.

front: How does tetracycline affect teeth and bone, and does the timing of exposure matter?
back: Calcium-tetracycline chelate is deposited in developing teeth and bone. Exposure from mid-pregnancy to about 5 months after birth causes brown discolouration and malformed deciduous teeth that are prone to caries. Exposure from about 3 months to 6 years affects the crowns of permanent anterior teeth, and repeated courses are worse. Late pregnancy or childhood exposure can temporarily suppress bone growth.

front: In which situations should tetracyclines be avoided or used with caution?
text: Avoid tetracyclines in {{pregnancy}}, {{lactation}} and {{children}}; avoid with {{diuretics}} (blood urea rises); caution in renal or hepatic insufficiency; never mix injectable tetracycline with {{penicillin}}.

front: How do aminoglycosides kill bacteria?
back: They must first cross the cell wall and cytoplasmic membrane by an oxygen-dependent, energy-driven transport, which is why anaerobes are not affected. Inside, they bind 30S ribosomes (others also bind 50S and the interface), freeze initiation, break up polysomes and cause misreading of the mRNA code. Faulty proteins damage the membrane, causing leakage and cell death, so the action is bactericidal.

front: Summarise the pharmacokinetics of systemically given aminoglycosides.
back: Highly ionised, so not absorbed orally; given i.m. or i.v., with peak levels in 30 to 60 minutes. They distribute only in extracellular fluid (volume about 0.3 L/kg), reach poor levels in CSF and aqueous humour, and high levels in the renal cortex and endolymph, which explains their toxicity. Not metabolised; excreted unchanged by glomerular filtration. Half-life 2 to 4 hours, prolonged in renal failure, the elderly and neonates. They cross the placenta.

front: Why are aminoglycosides increasingly given once daily?
back: They kill in a concentration-dependent way and have a long post-antibiotic effect, so a single high dose works as well as divided doses. Lower levels for longer each day let drug wash out of the endolymph and renal cortex, so single daily dosing is less nephrotoxic with equal efficacy, and it is cheaper. No regimen is less ototoxic than another. Avoid extended-interval dosing in renal insufficiency, in children, and when a beta-lactam is combined for endocarditis.

front: How is an aminoglycoside dose adjusted for reduced renal function?
back: Renal clearance parallels creatinine clearance (about two-thirds of it), so no reduction is needed while CLcr is above about 70 mL/min. Below that, reduce the daily dose or lengthen the interval according to measured CLcr. Elderly patients and neonates accumulate the drug, so they need the same adjustment.

front: Gentamicin: why is it important, what is the usual dose, and how is it combined?
back: It is the prototype and most widely used systemic aminoglycoside. Dose 3 to 5 mg/kg/day, given once daily or divided, i.m. or slow i.v. over 30 to 60 minutes. It covers aerobic Gram-negative bacilli (E. coli, Klebsiella, Proteus, Serratia, Pseudomonas) and some staphylococci, but not streptococci or enterococci on its own. It synergises with penicillin, ampicillin or vancomycin in enterococcal endocarditis and with a beta-lactam in Pseudomonas meningitis. It should not be used for community-acquired pneumonia.

front: What is streptomycin used for today?
back: Its use is now mostly restricted to tuberculosis, because of widespread resistance and lower potency. Other uses: plague (rapid cure in 7 to 12 days, alone or with a tetracycline), tularaemia (drug of choice), and subacute endocarditis in combination with penicillin. It is the least nephrotoxic aminoglycoside, but about one in five patients develop vestibular disturbance.

front: Amikacin: why is it kept in reserve?
back: A semisynthetic kanamycin derivative that resists most bacterial modifying enzymes, so it covers many gentamicin- and tobramycin-resistant Gram-negative bacilli. It is reserved for hospital-acquired gram-negative infections where local sensitivity shows resistance to gentamicin or tobramycin. Dose is 15 mg/kg/day in divided doses, and the toxicity is more cochlear than vestibular. It is used in multidrug-resistant tuberculosis.

front: Tobramycin: how does it differ from gentamicin?
back: Its spectrum, pharmacokinetics and dose (3 to 5 mg/kg/day) are almost identical to gentamicin, but it is 2 to 4 times more active against Pseudomonas and Proteus. Many gentamicin-resistant strains are cross-resistant, though some remain sensitive. It is not used with penicillin for enterococcal endocarditis; its main use is serious Pseudomonas and Proteus infection, as an alternative to gentamicin.

front: Classify the gut-acting aminoglycosides and their uses.
text: Oral {{neomycin}} is used for {{bowel preparation}} before surgery and for {{hepatic encephalopathy}}; {{paromomycin}} is given orally for intestinal {{amoebiasis}} and {{giardiasis}}. Neither is absorbed, but systemic use of neomycin is avoided because of {{ototoxicity}} and {{nephrotoxicity}}.

front: How do bacteria become resistant to aminoglycosides, and which mechanism matters most?
back: Most important: plasmid-encoded enzymes that phosphorylate, adenylate or acetylate the drug. The modified drug no longer binds ribosomes or enters cells well. These plasmids are common in hospital organisms and can carry multidrug resistance. Less common: mutation of ribosomal proteins, and reduced uptake. Cross-resistance is variable because enzyme susceptibility differs; amikacin resists most of these enzymes.

front: Describe the two types of aminoglycoside ototoxicity and which drugs favour each.
back: Cochlear: damage starts at the base of the cochlea, so high frequencies are lost first. It is often silent until audiometry, then tinnitus and permanent hearing loss, because hair cells do not regenerate. Kanamycin and amikacin are most cochlear. Vestibular: headache, nausea, vomiting, vertigo, ataxia and nystagmus. Partial recovery occurs over 1 to 2 years. Streptomycin and gentamicin are more vestibular.

front: How does aminoglycoside nephrotoxicity appear, and what increases the risk?
back: Proximal tubular damage: loss of urinary concentrating power, low GFR, nitrogen retention, albuminuria and casts. The drug accumulates in the renal cortex, so toxicity tracks total dose and duration. Risk is higher in the elderly and in pre-existing kidney disease. Single daily dosing is less toxic. Damage is reversible if the drug is stopped promptly. Reduced clearance raises levels and worsens ototoxicity. Streptomycin is the least nephrotoxic.

front: How is gentamicin monitored to limit toxicity?
back: By the trough plasma concentration. Vestibular damage becomes concentration-dependent above about 2 mcg/mL, so dosing should keep the measured trough below 1 mcg/mL. Dose by renal function.

front: Which drugs add to aminoglycoside toxicity?
text: Additive nephrotoxicity: {{amphotericin B}}, {{vancomycin}}, {{cyclosporine}}, {{cisplatin}} and {{NSAIDs}}. Additive ototoxicity (use cautiously): {{furosemide}} and {{minocycline}}.

front: When should aminoglycosides be avoided even though they are otherwise indicated?
back: In pregnancy, because they cross the placenta and reach fetal blood and amniotic fluid, risking hearing loss in the baby; streptomycin is contraindicated. Aminoglycoside ear drops are contraindicated with a perforated eardrum, because they cause ototoxicity. Neomycin is contraindicated when renal function is impaired.

front: How does erythromycin act, and which organisms does it cover?
back: It binds the 50S ribosome and blocks translocation of the growing peptide from the A site back to the P site. The ribosome stalls, and larger proteins are prematurely terminated. It is mainly bacteriostatic. Its narrow spectrum covers Gram-positive cocci (streptococci, pneumococci), Clostridia, C. diphtheriae, Listeria, plus Campylobacter, Legionella, Mycoplasma, Chlamydia and Gardnerella. Enterobacteriaceae and B. fragilis are not covered.

front: What are the main mechanisms of macrolide resistance, and what cross-resistance follows?
back: Efflux pumps in cocci; plasmid-encoded methylase that alters the ribosomal binding site (the most important mechanism in Gram-positives); erythromycin esterase in enterobacteria; chromosomal 50S mutation in some. Resistance extends to other macrolides, and partly to clindamycin and chloramphenicol, whose ribosomal binding sites lie close together.

front: Why is erythromycin dangerous with terfenadine, astemizole or cisapride?
back: Erythromycin (and clarithromycin) inhibits CYP3A4, raising levels of the co-prescribed drug. Terfenadine, astemizole and cisapride then cause QT prolongation, serious ventricular arrhythmias and death, and these drugs were withdrawn. Erythromycin also raises levels of theophylline, carbamazepine, valproate, ergotamine and warfarin. Azithromycin interacts much less.

front: Which erythromycin ester causes cholestatic hepatitis, and when does it appear?
back: The lauryl sulfate estolate. It causes hepatitis with cholestatic jaundice, resembling viral hepatitis or biliary obstruction, usually after 1 to 3 weeks. Pregnancy increases the risk. It is probably a hypersensitivity reaction and clears on stopping. Rarely seen with the ethylsuccinate or stearate esters. Erythromycin base or another ester can be given later without recurrence.

front: What makes azithromycin preferable to erythromycin, and how should it be taken?
back: It is acid-stable, better tolerated and has fewer CYP3A4 interactions. Tissue and intracellular concentrations are high, and the terminal half-life exceeds 50 hours, so short courses work once daily. Take it 1 hour before or 2 hours after food, because food reduces absorption. It is excreted mainly in bile, with little renal excretion. The child dose is 10 mg/kg/day.

front: Which sexually transmitted infections are treated with azithromycin, and at what regimen?
text: Urogenital chlamydia: {{single 1 g dose}}; chancroid and PPNG: {{single 1 g dose}}; lymphogranuloma venereum: {{1 g weekly for 3 weeks}}; donovanosis: {{500 mg daily for 7 days}} or 1 g weekly for 4 weeks; Legionnaires pneumonia: {{500 mg daily for 2 weeks}}.

front: Classify the newer macrolides and name one key feature of each.
text: {{Clarithromycin}} inhibits CYP3A4 and is used in H. pylori triple therapy and MAC infection; {{roxithromycin}} has a long half-life for twice daily dosing; {{telithromycin}} is a ketolide restricted because of hepatitis; {{azithromycin}} is an azalide given once daily; {{spiramycin}} limits transplacental toxoplasmosis.

front: Clindamycin: mechanism, spectrum and where it is most useful.
back: A lincosamide that binds the 50S ribosome like erythromycin, with partial cross-resistance. It covers most streptococci, penicillinase-producing staphylococci (not MRSA) and most anaerobes, especially Bacteroides fragilis. It is inactive against aerobic Gram-negative bacilli, enterococci, Mycoplasma, Chlamydia and Rickettsia. It penetrates bone and soft tissue well, but not the CSF, and it concentrates in neutrophils and macrophages.

front: What is the most serious adverse effect of clindamycin, and how is it managed?
back: Antibiotic-associated pseudomembranous colitis from Clostridioides difficile overgrowth, which can be fatal. Stop the drug at once. Current guidelines treat with oral vancomycin or fidaxomicin; oral metronidazole (first choice in older texts, including KDT) is now kept for mild cases when those are unavailable. Clindamycin is therefore reserved for anaerobic and mixed infections, such as B. fragilis abscesses, and skin infections in penicillin-allergic patients. Other effects include rash and rarely liver injury or phlebitis.

front: How does vancomycin kill bacteria, and how do enterococci resist it?
back: It binds the D-Ala-D-Ala end of peptidoglycan precursors, so they cannot be transferred and cross-linked at the cell membrane, and the cell wall weakens. It is bactericidal only against Gram-positive organisms, Neisseria and Clostridia; Gram-negative bacilli are inherently resistant. It is not absorbed orally. Enterococci resist (VRE) through a plasmid-mediated change in the D-Ala-D-Ala target, which lowers vancomycin binding.

front: What is red man syndrome, and how is it prevented?
back: An infusion reaction after rapid i.v. vancomycin. The drug directly releases histamine from mast cells, causing flushing of the face and upper body, urticaria, chills, fever and sometimes hypotension. Prevent it by infusing slowly; systemic doses are infused over about 1 hour.

front: What toxicities must be watched during vancomycin therapy?
back: Concentration-dependent nerve deafness, which may be permanent, and dose-related kidney damage. Its toxicity adds to aminoglycosides, so combined use needs care. Skin allergy and fall in blood pressure can occur with rapid infusion. Reduce the dose in renal insufficiency, because the drug is excreted unchanged in urine with a half-life of about 6 hours.

front: List the main uses of vancomycin.
text: Systemic: {{serious MRSA}} infection; {{enterococcal endocarditis}} with gentamicin in penicillin-allergic patients; empirical {{bacterial meningitis}} with a cephalosporin; surgical {{prophylaxis}} in MRSA areas. Oral: {{C. difficile}} colitis and {{staphylococcal enterocolitis}}.

front: How does linezolid differ from other protein-synthesis inhibitors?
back: It is an oxazolidinone that binds the 23S rRNA of the 50S subunit at the P site and blocks formation of the initiation complex, so protein synthesis never starts. It is mainly bacteriostatic and has no cross-resistance with other antibiotic classes; enterococci can become resistant through 23S rRNA mutation. Active against MRSA, VRE and penicillin-resistant pneumococci, but not Gram-negative bacilli.

front: Why is linezolid kept in reserve, and why is it unsuitable for enterococcal endocarditis?
back: It is reserved for serious drug-resistant Gram-positive infections, such as hospital-acquired pneumonia, febrile neutropenia, wound infection, and infection with VRE or vancomycin-resistant MRSA, to limit resistance. Because it is bacteriostatic, it is unsuitable for enterococcal endocarditis. It is also a reserve drug for extensively drug-resistant TB. Dose 600 mg twice daily, oral or i.v., with no renal adjustment.

front: Daptomycin: mechanism, indications and key toxicity.
back: A lipopeptide whose lipid tail inserts into the bacterial membrane, where molecules aggregate into pores. Potassium leaks out, the membrane depolarises, and DNA, RNA and protein synthesis stop. It is bactericidal only against Gram-positive bacteria, including MRSA and VRE. Indicated for complicated skin infections and S. aureus bacteraemia, not pneumonia. Dose 4 mg/kg daily for skin infection and 6 mg/kg daily for bacteraemia or endocarditis. Toxicity: myopathy and rhabdomyolysis, especially with statins; eosinophilic pneumonia after more than 2 weeks.

front: Which drugs are options for vancomycin-resistant Enterococcus (VRE)?
text: Options named in the chapter include {{linezolid}}, {{daptomycin}}, {{tigecycline}} and {{quinupristin-dalfopristin}}; the last is not active against {{E. faecalis}}, and {{teicoplanin}} works only on some VRE strains.

front: How do polymyxin B and colistin kill Gram-negative bacteria?
back: They are cationic polypeptides with a detergent-like action. They bind phospholipids in the outer membrane, distort it and form pseudopores, so ions and amino acids leak out; they may also neutralise endotoxin. They are rapidly bactericidal against most Gram-negative bacilli. Proteus, Serratia and Neisseria are not inhibited. Resistance has never been a major problem, and there is no cross-resistance with other classes.

front: Where are polymyxin B and colistin used, and why are they not given systemically?
back: They are barely absorbed from the gut or denuded skin, so they are used topically (skin, burns, otitis externa, conjunctivitis, corneal ulcer, often with other agents). Oral colistin treats gram-negative bacillary diarrhoea in infants (E. coli, Salmonella, Shigella) and Pseudomonas enteritis. They are not used systemically because of their toxicity.

front: Bacitracin, mupirocin and fusidic acid: where are these topical agents used?
text: {{Bacitracin}} is topical only, for wounds and eyes (kidney-toxic if given systemically); {{mupirocin}} treats impetigo and small wounds; {{fusidic acid}} treats penicillinase-producing staphylococcal boils and skin infection.

front: How does nitrofurantoin act, and why has its use narrowed?
back: Bacterial nitroreductases convert it into reactive intermediates that damage DNA and interfere with protein synthesis. It is mainly bacteriostatic but can be cidal at high concentration and in acid urine. Its broad Gram-negative activity has narrowed largely to E. coli, because of resistance; Pseudomonas and Proteus are resistant. Resistance does not emerge rapidly during treatment. It achieves antibacterial levels only in urine, not in blood or tissues.

front: What is the main indication for nitrofurantoin, and what are typical doses?
back: Uncomplicated lower urinary tract infection, not associated with prostatitis. Acute infection: 50 to 100 mg three times daily for 5 to 10 days, and not for more than 2 weeks at a time. Suppression of recurrent cystitis: 50 mg twice daily or 100 mg at bedtime, which can also be used after catheterisation. It is unsuitable for pyelonephritis, because it does not reach kidney tissue.

front: When must nitrofurantoin be avoided, and what are its main adverse effects?
back: Avoid in renal failure (poor excretion and rising toxicity), in pregnancy, and in neonates. The commonest effect is gastrointestinal intolerance. Others: acute chills, fever and leucopenia; peripheral neuritis with long use; haemolytic anaemia, especially in G6PD deficiency; rarely liver damage and chronic pulmonary fibrosis. Urine turns dark brown on standing. Probenecid reduces its concentration in urine.

front: Short note: Empirical treatment of urinary tract infection

points: Send urine for culture before starting empirical therapy
Choose the least toxic, cheapest drug likely to work; adjust to sensitivity
Lower UTI: about 3 days; pyelonephritis: 10 to 14 days, with a potent drug
Ciprofloxacin or ofloxacin (avoid in pregnancy)
Cotrimoxazole; cephalexin or cefpodoxime
Amoxicillin-clavulanate; nitrofurantoin for 5 to 7 days
Nitrofurantoin not used for pyelonephritis; parenteral options include gentamicin with a potent agent
Avoid methenamine and tetracyclines (except doxycycline); avoid potassium and acidifying agents
Bedtime cotrimoxazole, nitrofurantoin, norfloxacin or cephalexin

front: How does amphotericin B kill fungi?
back: It binds ergosterol in the fungal membrane. Several molecules line up to form a pore; ions and small water-soluble molecules then leak out, so the cell dies.

front: Why is amphotericin B so toxic to the patient even though it targets fungi?
back: Human cell membranes contain cholesterol, which resembles ergosterol. Amphotericin B binds cholesterol too, though with lower affinity, so its selectivity is poor. It is among the most toxic systemic antibiotics, although it is the least toxic of the polyenes.

front: What is the acute infusion reaction to amphotericin B and how is it managed?
back: Chills, fever, body aches, nausea, vomiting and breathlessness for 2 to 5 hours, probably from cytokine release (IL-1, TNF). Raise the dose gradually after a test dose. Hydrocortisone given with the infusion can blunt it, and it usually lessens with continued use. Thrombophlebitis of the vein can occur.

front: What is the most important long-term toxicity of conventional amphotericin B?
back: Dose-related nephrotoxicity: fall in GFR, azotaemia, hypokalaemia, renal tubular acidosis and loss of urine-concentrating ability. It recovers slowly and often incompletely after stopping. Anaemia from marrow depression is common but largely reversible.

front: Short note: Amphotericin B formulations

points: Polyene from Streptomyces nodosus
Gold standard for most systemic mycoses
Fungicidal at high concentration, fungistatic at low
Powder with deoxycholate, dispersed in glucose (not saline) before IV use
Test dose first, then slow infusion, titrated up toward about 0.7 mg/kg/day
Total course often 3 to 4 g over 2 to 3 months
Most toxic formulation
Lower infusion reaction and nephrotoxicity, less anaemia
Can be infused faster
Preferred for empirical febrile neutropenia, severe deep mycosis and kala-azar
Much costlier

front: Mucormycosis: which drug is first choice and which is the salvage option?
back: Amphotericin B is first choice. Posaconazole is the second choice and is kept for salvage. Fluconazole is not active against mucor.

front: Cryptococcal meningitis: which two drugs are combined and why?
back: Amphotericin B with flucytosine. Flucytosine acts synergistically with amphotericin B, which helps flucytosine enter the fungus, so the more toxic amphotericin dose can be reduced. Flucytosine is kept to about the first two weeks because of marrow toxicity.

front: Which fungal enzyme do echinocandins inhibit, and why are they less toxic than amphotericin B?
back: Beta-1,3-glucan synthase, so beta-1,3-glucan is not made in the fungal cell wall. The wall weakens, the fungus loses osmotic stability and dies. Human cells have no such wall, so toxicity is low.

front: Caspofungin: route, distribution and main uses
back: Not absorbed orally, so given IV as a freshly made solution. It distributes into tissues but does not enter CSF. Preferred for deep and invasive candidiasis, also used for oesophageal candidiasis and for aspergillosis not responding to other drugs. Well tolerated in neutropenic patients with fever.

front: What is the mechanism of azole antifungals and why are triazoles less toxic than imidazoles?
back: They inhibit fungal lanosterol 14-alpha-demethylase, a cytochrome P450 enzyme, so ergosterol synthesis fails and toxic sterol intermediates build up. Triazoles have lower affinity for mammalian CYP450 and sterol synthesis, so they are less toxic.

front: Short note: Classes of azole antifungals

points: Clotrimazole, miconazole, econazole, oxiconazole
Used for dermatophytes, candidiasis, pityriasis versicolor, otomycosis
Ketoconazole is the exception: also oral, but now rarely used systemically
Fluconazole, itraconazole, voriconazole, posaconazole
Fluconazole and itraconazole largely replaced ketoconazole
Voriconazole and posaconazole are newer, broader agents
Dermatophytes, Candida, most deep mycoses
Mucor is not covered by most azoles (posaconazole excepted)
Also active against Nocardia and Leishmania
Candida in advanced AIDS and fluconazole-resistant oesophageal candidiasis
Usually due to mutation of the 14-demethylase gene
Many fluconazole-resistant isolates respond to itraconazole or voriconazole

front: Why has oral ketoconazole been largely withdrawn from systemic use?
back: It suppresses testicular androgen synthesis and displaces testosterone from binding proteins, causing gynaecomastia, loss of libido and oligospermia. It suppresses cortisol synthesis at higher doses and disturbs oestradiol synthesis in women. Fluconazole and itraconazole avoid these effects.

front: Classify the interactions of ketoconazole: acid-dependent absorption, enzyme inducers and CYP inhibition
text: Ketoconazole needs {{gastric acid}} for absorption, so H2 blockers, PPIs and antacids reduce it. {{Rifampin}}, phenytoin and carbamazepine induce its metabolism. It inhibits {{CYP3A4}} and raises levels of drugs such as digoxin, warfarin, cyclosporine and statins.

front: Fluconazole: key pharmacokinetics and why it is the azole of choice for meningitis
back: Water-soluble and about 94% absorbed; food and gastric pH do not change this. Mostly excreted unchanged in urine, half-life 25 to 30 hours. It penetrates brain and CSF well, so it is preferred for cryptococcal and coccidioidal meningitis. Dose reduction is needed in renal impairment.

front: Name two deep mycoses that fluconazole does not treat.
back: Aspergillosis and mucormycosis. It is also inferior to itraconazole for histoplasmosis, blastomycosis and sporotrichosis, and for tinea unguium (nail infection).

front: Itraconazole: how do food and acid affect it, and why is it not used for meningitis?
back: Oral absorption is variable and improved by food and gastric acid, so antacids, H2 blockers and PPIs reduce it. It is highly protein bound with a large volume of distribution, but CSF penetration is poor. It is metabolised by CYP3A4 and its active metabolite is excreted in faeces.

front: Voriconazole: drug of choice for which infections, and what are its main toxicities?
back: Drug of choice for invasive aspergillosis, fluconazole-resistant invasive Candida, Fusarium, and febrile neutropenia not responding to antibacterials. Toxicities: rash, photosensitivity, raised liver enzymes, QTc prolongation; short-lived visual disturbances, especially after IV dosing.

front: Posaconazole: what is its distinctive role?
back: It is the only azole with proven efficacy in mucormycosis, used as salvage therapy. Because of cost and limited experience, it is kept for non-responding aspergillosis and invasive candidiasis. It can raise levels of CYP3A4 substrates.

front: Essay: Compare fluconazole, itraconazole, voriconazole and ketoconazole

points: All inhibit fungal lanosterol 14-alpha-demethylase
Triazoles preferred over the imidazole ketoconazole for systemic use
Fluconazole: Candida, cryptococcus, dermatophytes; poor against moulds
Itraconazole: adds some moulds; histoplasmosis, blastomycosis, sporotrichosis
Voriconazole: invasive aspergillosis, fluconazole-resistant Candida
Ketoconazole: now mainly topical
Fluconazole: well absorbed, renal excretion unchanged, good CSF penetration
Itraconazole: variable absorption needing food and acid, poor CSF
Voriconazole: well absorbed, avoid high-fat meal, CYP2C19 and CYP3A4 metabolism
Ketoconazole: hormonal effects, nausea
Itraconazole: dose above 400 mg/day poorly tolerated, hypokalaemia, can worsen LV function
Voriconazole: visual change, QTc prolongation, photosensitivity
Azoles inhibit CYP3A4 to varying degrees
Enzyme inducers such as rifampin, phenytoin and carbamazepine reduce levels
Fluconazole has the fewest interactions among them

front: Classify the first-choice drugs for systemic mycoses
text: Cryptococcal meningitis: first choice {{amphotericin B with flucytosine}}, second choice {{fluconazole}}. Invasive aspergillosis: first choice {{voriconazole}} or amphotericin B. Histoplasmosis: first choice {{itraconazole}} or amphotericin B.

front: Terbinafine: mechanism and why it is called fungicidal
back: It non-competitively inhibits squalene epoxidase, an early enzyme in ergosterol synthesis. Squalene accumulates inside the fungus, which is thought to kill it. The human enzyme is inhibited only at far higher concentrations.

front: Terbinafine: which infections does it treat, and for how long?
back: Topical 1% cream twice daily for tinea pedis, cruris, corporis and pityriasis versicolor, for 2 to 4 weeks. Oral 250 mg daily for onychomycosis, tinea capitis and widespread lesions, for 3 to 6 months or longer. Nail cure about 90%, better than griseofulvin or itraconazole. Oral route is not effective for pityriasis versicolor; it is weaker against candidiasis.

front: Flucytosine: mechanism and why it is never used alone
text: Flucytosine is converted inside fungal cells to {{5-fluorouracil}}, which blocks {{thymidylate synthesis}}. Mammalian cells convert it poorly, so it has {{no}} anticancer use. Resistance develops {{rapidly}} if it is used alone, so it is always given with amphotericin B.

front: How does griseofulvin act on dermatophytes, and why is it fungistatic?
back: It binds polymerised microtubules and disrupts mitosis, so hyphae become multinucleate and stunted. Daughter nuclei fail to separate properly. It is fungistatic, so the newly formed keratin is not invaded, but infected keratin stays infected until shed. It has no action on Candida, deep mycoses or bacteria.

front: Short note: Griseofulvin

points: Poorly water soluble, so absorption is incomplete; better with fatty food and microfine particles
Deposits in keratin-forming tissue and stays for weeks
Mainly metabolised by methylation; excreted in urine
Oral only; ineffective topically
Reserve for extensive tinea, tinea capitis and onychomycosis
Duration depends on keratin turnover: scalp about 4 weeks, palms and soles 6 to 8 weeks, fingernails 6 to 8 months, toenails 10 to 12 months
Headache and GI upset are commonest
Rash, photoallergy and hepatitis need stopping
Induces CYP450: lowers efficacy of oral contraceptives and speeds warfarin metabolism

front: Acyclovir: how does it selectively stop herpes virus replication?
back: A herpes-specific viral thymidine kinase converts acyclovir to its monophosphate; cellular kinases then make the triphosphate. The triphosphate competitively inhibits viral DNA polymerase and is incorporated into viral DNA, ending chain elongation. Infected cells activate it far more than uninfected cells, giving a high therapeutic index. CMV is practically unaffected.

front: Short note: Acyclovir in herpes infections

points: Topical therapy works only if started early in mild cases
Oral or IV therapy for severe or late disease
Suppressive oral therapy reduces recurrences and transmission but does not eliminate them
HSV encephalitis: IV acyclovir is the drug of choice; benefit depends on starting early
Disseminated HSV in immunocompromised patients: IV or oral
Zoster: IV in immunodeficient or severe cases; oral therapy must start early
Postherpetic neuralgia is not prevented
Chickenpox: specific treatment reserved for immunocompromised patients and neonates
Ointment for deep stromal keratitis, where corneal penetration helps
Slower than idoxuridine drops for superficial dendritic ulcers
