front: Acyclovir: main toxicity and who is at risk
text: The most important toxicity is a dose-dependent fall in {{GFR}}, especially in patients with {{kidney disease}}; it usually reverses on stopping. High IV doses can cause reversible {{neurotoxicity}} such as tremor, confusion and convulsions. No {{teratogenicity}} has been noted.

front: How do valacyclovir and famciclovir improve on acyclovir?
back: Valacyclovir is a valyl ester prodrug of acyclovir; intestinal peptide transporters raise oral bioavailability to about 55 to 70%, giving roughly three-fold higher acyclovir levels, and it is preferred for zoster. Famciclovir is a prodrug of penciclovir with good oral absorption and a long-lived intracellular active triphosphate; it does not work on acyclovir-resistant strains.

front: Ganciclovir and valganciclovir: main use and key toxicity
back: Most active against CMV. Reserved for severe CMV disease (retinitis, pneumonia, colitis) in immunocompromised patients such as those with AIDS or transplants. Valganciclovir is an oral valyl prodrug with about 60% bioavailability and has largely replaced IV ganciclovir for retinitis, except when vision is threatened. Main toxicity: bone marrow suppression, plus rash, fever and neuropsychiatric effects.

front: Cidofovir: why it can be given weekly, and its main safety rule
back: It is a nucleotide analogue active against most DNA viruses, including acyclovir-resistant HSV and ganciclovir-resistant CMV. Cellular enzymes make the active diphosphate, which persists in infected cells, so weekly dosing works. It is given IV with oral probenecid, which reduces its nephrotoxicity. Dose-related kidney damage means it is contraindicated in kidney disease.

front: Foscarnet: why is it reserved for resistant cases, and what are its toxicities?
back: It is a non-nucleoside phosphonate that inhibits viral DNA polymerase and reverse transcriptase, so it works on acyclovir- and ganciclovir-resistant strains, with minimal viral resistance. Toxicity is high: nephrotoxicity with a diabetes-like tubular defect and acute renal failure, anaemia, phlebitis, and hypocalcaemia causing tremor and convulsions.

front: Idoxuridine and trifluridine: class, use and limitation
text: Both are {{thymidine}} analogues used topically for {{herpes simplex keratitis}}. Trifluridine has low virus selectivity because it also blocks {{host cell kinases}}. Ocular {{irritation}} and lid oedema are common adverse effects.

front: Amantadine: mechanism, and why it is seldom used for influenza now
back: A tricyclic amine that blocks the M2 ion channel of influenza A, preventing uncoating of the viral genome. It has no action on influenza B or the H5N1 and H1N1 strains, and resistance arises through M2 mutation. Now rarely used for influenza; occasionally used for parkinsonism.

front: Oseltamivir: mechanism, and why timing of the first dose matters
back: A sialic acid analogue that inhibits viral neuraminidase, so progeny virions cannot leave the infected cell. It is an ester prodrug converted to oseltamivir carboxylate, about 80% bioavailable. Start within 48 hours of symptoms, because viral replication peaks in the first 2 days. Given within 2 days of exposure it can prevent illness in contacts.

front: Oseltamivir: treatment and prophylaxis doses
text: Treatment is {{75 mg}} orally twice daily for {{5 days}}; prophylaxis is {{75 mg}} once daily. Dose is reduced in {{renal insufficiency}}. Taking it with {{food}} reduces nausea and abdominal pain.

front: Zanamivir and peramivir: how they are given, and the key caution
back: Zanamivir is inhaled as a powder because oral bioavailability is very low; it is kept for oseltamivir-resistant or severe cases. It can cause bronchospasm, so it is contraindicated in asthma. Peramivir is a single IV dose (600 mg) given within 48 hours of onset, cleared by the kidney, and useful when other drugs cannot be given.

front: Ribavirin: uses and toxicity
text: In hepatitis C, oral ribavirin is combined with injected {{peginterferon alpha}} for {{6 to 12}} months. Its major toxicity is dose-related {{haemolytic anaemia}}. It is teratogenic, so contraception is needed during treatment and for {{3 months}} afterwards.

front: Interferon alpha: mechanism and major adverse effects
back: Host cytokines that signal through JAK-STAT receptors and induce antiviral proteins, which mainly block viral protein synthesis. Given by SC or IM injection; pegylated forms are given weekly. Adverse effects: flu-like symptoms after each dose, neuropsychiatric effects, neutropenia and thrombocytopenia, thyroid dysfunction, alopecia. Contraindicated in pregnancy, decompensated cirrhosis and autoimmune disease.

front: Entecavir: administration and dosing in chronic hepatitis B
text: Entecavir is a {{guanosine}} analogue and is taken on an {{empty stomach}}, since food reduces absorption. The dose is {{0.5 mg}} once daily, or {{1 mg}} once daily if the patient is lamivudine-resistant. Lactic acidosis can occur in {{decompensated cirrhosis}}.

front: Short note: Nucleoside analogues for chronic hepatitis B

points: 300 mg once daily; a first-line drug
Effective even in lamivudine-resistant disease; resistance rare
Watch renal function: creatinine rise is common
Current first-line option; faster viral fall than lamivudine
Resistance rare, mainly in lamivudine-resistant patients
Least active of the nucleotide analogues; not first-line
Resistance in about 30% of patients
Nephrotoxic at higher doses
Telbivudine: not first-line; resistance frequent, especially after lamivudine resistance
Lamivudine: no longer first-line for HBV because resistance reaches up to 70% in 1 to 5 years
Do not stop abruptly: flare of hepatitis can follow
Continue nucleos(t)ide therapy until about 6 months after seroconversion
Combinations are not superior; drugs are used sequentially

front: Sofosbuvir: mechanism and main cautions
back: A uridine analogue prodrug converted in hepatocytes to its triphosphate, which inhibits the HCV NS5B RNA polymerase and terminates the viral RNA chain. Active against all six genotypes, always used in combination. It is a P-glycoprotein substrate, so avoid P-gp inducers such as rifampin and phenytoin, and avoid it in severe renal impairment. Severe bradycardia has been reported with amiodarone.

front: Classify the newer direct-acting HCV drugs by target
text: Sofosbuvir inhibits {{NS5B polymerase}}. Simeprevir inhibits {{NS3/4A protease}}. Daclatasvir, ledipasvir and velpatasvir inhibit {{NS5A}}. All are used in {{combination}}, never alone, to reach sustained viral response.

front: Essay: Treatment of chronic hepatitis C

points: Sustained viral response: undetectable HCV-RNA 6 months after completing therapy
Relapse only about 5% once achieved
Peginterferon alpha plus oral ribavirin
Response about 50 to 80%; long course and poor tolerability
NS5B, NS3/4A and NS5A inhibitors
Used in combination; monotherapy causes resistance
SVR up to 99% with 12 to 24 weeks of therapy
Sofosbuvir with daclatasvir, simeprevir or ledipasvir
Velpatasvir with sofosbuvir covers all six genotypes
Ribavirin added in cirrhosis or in genotype 3 with some regimens
Many interactions via P-gp and CYP3A4; check before co-prescribing
Acid suppressants reduce ledipasvir and velpatasvir absorption
Access in India limited by cost

front: Which two viral enzymes are the established drug targets in HIV, and what does each do?
back: Reverse transcriptase, which copies viral RNA into proviral DNA, and protease, which cuts the large viral polyprotein into functional proteins. Newer targets include viral fusion with the CD4 cell, the CCR5 co-receptor and integrase, which inserts proviral DNA into the host genome.

front: Zidovudine: mechanism, main toxicity and key interaction
back: A thymidine analogue; after phosphorylation it inhibits HIV reverse transcriptase and terminates the DNA chain. Dose-related anaemia and neutropenia are the main toxicities; myopathy and lactic acidosis are less common. Paracetamol increases its toxicity by competing for glucuronidation. Never used alone.

front: Classify the toxicities of stavudine and didanosine
text: Stavudine causes {{lipodystrophy}}, {{lactic acidosis}} and {{peripheral neuropathy}}, so it is largely avoided. Didanosine's main dose-related toxicity is {{peripheral neuropathy}}, and it does not cause {{myelosuppression}}. Stavudine and zidovudine should not be combined because they compete for the same activation step.

front: Lamivudine: why is it used for both HIV and hepatitis B, and why is it no longer first-line for HBV?
back: It inhibits both HIV reverse transcriptase and HBV DNA polymerase. It is well absorbed, has low systemic toxicity, is mostly excreted unchanged (so usable in hepatic insufficiency) and is an essential part of most first-line HIV triple regimens. For HBV, resistance by point mutation reaches up to about 70% within 1 to 5 years, so it is no longer a first-line HBV drug.

front: Abacavir: main safety issue and what must happen when it occurs
back: Hypersensitivity reaction in about 2 to 5% of adults: fever, rash, abdominal pain, GI upset and flu-like respiratory symptoms. Stop immediately and never rechallenge, because fatal reactions followed re-exposure. A genetic basis has been proposed. Avoid in patients with cardiovascular risk factors.

front: Tenofovir disoproxil: why is it widely used, and what should be monitored?
back: It is the only nucleotide (not nucleoside) reverse transcriptase inhibitor in common use and is also active against HBV. It is well tolerated, with few GI side effects, and is in preferred first-line WHO regimens. Monitor renal function: creatinine rise is common and acute or chronic kidney injury is possible. Dose 300 mg daily.

front: Emtricitabine: what distinguishes it from lamivudine?
back: A cytidine analogue with a long intracellular half-life of the triphosphate (about 40 hours), so it is dosed once daily. Renally excreted and needs dose adjustment in renal impairment. It is one of the least toxic ARVs and is supplied only as fixed-dose combinations. It must not be combined with lamivudine, and stopping it in HIV-HBV coinfection can cause rebound hepatitis.

front: NNRTIs: mechanism and rules of use
text: NNRTIs bind HIV reverse transcriptase {{non-competitively}} and do not need {{intracellular phosphorylation}}. They act on HIV-1 but not {{HIV-2}}. Resistance appears {{rapidly}} if used alone, so they are always given with two other drugs. Nevirapine and efavirenz show {{cross-resistance}} with each other, but not with NRTIs or PIs.

front: Short note: Efavirenz versus nevirapine

points: Both are enzyme inducers that autoinduce their own metabolism
Nevirapine: 200 mg daily for 2 weeks, then 200 mg twice daily
Efavirenz: no lead-in; long half-life so occasional missed doses are less harmful
Nevirapine: rash (can be severe), fever, transaminase rise; potentially hepatotoxic; avoid in hepatic dysfunction
Efavirenz: headache, dizziness, insomnia, neuropsychiatric effects; gynaecomastia; teratogenicity not confirmed in humans
Rifampin lowers nevirapine levels: switch to efavirenz if TB needs treatment
Efavirenz is metabolised mainly by CYP2B6 and also inhibits CYP3A4
Efavirenz is preferred first-line, including in pregnancy and breastfeeding
Nevirapine is an alternative but avoided with liver disease or rifampin

front: Protease inhibitors: mechanism, and why they act on both new and old infected cells
back: They block the aspartic protease that cleaves the viral polyprotein at the maturation step, so new virions are immature and non-infectious. They do not need intracellular activation, so they work in newly and chronically infected cells. They are not used alone because resistance develops within months.

front: What is ritonavir boosting, and which protease inhibitor is not boosted?
back: Low-dose ritonavir (100 mg) strongly inhibits CYP3A4, raising the partner PI's levels and allowing fewer tablets a day. Nelfinavir is not boosted because it is metabolised mainly by CYP2C19, which ritonavir does not inhibit. Full-dose ritonavir is rarely used as an antiretroviral because of its side effects.

front: Classify the adverse effects of protease inhibitors
text: PIs cause {{lipodystrophy}} (abdominal fat gain, buffalo hump, limb wasting), {{dyslipidaemia}} and {{insulin resistance}}, plus GI intolerance. Indinavir can crystallise in {{urine}} and cause {{nephrolithiasis}}. Atazanavir can cause {{jaundice}} without liver damage by inhibiting glucuronyl transferase.

front: Integrase inhibitors (raltegravir, dolutegravir): action and key interactions
back: They prevent the proviral DNA from being inserted into host chromosomal DNA. Both act on HIV-1 and HIV-2 with no cross-resistance to other classes; dolutegravir also works against some raltegravir-resistant virus. Dolutegravir (50 mg once daily) is a preferred option where cost allows. Calcium, magnesium and iron antacids or supplements chelate them and should be avoided or staggered. Double the dose with rifampin.

front: Enfuvirtide and maraviroc: where each blocks HIV entry and when each is used
back: Enfuvirtide is a synthetic peptide that binds gp41 and blocks fusion of the viral and cell membranes; given SC twice daily to multidrug-resistant patients with no other option, and causes painful injection-site nodules. Maraviroc blocks the host CCR5 co-receptor, so it works only on CCR5-tropic virus and tropism must be proven first.

front: Essay: First-line ART for a treatment-naive adult

points: Start ART as soon as HIV is confirmed, whatever the CD4 count (WHO 2016)
Always at least three drugs from at least two classes
Target: HIV-RNA below 50 copies/mL and near-normal CD4 within 6 months
Lifelong therapy, even after viral suppression
Two NRTIs plus one NNRTI
Tenofovir + lamivudine (or emtricitabine) + efavirenz
Efavirenz preferred over nevirapine; etravirine reserved for NNRTI failure
Zidovudine-based regimens with efavirenz or nevirapine
Tenofovir or abacavir with lamivudine plus dolutegravir
Dolutegravir-based regimens favoured where cost allows
Monotherapy and three-NRTI regimens
Nevirapine with hepatic dysfunction or rifampin
PI-sparing regimens preferred for treatment-naive patients
Adherence is the main determinant of outcome
If toxicity develops, change the offending drug or regimen; do not reduce doses
Watch for IRIS when treating latent opportunistic infection

front: After failure of first-line ART, what should change and what are the WHO 2016 second-line options?
back: Change the entire failed regimen, not a single drug, and avoid cross-resistant drugs (for example nevirapine for efavirenz, emtricitabine for lamivudine). Use two NRTIs plus one ritonavir-boosted PI. After failure on tenofovir plus lamivudine or emtricitabine, use zidovudine plus lamivudine; after failure on zidovudine or stavudine plus lamivudine, use tenofovir plus lamivudine or emtricitabine. Preferred boosted PIs are atazanavir or lopinavir.

front: PrEP: which drugs are used and who should be offered it?
back: Tenofovir 300 mg with emtricitabine 200 mg taken once daily. Meta-analysis of 10 trials showed about a 51% reduction in HIV risk compared with placebo. WHO recommends offering it to people at high risk: men who have sex with men, sex workers, people who inject drugs, transgender people, and uninfected partners of serodiscordant heterosexual couples.

front: Short note: Post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) for HIV

points: High: source symptomatic with high viral load or low CD4 and not on ART; deep or large-bore needle; visible blood on needle; sexual exposure
Low: source on ART or asymptomatic with low viral load and high CD4; superficial or small exposure
None: source HIV-negative; intact skin; urine, sweat, non-bloody saliva
Preferred: tenofovir + emtricitabine daily, plus lopinavir/r or atazanavir/r
Alternative third drug: darunavir/r, raltegravir or efavirenz
Nevirapine is not recommended for PEP in adults
Zidovudine + lamivudine as the preferred NRTI pair, with lopinavir/r
Check the age band against the WHO table; the extracted text is garbled here
Course is 4 weeks
Minimum two NRTIs, ideally with a third drug of another class

front: PEP: how soon must it start, and what is the regimen after sexual exposure?
back: Start as soon as possible, ideally within 1 to 2 hours. Benefit falls with delay, and it is generally not started beyond 72 hours. After sexual exposure the same regimen as for needle-stick is used; a popular US option is tenofovir plus emtricitabine daily with raltegravir 400 mg twice daily.

front: Essay: Prevention of mother-to-child transmission (PMTCT) of HIV

points: Transmission in utero, during delivery, or by breastfeeding
Highest risk is during the birth process
All HIV-positive women not on ART start standard triple ART
Continue through delivery and into the postnatal period
Benefits the mother's own health too
Tenofovir 300 mg + lamivudine 300 mg + efavirenz 600 mg as one daily tablet
WHO 2016 keeps efavirenz in the preferred first-line regimen for pregnant and breastfeeding women
Nevirapine syrup for 6 weeks
Caesarean section advised if HIV-RNA is above 1000 copies/mL near delivery

front: Classify the ARV combinations to avoid
text: Avoid zidovudine with {{stavudine}} (pharmacodynamic antagonism); stavudine with {{didanosine}} (neuropathy and lactic acidosis); lamivudine with {{emtricitabine}} (similar drugs); lamivudine with {{didanosine}} (not additive); tenofovir with {{didanosine}} (lower efficacy).

front: Short note: Classification of antimalarial drugs by stage of action

points: Liver stages (pre-erythrocytic, and exo-erythrocytic for P. vivax)
Blood stage (erythrocytic schizogony)
Gametocytes
Causal prophylactics: act on the pre-erythrocytic stage
Tissue schizontocides: act on liver forms, including vivax and ovale hypnozoites
Erythrocytic schizontocides: end the attack; used for clinical cure and suppressive prophylaxis
Gametocides: kill gametes and reduce mosquito transmission
Primaquine: causal prophylactic, tissue schizontocide and gametocide
Artemisinins: fastest blood schizontocides, but weak on mature gametes
Chloroquine: blood schizontocide with no liver-stage action

front: Cloze: four aims of antimalarial therapy
text: Antimalarial therapy aims at {{prophylaxis}} against clinical attacks, {{clinical cure}} of an attack, {{radical cure}} to remove all parasites from the body, and {{gametocidal}} action to cut transmission to mosquitoes.

front: Cloze: why a blood schizontocide alone can leave relapse in vivax malaria
text: P. vivax and P. ovale leave {{hypnozoites}} in the liver, so a blood schizontocide alone is followed by {{relapse}}. In falciparum malaria no such tissue stage persists, so clearing the blood adequately is a radical cure.

front: Why are proguanil and pyrimethamine called low-efficacy clinical curatives?
back: They are slow-acting blood schizontocides, too slow to be used alone in a non-immune patient, and parasites quickly develop resistance to them. They are therefore used only in combination, for example sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine, for clinical cure.

front: Essay: Chemoprophylaxis of malaria

points: Non-immune travellers and non-immune residents on fixed postings
Infants, children and pregnant women
Falciparum malaria carries serious risk in pregnancy
Short-term use in special risk groups
Choose the drug according to local resistance
Start before travel so that tolerance can be checked
Chloroquine: only where P. falciparum is still sensitive; no longer used in India
Mefloquine: weekly, for chloroquine-resistant areas; not for residents
Doxycycline: daily, for short trips; avoid in pregnancy and under 8 years
Atovaquone with proguanil: daily, used by western travellers
Proguanil with chloroquine: weekly, gives moderate protection against resistant falciparum
Primaquine protects against all species, but is not used in mass programmes because of its toxicity
Artemisinins: widespread prophylactic use would drive resistance
Proguanil alone: weak liver-stage action and rapid resistance

front: How does chloroquine kill the malaria parasite inside the red cell?
back: As a weak base it concentrates in the parasite's acidic food vacuole and raises its pH, which interferes with haemoglobin digestion. It also blocks conversion of toxic haem into inert haemozoin, so free haem or the haem-drug complex damages the parasite membrane.

front: What is the main mechanism of chloroquine resistance in P. falciparum?
back: A mutant transporter (encoded by the pfcrt gene) in the membrane of the acidic vacuole pumps chloroquine out, so less drug reaches haem. The P-glycoprotein encoded by pfmdr1 contributes and also reduces the activity of quinine and mefloquine.

front: Short note: Adverse effects of chloroquine

points: Nausea, vomiting, anorexia and epigastric discomfort
Intense itching, which is the most frequent complaint
Headache and difficulty in accommodation
Retinal damage with loss of vision (seen with long courses for rheumatoid arthritis or lupus)
Corneal deposits, which are reversible on stopping
Myopathy, hearing loss, rashes, photoallergy, mood change, greying of hair
Liver damage, severe GI, neurological, retinal or blood disorders
Can precipitate seizures, porphyria and psoriasis
Must not be combined with mefloquine, amiodarone or other antiarrhythmics
Usable for treating malaria; no abortifacient or teratogenic effect reported

front: Cloze: pharmacokinetics of chloroquine
text: Chloroquine binds {{tightly}} to melanin and nuclear chromatin, so it concentrates in the {{liver, spleen, kidney and lungs}} and in the {{retina}}. Its terminal half-life can extend to {{1-2 months}}.

front: Short note: Mefloquine

points: Effective against chloroquine-resistant falciparum
Used with artesunate as an ACT, though this combination is now less favoured
Weekly prophylaxis for travellers to multidrug-resistant areas, not for residents
GI upset, dizziness, sinus bradycardia and QT prolongation
Neuropsychiatric effects: loss of balance, ataxia, anxiety, hallucinations, rarely convulsions
Convulsions are more likely in patients recovering from cerebral malaria
Anxiety, depression, psychosis, neuropsychiatric illness or convulsions
Cardiac conduction defects or heart disease
Avoid in the first trimester unless essential
Do not give quinine, quinidine, halofantrine or chloroquine within 12 hours of a dose (QT risk)
Cannot be given parenterally; not used in severe malaria

front: Short note: Quinine, uses and toxicity

points: Oldest antimalarial still in use; used when an ACT is unsuitable
Oral quinine (with doxycycline or clindamycin) for resistant falciparum
Drug of choice in the first trimester of pregnancy, with clindamycin
Tinnitus, nausea, vomiting, headache, confusion, vertigo, hearing and visual disturbance
Caused by a single large dose or several days of therapeutic doses; resolves on stopping
Rapid i.v. injection: hypotension and cardiac arrhythmia
Hypoglycaemia from insulin release; watch glucose, especially with i.v. infusion
Haemolysis with haemoglobinuria (blackwater fever), in pregnancy or falciparum infection
Single dose of about 8-10 g may be fatal
Narrow therapeutic index and a 7-day course make it less convenient than an ACT

front: Which drug gives radical cure of vivax malaria, what dose, and what must be checked first?
back: Primaquine 15 mg daily for 14 days, given with a full curative dose of chloroquine or another blood schizontocide. Test for G6PD deficiency before starting, and take the tablets with food to reduce GI upset.

front: Short note: Primaquine toxicity and G6PD deficiency

points: Dose-related haemolysis
Methaemoglobinaemia, with tachypnoea and cyanosis
Its reactive metabolites are more oxidant than the parent drug
Highly susceptible patients can develop haemolytic anaemia at 15-30 mg daily
Variants differ in severity; the Mediterranean variant causes massive haemolysis
Spot tests can detect deficiency; stop the drug if dark urine appears
Rheumatoid arthritis, SLE and acute illness raise the risk
Leucopenia can occur with larger doses
Avoid, because the foetus may also be G6PD deficient
Abdominal pain, GI upset, weakness and chest discomfort; fewer with meals

front: What single primaquine dose is given after falciparum treatment to reduce transmission, and where do national and WHO guidance differ?
back: A single gametocidal dose given on day 2 with the clinical cure. The national programme uses 45 mg (0.75 mg/kg), while WHO (2015) recommends 15 mg (0.25 mg/kg) as safer for mass use. It is given even when an artemisinin is used, because artemisinins do not kill all gametes.

front: Cloze: tafenoquine
text: Tafenoquine is a long-acting {{8-aminoquinoline}} with a terminal half-life of about {{14-19 days}}, so a single dose can cover relapse prevention. Primaquine has a half-life of only {{6-8 hours}}. Tafenoquine still carries the {{G6PD-linked haemolysis}} risk.

front: Cloze: how primaquine differs from other antimalarials
text: Primaquine is a poor {{blood}} schizontocide, but it is highly active against {{hypnozoites}} of P. vivax and ovale, against {{gametocytes}} of all species, and against the {{pre-erythrocytic}} stage of P. falciparum.

front: How do artemisinins act on the parasite?
back: Their endoperoxide bridge is cleaved by iron derived from haem, releasing free radicals that damage parasite membranes and proteins. A parasite calcium pump (PfATP6) is also reported to be inactivated. The result is rapid killing across ring to early schizont stages.

front: Cloze: artemisinin derivatives by route
text: {{Artesunate}} is water soluble and can be given orally, i.m. or {{i.v.}}. {{Artemether}} is lipid soluble and given orally or i.m., not i.v. {{Arteether}} is an i.m. oil injection for adults only. {{Arterolane}} is an oral synthetic trioxolane, used only with a partner drug.

front: Why must an artemisinin never be given alone for uncomplicated falciparum malaria?
back: It is short-acting, so recrudescence is common: about 50% after a 3-day course alone. A long-acting partner with a different mechanism clears the remaining parasites and prevents resistance. Monotherapy with oral artemisinins is prohibited in India.

front: Artemether-lumefantrine: why must it be taken with fatty food, and what are its key interactions?
back: Lumefantrine is highly lipophilic, and its absorption is poor without fat; inadequate absorption can lead to recrudescence. It inhibits CYP2D6, so drugs such as metoprolol, neuroleptics and tricyclics are affected, and it should not be given with other QT-prolonging drugs. Avoid it in the first trimester and during breastfeeding.

front: Essay: Artemisinin-based combination therapy (ACT) for uncomplicated falciparum malaria

points: The artemisinin kills more than 95% of parasites quickly, which leaves little biomass for resistance to select
The partner drug's longer action clears the remaining parasites
Each component protects the other from resistance
Rapid clinical and parasitological cure
High cure rate with low recrudescence
Good tolerability
Partner half-life matters: a long half-life allows a short course but risks subinhibitory levels that select resistant parasites
Short-acting partners need about 7 days of therapy
Artemether-lumefantrine: used in north-east India under the national programme
Artesunate with sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine: first line in most of India
Artesunate-amodiaquine, dihydroartemisinin-piperaquine, arterolane-piperaquine; artesunate-mefloquine is less favoured
Not for severe malaria, where parenteral artemisinins are used
Not for prophylaxis
In pregnancy, preferred in the 2nd and 3rd trimester; first-trimester safety unproven

front: What is the chapter's regimen for uncomplicated chloroquine-sensitive vivax malaria?
back: Chloroquine 600 mg base, then 300 mg after 8 hours, then 300 mg daily for 2 more days (about 25 mg/kg over 3 days), plus primaquine 15 mg daily for 14 days. For chloroquine-resistant vivax, use quinine with doxycycline or clindamycin for 7 days (or an ACT other than artesunate-sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine), followed by primaquine.

front: Chloroquine-resistant falciparum malaria in India: which regimens does the chapter list?
back: The national programme treats all P. falciparum cases with an ACT, plus a single primaquine dose of 0.75 mg/kg on day 2. Options: artesunate with sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine (first line, except north-east India); artemether-lumefantrine (north-east India); artesunate-mefloquine; artesunate-amodiaquine; dihydroartemisinin-piperaquine; arterolane-piperaquine. Non-ACT option: quinine with doxycycline or clindamycin for 7 days.

front: Severe falciparum malaria: first-choice regimen and when to switch to oral therapy
back: Artesunate i.v. or i.m. 2.4 mg/kg at 0, 12 and 24 hours, then once daily for 7 days. WHO (2015) uses 3 mg/kg for children under 20 kg. Switch to a 3-day oral ACT as soon as the patient can take tablets. Alternatives are i.m. artemether or i.m. arteether (adults) and i.v. quinine; chloroquine i.v. is a last resort in adults.

front: Short note: Falciparum malaria in pregnancy

points: Serious risk to both mother and foetus; treat promptly and aggressively
Quinine with clindamycin for 7 days; the safer option in the first trimester
Safety of artemisinins in the first trimester is unproven
A 3-day ACT is preferred over the 7-day quinine course
Intermittent preventive treatment with sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine in high-transmission areas
Treat with chloroquine as in non-pregnant patients
Defer radical cure with primaquine until after delivery
Primaquine, because the foetus may be G6PD deficient
Doxycycline, which is contraindicated in pregnancy

front: What is the role of doxycycline and clindamycin in malaria?
back: Both are slow-acting schizontocides with no useful effect on liver stages or gametocytes. They are never used alone for malaria; they are added to quinine or an artemisinin to potentiate it. Doxycycline is a second-line prophylactic for short trips to chloroquine-resistant areas, but is not used in children or pregnancy. Clindamycin can be used in children and pregnancy.

front: How does metronidazole kill anaerobic protozoa and bacteria?
back: It diffuses into the organism, where anaerobic electron-transport proteins reduce its nitro group to a reactive nitro radical. The radical damages cell components and competes for electrons from the pyruvate-ferredoxin pathway, disrupting energy metabolism. Oxygen blocks this activation, which is why aerobic organisms are spared.

front: Short note: Metronidazole, uses and adverse effects

points: First line for all forms of amoebiasis
Giardiasis and trichomoniasis
Anaerobic infections, including post-surgical and brain abscess, and C. difficile colitis
H. pylori eradication in triple therapy; ANUG
Anorexia, nausea, metallic taste and abdominal cramps
Headache, glossitis and dry mouth
Allergic urticaria or fixed drug eruption: stop, and avoid all nitroimidazoles afterwards
Peripheral neuropathy and CNS effects with prolonged use; seizures at very high doses
Leucopenia with repeated courses
Thrombophlebitis if the i.v. solution is not well diluted
Neurological disease, blood dyscrasias and first trimester
Use with caution in chronic alcoholics
Potentiates warfarin by blocking its metabolism
Reduces lithium clearance, risking toxicity
Enzyme inducers reduce its effect

front: Cloze: metronidazole and alcohol
text: Some patients taking metronidazole develop a {{disulfiram-like}} reaction when they drink {{alcohol}}, but most patients can drink without reaction. Because of this, alcohol is avoided during treatment and for a period afterwards.

front: Cloze: tinidazole compared with metronidazole
text: Tinidazole has a half-life of about {{12 hours}}, so it suits {{single-dose or once-daily}} regimens. It is {{equally efficacious}} but has {{fewer}} side effects than metronidazole.

front: What is the role of diloxanide furoate in amoebiasis?
back: It is a luminal amoebicide that kills intestinal trophozoites which would otherwise form cysts. The ester is hydrolysed in the gut and the released diloxanide is absorbed, but it has no useful systemic amoebicidal action. It is the preferred drug for mild intestinal disease and asymptomatic cyst passers, given with or after a tissue amoebicide, with 80-90% cure in mild disease.

front: Why are emetine and dehydroemetine now restricted in amoebiasis?
back: They are potent direct tissue amoebicides, but they must be given by injection because they cause vomiting. Cardiotoxicity (ECG changes, myocarditis, hypotension) and cumulative toxicity limit their use. They are reserved for patients who cannot take metronidazole, for no more than about 10 days, and a luminal amoebicide must always follow. Dehydroemetine is preferred because it is less cardiotoxic.

front: Cloze: chloroquine in amoebiasis
text: Chloroquine kills {{trophozoites}} and is concentrated in the {{liver}}, so it is used only for {{hepatic amoebiasis}}. It does not clear the intestinal cyst reservoir, so a {{luminal amoebicide}} must always follow.

front: Essay: Amoebic liver abscess

points: Trophozoites reach the liver via the portal vein from an intestinal focus
Fever, right upper quadrant pain and hepatomegaly; ultrasound shows the abscess, and stool may be negative
Metronidazole 800 mg TDS for 10 days (i.v. 500 mg 6-hourly in severe cases) followed by oral therapy
Tinidazole 2 g daily for 3-6 days; i.v. tinidazole in severe cases
Dehydroemetine, only if metronidazole cannot be used or fails
Chloroquine after a nitroimidazole or emetine, if response is incomplete
Large abscesses can take months to resolve even after trophozoites are killed
Aspiration may be needed for a large abscess
Give a luminal amoebicide to clear the intestinal reservoir and prevent a carrier state

front: Why were 8-hydroxyquinolines withdrawn in some countries?
back: Prolonged, high-dose quiniodochlor caused an epidemic of subacute myelo-optic neuropathy (SMON) in Japan in the 1970s, and other members caused neuropathy and visual impairment. They were banned in Japan and some other countries. In India their use is prohibited in children, because chronic use has caused blindness.

front: Cloze: drugs for giardiasis
text: {{Metronidazole}} 400 mg TDS for 5-7 days, {{tinidazole}} as a 2 g single dose, or {{secnidazole}} as a 2 g single dose are first-choice options. {{Nitazoxanide}} 500 mg BD for 3 days is an alternative, and about {{10%}} of patients may need a second course.

front: Trichomoniasis: first-choice oral drugs and how to prevent reinfection
back: Metronidazole 2 g as a single dose (or 400 mg TDS for 7 days), tinidazole, or secnidazole 2 g single dose. Recurrence is common; repeat a course after 4-6 weeks if needed. Treat the male partner at the same time to prevent reinfection. Intravaginal agents are reserved for refractory cases.

front: Which drug is first line for visceral leishmaniasis in India now, and why is sodium stibogluconate no longer used?
back: Oral miltefosine is the first-line drug under the national programme. Leishmania donovani in Bihar and nearby areas is resistant to sodium stibogluconate (SSG); over 60% of cases in Bihar did not respond, so SSG is no longer used in India.

front: Miltefosine: dosing, key adverse effects and pregnancy warning
back: Given orally with meals for 28 days. Under the national programme: 100 mg daily for adults over 25 kg, 50 mg daily for adults under 25 kg, and 2.5 mg/kg daily for children aged 2-11. Common effects are anorexia, vomiting and diarrhoea; transaminase rise and renal dysfunction are usually reversible. It is teratogenic and contraindicated in pregnancy; prevent pregnancy during treatment and for 3 months after.

front: Cloze: drug options for visceral leishmaniasis
text: {{Miltefosine}} is the first-line oral drug in India. {{Amphotericin B deoxycholate}} is the second-line drug under the national programme, while WHO prefers {{liposomal amphotericin B}}. {{Paromomycin}} given i.m. for 21 days is an alternative, and {{sodium stibogluconate}} is used only where the parasite is still sensitive.

front: How does amphotericin B act on Leishmania, and why is it the drug of choice in pregnancy?
back: Leishmania, like fungi, has ergosterol in its membrane, and amphotericin B binds ergosterol to damage the membrane. It is the preferred drug in pregnant and breastfeeding women because miltefosine is teratogenic.

front: Short note: Treatment of visceral leishmaniasis

points: Miltefosine: oral, 28 days, first line in India
Amphotericin B deoxycholate: 0.75-1 mg/kg on alternate days to 15 mg/kg total; second line in India
Liposomal amphotericin B: 3-5 mg/kg daily for 3-5 days (total 15 mg/kg); WHO first preference, with a single 10 mg/kg option
Paromomycin: 15 mg/kg daily i.m. for 21 days
Sodium stibogluconate: 20 mg Sb/kg for 30 days, only where the parasite is still sensitive
Liposomal amphotericin 5 mg/kg single dose plus miltefosine for 7 days
Liposomal amphotericin 5 mg/kg single dose plus paromomycin for 10 days
Miltefosine plus paromomycin, each for 10 days; cure about 98-99%
Failures are treated with higher doses of amphotericin B or liposomal amphotericin B
Cure: clinical improvement with no relapse for 6 months; spleen aspirate negative
Poorer response to both antileishmanial and anti-HIV drugs and higher mortality; intensive therapy needed
Local sodium stibogluconate or 15% paromomycin ointment for small dermal lesions; systemic drugs for multiple or severe lesions

front: How does mebendazole kill intestinal worms?
back: It binds the parasite's beta-tubulin with high affinity and blocks microtubule formation, which also reduces glucose uptake and glycogen stores. Worms are immobilised and die slowly, over 2-3 days, and hatching of nematode eggs is inhibited. It is poorly absorbed, so it acts in the gut.

front: Cloze: albendazole pharmacokinetics
text: Albendazole is converted by first-pass metabolism to an active {{sulfoxide}} metabolite, which is widely distributed and enters the {{brain}}. Absorption is improved by a {{fatty}} meal, which is why it is given with food for cysticercosis and hydatid disease.

front: Cloze: first-choice anthelmintic for selected worms
text: Strongyloides: {{ivermectin}}. Trichuris: {{mebendazole}}. Trichinella and hydatid disease: {{albendazole}}. Tapeworms (Taenia, Hymenolepis): {{praziquantel}}. Wuchereria and Brugia: {{diethylcarbamazine}} or ivermectin.

front: Pyrantel: mechanism, and why it should not be combined with piperazine
back: Pyrantel activates nicotinic receptors on worm muscle, causing persistent depolarisation that leads to slow spastic paralysis and expulsion. Piperazine has the opposite effect, hyperpolarising worm muscle, so it antagonises pyrantel and the two should not be used together.

front: Piperazine: mechanism and contraindications
back: It acts as a GABA agonist on Ascaris muscle, opening chloride channels. This hyperpolarises the muscle, producing flaccid paralysis, so worms are expelled alive. It is contraindicated in renal insufficiency and epilepsy, and is considered safe in pregnancy.

front: Levamisole: current role in helminthiasis
back: It is a second-line anthelmintic restricted to ascariasis and ancylostomiasis (hookworm). It stimulates worm ganglia, causing tonic paralysis and expulsion of live worms. Its immunomodulatory use in other diseases has been abandoned because repeated doses cause severe reactions.

front: Diethylcarbamazine: which filarial stages does it kill?
back: It is highly selective for microfilariae and clears them from blood within about a week, but does not clear those in nodules or fluid collections. Prolonged courses slowly kill adult worms, so it is repeated to achieve a radical cure. It is also used in tropical pulmonary eosinophilia.

front: Diethylcarbamazine: how is the febrile reaction reduced?
back: Mass death of microfilariae and adult worms causes fever, rash, itching, lymphadenopathy, bronchospasm and fall in blood pressure. Start with a low dose (about 0.5 mg/kg) and escalate to full dose over 4 days. If a reaction occurs, hold DEC and give an antihistamine or corticosteroid. Loa loa and onchocerciasis reactions can be dangerous, so a test dose or ivermectin is used first.

front: Ivermectin: mechanism and main indications
back: It opens invertebrate glutamate-gated chloride channels, paralysing nematodes; it also kills scabies mites and lice. It poorly enters the mammalian CNS because of P-glycoprotein efflux. Key uses: onchocerciasis (repeated doses every 6-12 months), strongyloidiasis, scabies, pediculosis and cutaneous larva migrans. It is microfilaricidal but not macrofilaricidal.

front: Praziquantel: mechanism and spectrum
back: It causes calcium leakage in susceptible worms, producing contracture and paralysis; at higher concentrations it vacuolates the tegument, so the host's immunity destroys the worm. It acts on schistosomes, most flukes and cestodes (adult and larval stages), but not on nematodes.

front: Short note: Niclosamide and the Taenia solium precaution

points: Blocks oxidative phosphorylation in the tapeworm, which is then partly digested in the gut
Poorly absorbed, so little systemic toxicity; tasteless
After a light breakfast: 2 g chewed over one day (2 tablets, then 2 more an hour later)
Saline purge 2 hours after the last dose
Search the stool for the scolex to confirm expulsion
Digestion of T. solium segments can release eggs that develop into larvae and cause visceral cysticercosis
A thorough purge is needed; praziquantel is preferred for T. solium
H. nana: 2 g daily for 5 days, as the cysticerci of H. nana are not affected in one dose

front: Essay: Management of neurocysticercosis

points: Treat active cysts, multiple parenchymal cysts, and intraventricular cysts likely to cause hydrocephalus
Inactive or calcified cysts may be left alone
Seizures are controlled symptomatically in all cases
Albendazole is preferred: shorter course (8-15 days), cure of 75-85% against 50-60% for praziquantel, and cheaper
Praziquantel, 50 mg/kg daily in 3 divided doses for 15-30 days, is the second choice
Phenytoin and carbamazepine lower praziquantel levels, so a higher dose may be needed
Corticosteroids raise albendazole absorption but lower praziquantel levels
Start a corticosteroid 2 days before and continue for 2 weeks after the anthelmintic course
Start an anticonvulsant before the anthelmintic and continue for 1-6 months after it
Do not give an anthelmintic for ocular cysticercosis: the reaction can cause blindness
Intraventricular or subarachnoid cysts may need a month or longer of treatment
Expelling the adult tapeworm from the gut removes the source of future cysts

front: Why is albendazole preferred over praziquantel for neurocysticercosis?
back: It needs a shorter course (8-15 days, against 15-30 days for praziquantel), gives higher cure rates in symptom resolution and cyst disappearance (75-85% against 50-60%), and is cheaper. Praziquantel is therefore the second choice.

front: Hydatid disease: albendazole regimen and its role around surgery
back: 400 mg twice daily for 4 weeks, repeated after 2 weeks if needed, for up to 3 courses. It is given before and after surgery and is the treatment for inoperable cysts. Mebendazole is less effective.

front: Classify: control of PTH secretion
text: Parathyroid cells sense plasma Ca2+ through a {{calcium-sensing receptor}}, a {{G-protein coupled}} receptor. Falling Ca2+ {{stimulates}} PTH release; rising Ca2+ {{suppresses}} it by lowering cAMP in the cell.

front: Short note: Actions of PTH that raise plasma calcium

points: Increases bone remodelling and osteoclast activity when levels are high and continuous
Intermittent low doses favour new bone formation
Increases distal tubular calcium reabsorption
Increases phosphate excretion
Activates renal 1-hydroxylase, which makes calcitriol
No direct effect; raises absorption indirectly through calcitriol
Hypoparathyroidism: low Ca2+, tetany, cataract
Hyperparathyroidism: hypercalcaemia, renal stones, bone deformity

front: Osteoclasts lack PTH receptors. How does PTH still activate them?
back: PTH acts on osteoblasts, which then make RANKL. RANKL binds RANK on osteoclast precursors, driving their differentiation and activity. Osteoblasts also secrete osteoprotegerin, a decoy that binds RANKL and blocks it.

front: What is teriparatide, and how does it differ from other osteoporosis drugs?
back: A recombinant fragment of PTH (residues 1 to 34) with the same actions as full-length PTH. Given once daily by subcutaneous injection, its action is intermittent, so bone formation outweighs resorption. It is the only osteoporosis drug that builds new bone. Reserve it for severe osteoporosis, previous osteoporotic fracture or multiple fracture risk factors. Contraindicated in Paget's disease and hypercalcaemia. Not recommended beyond 2 years; a bisphosphonate may follow. Side effects: dizziness, headache, leg cramps.

front: Short note: Cinacalcet

points: Oral fluorinated calcimimetic
Allosterically activates the calcium-sensing receptor on parathyroid cells and other tissues
Suppresses PTH secretion
Lowers plasma Ca2+ and phosphate as a result
Secondary hyperparathyroidism in renal disease, including long-term dialysis
Lowering Ca2+ in inoperable parathyroid carcinoma
Hypocalcaemia is the main risk; titrate the dose carefully
Long half-life of about 30 to 40 hours

front: Classify: steps in vitamin D activation
text: Skin: 7-dehydrocholesterol becomes {{cholecalciferol}} (D3) under UV light. Liver: 25-hydroxylation gives {{calcifediol}}. Kidney: 1-hydroxylation, the rate-limiting step, gives {{calcitriol}}, the active form.

front: How does calcitriol increase intestinal calcium absorption?
back: It binds the cytoplasmic vitamin D receptor, moves to the nucleus and changes gene transcription. This increases calcium channels and calbindin, a calcium-binding carrier, so calcium can be transported across the cell. A faster effect within minutes does not need gene transcription.

front: Why is alfacalcidol useful in renal bone disease and in liver disease?
back: Alfacalcidol (1-alpha-hydroxy vitamin D3) is a prodrug that the liver converts to calcitriol. It bypasses the rate-limiting renal 1-hydroxylation, so it works when the kidney cannot make calcitriol, and activation is not impaired by severe liver disease. It is orally active and is used in renal bone disease, vitamin D-dependent or resistant rickets, and hypoparathyroidism. Calcium must be monitored and the drug stopped for a few days if hypercalcaemia develops.

front: Short note: Hypervitaminosis D

points: Chronic intake of large doses, around 50,000 IU/day
Increased tissue sensitivity to vitamin D
Hypercalcaemia with weakness, fatigue, vomiting, diarrhoea and polyuria
Ectopic calcification of soft tissues, blood vessels and organs
Renal stones, nephrocalcinosis and hypertension
Growth retardation in children; coma in severe cases
Stop the vitamin
Low-calcium diet with plenty of fluids
Corticosteroids; recovery may be incomplete

front: Classify: calcium salts and their properties
text: Calcium {{carbonate}} (40% elemental) is the most common supplement salt but needs gastric acid to be absorbed. Calcium {{gluconate}} is the preferred injectable salt and causes warmth on IV injection, so extravasation must be avoided. Calcium {{chloride}} (27%) is too irritant to give orally.

front: Classify: drugs that impair vitamin D action or absorption
text: Phenytoin and phenobarbitone reduce target tissue response to {{calcitriol}}, although its plasma level is normal; long-term use can cause {{rickets}} or {{osteomalacia}}. Cholestyramine and liquid paraffin reduce {{vitamin D absorption}}.

front: How does calcitonin lower plasma calcium, and what controls its release?
back: Thyroid parafollicular C cells release calcitonin in proportion to plasma Ca2+. It acts through a G-protein coupled receptor that raises cAMP and directly inhibits osteoclasts, reducing their ruffled border and bone resorption. Its role in day-to-day calcium control is minor. The hypocalcaemic effect lasts about 8 hours.

front: What are the main clinical uses of calcitonin?
back: Acute hypercalcaemia (hyperparathyroidism, hypervitaminosis D, malignancy), given with IV fluids while bisphosphonates take effect. It responds within about 4 hours, peaks around 48 hours, then refractoriness develops. It also relieves bone pain from osteolytic lesions. Paget's disease gives only short-term benefit because antibodies develop; bisphosphonates are preferred. Raised serum levels help diagnose medullary thyroid carcinoma. It is no longer recommended for postmenopausal osteoporosis in British guidelines, because of malignancy risk with long-term use.

front: Classify: adverse effects of calcitonin
text: Frequent: nausea, {{flushing}} and tingling of the fingers. Less common: bad taste, {{flu-like symptoms}}, allergic reactions and {{joint pain}}.

front: Classify: bisphosphonates by generation
text: First generation (simple side chains, least potent): {{etidronate}}. Second generation (nitrogen-containing side chain): {{pamidronate}}, {{alendronate}}, {{ibandronate}}. Third generation: {{risedronate}}, {{zoledronate}}.

front: How do bisphosphonates act on osteoclasts?
back: They bind strongly to bone mineral and concentrate at resorption sites. When the acidic resorption zone releases them, osteoclasts take them up, which triggers apoptosis and disrupts the ruffled border and cytoskeleton. They also inhibit osteoclast precursor differentiation. Second and third generation agents also block the mevalonate pathway, impairing prenylation of GTP-binding proteins needed for vesicle function.

front: Oral bisphosphonates: what limits them and how must they be taken?
back: Oral bioavailability is about 1%, and they irritate the oesophagus and stomach (oesophagitis, erosions, ulcers). Take them on an empty stomach each morning with a full glass of water, stay upright and eat for at least 30 minutes, and do not chew. Calcium, iron, antacids, mineral water, tea, coffee and juice reduce absorption. Avoid in gastro-oesophageal reflux, peptic ulcer and renal impairment. NSAIDs add to gastric irritation.

front: Short note: Osteonecrosis of the jaw with bisphosphonates and denosumab

points: Necrosis of the jawbone, a rare complication
Mainly with high-dose intravenous bisphosphonate therapy
Rarely reported with denosumab
Dental review before starting therapy; avoid invasive dental work where possible
Refer to dental or oral surgery if it develops

front: What is an atypical femoral fracture linked to long-term bisphosphonate use?
back: A low-energy fracture of the femoral shaft or subtrochanteric region, occurring after prolonged suppression of bone turnover. Thigh or groin pain may come before it. It is uncommon, but the risk rises with duration of therapy, so the need for continued treatment should be reviewed after several years.

front: What is denosumab, and when is it preferred over a bisphosphonate?
back: A fully human monoclonal antibody against RANKL. By blocking RANKL it prevents RANK activation, reducing osteoclast formation and function, with an effect equal to or greater than potent bisphosphonates. Used for osteoporosis in women and men, bone loss from hormone-suppressing cancer therapy, and bone metastases in breast and prostate cancer. It can be used in severe renal disease, where bisphosphonates are contraindicated. Dose: 60 mg subcutaneously every 6 months.

front: Why is strontium ranelate only a reserve drug for osteoporosis?
back: It reduces resorption by blocking osteoclast differentiation and promoting their apoptosis, and it also stimulates bone formation. It lowers vertebral and hip fracture risk. However, it raises the risk of myocardial infarction, stroke and thromboembolism. It is reserved for severe osteoporosis in elderly women or high-risk men when bisphosphonates and other drugs are contraindicated or not tolerated. Other effects: headache, GI upset, rashes and serious skin reactions.

front: Essay: Drug treatment of postmenopausal osteoporosis

points: Remodelling imbalance; estrogen lack mainly removes trabecular bone
Typical fracture sites: vertebrae, wrist and femoral neck
Second and third generation bisphosphonates are the first choice; they cut vertebral and hip fracture risk
Denosumab for patients with severe renal disease
Estrogen (HRT) prevents vertebral but not other fractures; calcitonin is weaker
Teriparatide is the only bone-building agent
Reserved for severe osteoporosis; limited to about 2 years
Calcium and vitamin D are adjuvants, mainly where dietary calcium is low
Supplements alone do not clearly reduce fracture risk; a meta-analysis linked them to more MI
Bisphosphonates: oesophagitis, osteonecrosis of the jaw, atypical femoral fracture
Denosumab: flu-like symptoms, transient fall in Ca2+, infection risk
Teriparatide: dizziness, headache, leg cramps

front: Essay: Management of hypercalcaemia of malignancy

points: Common in malignancy and a medical emergency
Causes dehydration and altered consciousness
Rapid IV saline to restore volume; this alone lowers Ca2+
Furosemide after rehydration to increase calcium excretion without causing overload
IV zoledronate (4 mg over 15 minutes) is the drug of choice: faster and more potent
IV pamidronate (60 to 90 mg over 2 to 4 hours) is the alternative
Bisphosphonates take 24 to 48 hours; oral forms are not useful here
IM calcitonin 6 to 12 hourly for 2 days for quick effect
Glucocorticoids take 1 to 2 weeks; adjuvant in lymphoma, myeloma and breast carcinoma
Gallium nitrate for resistant cases
Repeated serum calcium levels
Renal function, since zoledronate can cause renal toxicity

front: What is Paget's disease of bone, and how is it treated?
back: Excess osteoclast activity causes disordered remodelling and a honeycomb-like bone architecture. Bisphosphonates are preferred (alendronate, risedronate, ibandronate, zoledronate): they arrest lytic lesions, relieve bone pain and can give long remissions. Calcitonin is second line, with short-lived benefit. A bisphosphonate course should not exceed 6 months; courses can be repeated after a gap.

front: Gallium nitrate: mechanism and main limitation?
back: It inhibits bone resorption by depressing the ATP-dependent proton pump on the osteoclast ruffled membrane. It is given as a continuous IV infusion for about 5 days in malignancy-associated hypercalcaemia that does not respond to other drugs. It is nephrotoxic, so it is kept as a reserve drug.

front: Cell-cycle non-specific vs cell-cycle specific cytotoxic drugs: give one example of each and the key difference.
back: Non-specific drugs kill resting as well as dividing cells (e.g. alkylating agents, cisplatin, anthracyclines, actinomycin D). Specific drugs kill only cycling cells, usually in one phase (e.g. antimetabolites in S phase, vinca alkaloids and taxanes in M phase).

front: Why are cell-cycle specific drugs given in short pulses, and where do they sit in a regimen?
back: Resting cells are less drug-sensitive and re-enter the cycle between courses, so repeated pulses catch more of the tumour. Specific drugs are usually scheduled after a course of non-specific drugs to improve the kill.

front: Why do large solid tumours respond poorly to cytotoxic drugs compared with leukaemias and lymphomas?
back: Most large solid tumours have a low growth fraction, so few cells are dividing at any moment and cycle-dependent drugs have fewer targets. Leukaemias and lymphomas have a high growth fraction and respond better.

front: Complete: phase of action of selected anticancer drugs.
text: Methotrexate and fluorouracil act mainly in the {{S phase}}; vinca alkaloids and taxanes act in the {{M phase}}; etoposide acts in {{late S and G2}} (KDT lists it under both G1 and G2); bleomycin acts in {{G2}}.

front: How do tumours become resistant to a drug used repeatedly, and what is the main multidrug resistance mechanism?
back: Repeated use of a single drug, especially at low dose, selects for less sensitive clones. Mutations in the target give drug-specific resistance. Overexpression of the MDR1 gene raises P-glycoprotein, an efflux pump that expels vinca alkaloids, anthracyclines and taxanes.

front: Which malignancies can chemotherapy cure or put into long remission, and which does it only palliate?
back: Cure or long remission: childhood acute leukaemias, Wilms tumour, Ewing sarcoma, retinoblastoma, rhabdomyosarcoma, choriocarcinoma, Hodgkin and Burkitt lymphoma, testicular teratoma and seminoma, mycosis fungoides. Palliation (shrinks tumour, prolongs life): breast, ovary, endometrium, prostate, myeloma, CLL, CML, non-Hodgkin lymphoma, small cell lung and head and neck cancers.

front: Essay: Principles of combination cancer chemotherapy

points: A single drug seldom cures; combinations give greater total kill
Each drug kills a fixed fraction of cells, so more drugs leave fewer survivors
Intensive regimens early in disease work best
Each agent active when used alone
Different mechanisms and different toxicities
Non-overlapping resistance mechanisms
Known synergy, e.g. 5-FU with leucovorin, or with cisplatin or oxaliplatin
Kinetic scheduling: non-specific drugs first, then cycle-specific drugs in pulses
Pulses 2 to 3 weeks apart let normal tissue recover, while tumour cells recover more slowly
KDT: about 6 to 11 cycles for best response; extra maintenance adds little for most solid tumours (exceptions: ALL, myeloma)
Palliative: large tumour burden shrinks
Adjuvant: clears micrometastases after surgery or radiotherapy
Combined modality with surgery, radiation and immunotherapy
ABVD for Hodgkin disease
CHOP-R for non-Hodgkin lymphoma
BEP for testicular cancer
FOLFOX and FOLFIRI for colorectal cancer

front: Essay: General toxicities of cytotoxic drugs and their supportive care

points: Granulocytopenia, thrombocytopenia and anaemia; usually the dose-limiting toxicity
Consequences: infection and bleeding
Lymphocytopenia and loss of cell-mediated and humoral immunity
Opportunistic infection: Candida and other deep mycoses, herpes zoster, CMV, Pneumocystis, Toxoplasma
Mucositis with fluorouracil, methotrexate, anthracyclines, bleomycin, actinomycin D; xerostomia and caries
Nausea and vomiting from direct chemoreceptor and upper GI effects
Diarrhoea and mucosal shedding
Alopecia and dermatitis
Oligospermia, impotence, amenorrhoea
Teratogenic and abortifacient in pregnancy
Secondary leukaemias and lymphomas years later
Hyperuricaemia and tumour lysis from massive cell death: acute kidney injury, gout, urate stones
Prevention: hydration, allopurinol; rasburicase (recombinant urate oxidase) for high-risk tumour lysis
Urinary alkalinisation is an older measure, now largely abandoned
Antiemetics; G-CSF or GM-CSF to shorten neutropenia
Platelet and granulocyte transfusion when needed
Mesna, leucovorin, dexrazoxane and amifostine as specific protectors

front: Why is cisplatin highly emetogenic, and what is the antiemetic approach?
back: Cisplatin stimulates the chemoreceptor trigger zone directly and releases 5-HT from the upper gut, causing both acute and delayed vomiting. Current practice for highly emetogenic regimens is a four-drug prophylaxis given before each cycle: a 5-HT3 antagonist (ondansetron or palonosetron), an NK1 antagonist (aprepitant or fosaprepitant), dexamethasone and olanzapine. Older texts: ondansetron replacing metoclopramide, with dexamethasone or lorazepam added.

front: How do alkylating agents damage DNA, and what is their cell-cycle profile?
back: They form reactive carbonium ions that covalently alkylate macromolecules, most often at guanine N7. The result is cross-linking, abnormal base pairing or strand breaks. They are radiomimetic and mostly cell-cycle non-specific.

front: Cyclophosphamide: why is it not directly toxic, and what are its characteristic toxicities?
back: It is a prodrug, activated by hepatic CYP enzymes to aldophosphamide and then phosphoramide mustard (the cytotoxic alkylator). Another metabolite, acrolein, causes haemorrhagic cystitis, prevented by mesna and generous fluids. Alopecia is prominent. It spares platelets better than most alkylators and is strongly immunosuppressive.

front: Ifosfamide versus cyclophosphamide, and why is mesna given with ifosfamide?
back: Ifosfamide has a longer, dose-dependent half-life and causes more neurotoxicity (confusion, hallucinations, seizures, coma) and haemorrhagic cystitis, but less alopecia and less emesis. Mesna is a sulfhydryl compound excreted in urine that binds the bladder-toxic metabolites and protects the bladder.

front: Complete: uses of selected alkylating agents.
text: Chlorambucil was the classic maintenance drug for {{chronic lymphatic leukaemia}} (now mainly for elderly or unfit patients; BTK inhibitors and venetoclax have largely replaced it); busulfan is the most myeloid-selective alkylator, once second-line to imatinib in {{CML}} and now used mainly in stem-cell transplant conditioning; {{temozolomide}}, given with radiotherapy, is the drug of choice for {{glioblastoma and other gliomas}}.

front: Short note: Cisplatin

points: Hydrolysed inside cells to a reactive species that cross-links DNA, mainly at guanine N7
Also binds sulfhydryl groups of proteins
Enters via the copper transporter CTR1; resistance from efflux (MRP1) and altered transport
Metastatic testicular and ovarian cancer
Lung, bladder, oesophagus, stomach, liver, head and neck cancers
Cumulative, dose-dependent nephrotoxicity (the dose-limiting problem); magnesium and potassium wasting
Highly emetic, with delayed vomiting
Ototoxicity (tinnitus, high-tone deafness), sensory neuropathy, hyperuricaemia
Shock-like reaction during infusion (rare)
Saline hydration before and after infusion (about 1 to 2 L), with magnesium replacement
Full antiemetic cover
Amifostine, a thiophosphate activated by alkaline phosphatase, for nephro- and neurotoxicity

front: Carboplatin and oxaliplatin: how do their toxicity profiles differ from cisplatin?
back: Carboplatin has less nephro-, oto- and neurotoxicity and milder, delayed emesis; its dose-limiting toxicity is thrombocytopenia. Oxaliplatin's dose-limiting toxicity is peripheral neuropathy, with an acute form triggered by cold. It is not affected by cisplatin resistance and synergises with fluorouracil in colorectal cancer.

front: Short note: Methotrexate

points: Inhibits dihydrofolate reductase, so tetrahydrofolate is not regenerated
Retained in cells as polyglutamates; also inhibits thymidylate synthase
S-phase specific
Choriocarcinoma (can be curative)
Childhood acute lymphoblastic leukaemia (high dose with rescue)
Non-Hodgkin lymphoma, breast, bladder, head and neck, osteosarcoma
Immunosuppression in rheumatoid arthritis and psoriasis
Megaloblastic anaemia with low repeated doses; pancytopenia with high doses
Mucositis, diarrhoea, GI bleeding
High dose: crystal nephropathy (prevented by hydration and urinary alkalinisation)
Long-term low dose: liver fibrosis, pneumonitis; teratogenic
Salicylates, sulfonamides and dicoumarol displace it from plasma proteins
NSAIDs, penicillins, probenecid and PPIs reduce its renal clearance and raise toxicity
Folinic acid (leucovorin) rescues normal cells; folic acid does not
Glucarpidase (carboxypeptidase G2) clears methotrexate when renal excretion is delayed

front: Folinic acid (leucovorin) rescue: why does it work after high-dose methotrexate when folic acid does not, and how is it given?
back: Methotrexate blocks dihydrofolate reductase, so folic acid cannot be reduced to tetrahydrofolate. Folinic acid (5-formyl tetrahydrofolate) is already reduced, so it bypasses the block and restores folate coenzymes. In rescue, leucovorin is started about 24 hours after the start of the methotrexate infusion and repeated every 6 hours, guided by plasma methotrexate levels, until the level falls to a safe value. Delayed rescue fails. Normal cells are thought to be rescued more than tumour cells, which widens the therapeutic index. Older texts (KDT): leucovorin within 3 hours of a 6-hour infusion.

front: Short note: Thiopurines (mercaptopurine and thioguanine)

points: Converted to nucleotides that block purine synthesis
Incorporated into DNA and RNA, causing dysfunction
Partial feedback inhibition of de novo purine synthesis
Childhood acute leukaemia: induction with thioguanine and maintenance with mercaptopurine
Choriocarcinoma and some solid tumours
Xanthine oxidase inactivates mercaptopurine (and azathioprine, via mercaptopurine)
With allopurinol (or febuxostat), cut the mercaptopurine or azathioprine dose to about one-quarter to one-third
Thioguanine is not a xanthine oxidase substrate: no dose change
TPMT (and NUDT15) deficiency raises myelosuppression risk, so genotype or phenotype before starting; TPMT overexpression causes resistance
Slowly developing bone marrow depression
Mercaptopurine: more nausea and vomiting, reversible jaundice
Hyperuricaemia with both

front: Fluorouracil: how does it block DNA synthesis, what modulates it, and what determines its toxicity?
back: Its nucleotide FdUMP forms a stable ternary complex with thymidylate synthase and methylene-tetrahydrofolate, irreversibly blocking thymidylate synthesis (thymineless death). Its triphosphate is also built into RNA. Leucovorin enhances the effect by stabilising the complex, and cisplatin or oxaliplatin synergise (FOLFOX). It is degraded by dihydropyrimidine dehydrogenase (DPD); DPD deficiency causes severe, sometimes fatal toxicity, so DPYD testing is advised. Capecitabine is an oral prodrug converted finally to fluorouracil by thymidine phosphorylase, which is rich in tumour tissue.

front: Cytarabine: which cancers respond, why is it given as repeated boluses or infusion, and what is its main toxicity?
back: Used for induction in acute myeloid and lymphoblastic leukaemia, blast crisis of CML and non-Hodgkin lymphoma; ineffective in solid tumours. It is S-phase specific and is rapidly deaminated, so it is given as repeated i.v. bolus or continuous infusion over days. Toxicity: marrow suppression, mucositis, diarrhoea and delayed pulmonary complications.

front: L-asparaginase: mechanism, and why its toxicity profile differs from other cytotoxic drugs.
back: It hydrolyses circulating L-asparagine, starving asparagine-dependent leukaemic cells. It lacks marrow, alopecia and mucosal toxicity, but causes effects of defective protein synthesis: hyperglycaemia, raised triglycerides, pancreatitis, liver damage, clotting defects and CNS effects. Hypersensitivity and anaphylaxis occur, and neutralising antibodies limit repeat use; the PEG-conjugated form lasts longer and is less antigenic.

front: Short note: Vinca alkaloids (vincristine and vinblastine)

points: Bind tubulin and block microtubule assembly
Disrupts the mitotic spindle: metaphase arrest
M-phase specific
Rapid remission in childhood ALL; poor for maintenance
Also acute myeloid leukaemia, Hodgkin, Wilms, Ewing, neuroblastoma, lung
Peripheral neuropathy, ataxia, autonomic effects (postural hypotension, paralytic ileus, urinary retention); little marrow depression
Hodgkin disease, Kaposi sarcoma, non-Hodgkin lymphoma, testicular and breast cancer
More marrow depression, less neurotoxicity and alopecia
Local necrosis if extravasated
Syndrome of inappropriate ADH secretion can occur
Vesicants: extravasation causes local necrosis
Vincristine is fatal if given intrathecally: for i.v. use only

front: How do taxanes differ mechanistically from vinca alkaloids?
back: Taxanes bind beta-tubulin and promote excess polymerisation while stabilising microtubules against depolymerisation. Vinca alkaloids do the opposite. Both arrest mitosis, but taxanes produce abnormal microtubule bundles throughout the cell cycle.

front: Short note: Paclitaxel

points: Diterpene taxane from yew bark
Given in a polyoxyethylated castor oil vehicle, which causes anaphylactoid reactions
Dexamethasone plus H1 and H2 antihistamines before each dose
Ovarian cancer (first-line with carboplatin) and breast cancer; older texts: after failure of first-line drugs
Non-small cell and small cell lung, head and neck, oesophageal, bladder and prostate cancer
AIDS-related Kaposi sarcoma
Reversible granulocytopenia
Stocking-and-glove neuropathy; arthralgia, myalgia, mucositis, oedema
Docetaxel is more potent, uses a polysorbate vehicle (fewer hypersensitivity reactions), causes more neutropenia and less neuropathy

front: Etoposide versus topotecan and irinotecan: which enzyme does each act on?
back: Etoposide inhibits topoisomerase II (G2 arrest) and prevents resealing of DNA breaks. Topotecan and irinotecan inhibit topoisomerase I, leaving single-strand breaks that become lethal during replication. Irinotecan is a prodrug activated to SN-38; its inactivation depends on UGT1A1, and the UGT1A1*28 allele raises the risk of diarrhoea and neutropenia. Irinotecan can cause early cholinergic effects, which atropine suppresses.

front: Short note: Anthracycline cardiotoxicity and its prevention

points: Intercalate DNA and poison topoisomerase II
Generate quinone-type free radicals
Within 2 to 3 days: ECG changes, arrhythmias, hypotension
Usually reversible
Cumulative, dose-related dilated cardiomyopathy and heart failure, which can be fatal and appear years later
Risk rises steeply above a lifetime doxorubicin dose of about 450 to 550 mg/m2 (KDT quotes over 300 mg/m2, where risk begins)
Lower thresholds with prior chest irradiation, trastuzumab, age extremes and existing heart disease
Respect lifetime limits: doxorubicin about 450 to 550 mg/m2, daunorubicin about 550 mg/m2, epirubicin about 900 mg/m2, mitoxantrone about 140 mg/m2
Baseline and serial LVEF (echocardiography or MUGA)
Dexrazoxane, an iron chelator given before doxorubicin, reduces cardiotoxicity; it is also used for extravasation
Slow infusion and liposomal doxorubicin are less cardiotoxic; idarubicin and mitoxantrone are claimed to be less cardiotoxic

front: Complete: cytotoxic antibiotics and their key features.
text: Mitomycin C is now used mainly in {{anal cancer}} and intravesically for {{superficial bladder tumours}}; bleomycin causes {{pulmonary fibrosis}} with little {{myelosuppression}}; actinomycin D is used in {{Wilms' tumour}} and childhood {{rhabdomyosarcoma}}.

front: Imatinib: which kinases does it block, and which tumours respond?
back: It inhibits the Bcr-Abl tyrosine kinase of CML and also PDGF receptor and c-KIT. It is the drug of choice for metastatic c-KIT-positive GIST, and produces remission in over 90% of chronic-phase CML. It is also used in dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans. Resistance arises from point mutations in Bcr-Abl.

front: Complete: newer kinase inhibitors.
text: Dasatinib and nilotinib are second-generation {{Bcr-Abl}} inhibitors, used when imatinib fails and now also first-line in CML; both can cause {{QT prolongation}}, and dasatinib causes pleural effusion. Sunitinib and sorafenib are oral multi-kinase inhibitors that block the {{VEGF receptor}}, used in {{renal cell carcinoma}}; sorafenib is also used in hepatocellular carcinoma and sunitinib in imatinib-resistant GIST.

front: Gefitinib: which lung cancer patients respond, and what are its key adverse effects?
back: It is a first-generation EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitor, effective mainly in non-small cell lung cancer with activating EGFR mutations (exon 19 deletion, L858R), which are more common in non-smokers, women and East Asians. Common effects are acneiform rash and diarrhoea; interstitial lung disease is uncommon but serious. It is metabolised by CYP3A4. Resistance often comes from the T790M mutation; the third-generation inhibitor osimertinib overcomes it and is now the preferred first-line drug.

front: Trastuzumab: target, main indications, and what must be monitored?
back: A humanised monoclonal antibody against the extracellular domain of HER2. Used in HER2-positive breast cancer (adjuvant, neoadjuvant and metastatic) and HER2-positive gastric cancer, usually with a taxane. Infusion reactions (fever, chills, dyspnoea) are common with the first dose. Its cardiotoxicity is a fall in LVEF that is not dose-related and usually reverses on stopping, unlike anthracycline damage; the risk is much higher when combined with anthracyclines. LVEF is checked at baseline and every 3 months.

front: Rituximab: target antigen, how it kills cells, and key adverse effects.
back: A chimeric anti-CD20 antibody acting on B cells. It kills by inducing apoptosis, antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity and complement-dependent cytotoxicity. Used in B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma and CLL, and in rheumatoid arthritis and other autoimmune diseases. Adverse effects: infusion reactions (worst with the first dose; premedicate with antihistamine, paracetamol and steroid), tumour lysis, late neutropenia, hepatitis B reactivation (screen before use), progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy and severe mucocutaneous reactions.

front: Essay: Targeted anticancer therapy

points: Attacks specific pathways or surface antigens rather than all dividing cells
Small molecules are oral; monoclonal antibodies are given parenterally
Some tumours still respond poorly, and resistance can develop
Imatinib: Bcr-Abl, PDGF receptor, c-KIT
Dasatinib and nilotinib: second-generation Bcr-Abl inhibitors
Gefitinib, erlotinib: EGFR, in mutant lung cancer
Sunitinib, sorafenib: VEGF receptor and other kinases
Trastuzumab: HER2 (breast, gastric); cardiac monitoring needed
Cetuximab: EGFR (head and neck, colorectal); acneiform rash, hypomagnesaemia
Bevacizumab: VEGF-A; hypertension, arterial thromboembolism, bleeding, GI perforation, poor wound healing
Rituximab: CD20 on B cells
Bortezomib: boron-containing; stops NF-kB release, so survival signals fall
Used in multiple myeloma and mantle cell lymphoma
Peripheral neuropathy most prominent; thrombocytopenia also
Resistance through target mutation
Multi-kinase inhibitors have wider adverse effects
Anti-angiogenics carry bleeding and healing risks

front: Why are glucocorticoids used in cancer therapy, and what limits their use?
back: Their lympholytic action makes them key in acute childhood leukaemia and lymphomas: remission is rapid but relapse eventually occurs. They also help in Hodgkin disease, manage complications such as hypercalcaemia, haemolysis, retinoic acid syndrome, raised intracranial pressure and mediastinal oedema, and potentiate antiemetics. Long-term corticosteroid toxicity limits use.

front: Complete: hormonal drug classes for breast cancer.
text: The three main classes are {{selective oestrogen receptor modulators}} such as tamoxifen, {{selective oestrogen receptor down-regulators}} such as fulvestrant, and {{aromatase inhibitors}} such as letrozole; they form the backbone of adjuvant and palliative breast cancer hormone therapy.

front: Where do estrogens, antiandrogens, GnRH analogues and progestins fit in cancer therapy?
back: Estrogens once gave symptomatic relief in prostate cancer but have been replaced by GnRH analogues. A GnRH agonist causes an initial testosterone flare, so an antiandrogen (flutamide, bicalutamide) is given for the first weeks; antiandrogens alone raise LH and need orchiectomy or a GnRH analogue for full effect. Progestins give temporary remission in endometrial cancer at high doses and are sometimes used in breast cancer that stops responding to tamoxifen. Finasteride and dutasteride are only occasionally used in prostate cancer.

front: Cyclosporine: how does it suppress T-cell activation?
back: It binds cyclophilin, and the complex inhibits calcineurin. NFAT then cannot enter the nucleus, so IL-2 and other cytokine genes are not transcribed and the helper T-cell response fails. It spares marrow and humoral immunity, mainly suppressing cell-mediated immunity. It is most active when given before antigen exposure.

front: Short note: Cyclosporine toxicity and drug interactions

points: Main dose-limiting problem
Also impairs liver function
Sustained hypertension and diabetes
Hyperkalaemia, hyperuricaemia, hirsutism, gum hyperplasia
Tremor, seizures, anorexia, lethargy, opportunistic infection
Aminoglycosides, vancomycin, amphotericin B and NSAIDs
Reduced renal function slows excretion of other drugs
Enzyme inducers (phenytoin, phenobarbitone, rifampin) lower levels: risk of rejection
CYP3A4 inhibitors (erythromycin, ketoconazole) raise levels: toxicity
Potassium supplements and potassium-sparing diuretics cause marked hyperkalaemia

front: Why does cyclosporine need blood-level monitoring, and why is a microemulsion formulation preferred?
back: Oral absorption is variable and depends on bile, so the older soft-gelatin capsules were erratic. The microemulsion gives more consistent bioavailability. It is metabolised by CYP3A4 and excreted in bile, with a biphasic half-life. The intravenous form uses a polyoxyethylated castor oil vehicle that causes chills, fever and dyspnoea, so it is reserved for emergencies.

front: Tacrolimus versus cyclosporine: what is shared, what differs, and why is tacrolimus often preferred?
back: Both inhibit calcineurin through an immunophilin: cyclophilin for cyclosporine, FKBP for tacrolimus. Tacrolimus is a macrolide about 100 times more potent. It is preferred in transplantation for potency and easier monitoring, and its absorption does not depend on bile, which suits liver transplant. It causes more diabetes, neurotoxicity, alopecia and diarrhoea, and less hypertension, hirsutism and gum hyperplasia. Its dose-limiting toxicity is renal.

front: Short note: Sirolimus and everolimus (mTOR inhibitors)

points: Binds FKBP like tacrolimus, but the complex inhibits mTOR, not calcineurin
Acts later in the IL-2 signalling cascade, so it is antiproliferative
CYP3A4 handles it; cyclosporine raises its levels
Kidney transplant prophylaxis and rescue, often in calcineurin-sparing combinations with mycophenolate and steroid
Not recommended for liver transplant
Coated stents to limit restenosis
Not nephrotoxic
Thrombocytopenia, raised lipids, diarrhoea, liver damage, pneumonitis, impaired wound healing
Better and more consistent oral absorption; shorter half-life
Transplant use in kidney and liver
Also used in advanced renal cell cancer, HR-positive HER2-negative breast cancer and pancreatic neuroendocrine tumours

front: Complete: temsirolimus.
text: Temsirolimus is an intravenous {{ester}} of sirolimus that is converted in the body to {{sirolimus}}, an mTOR inhibitor; it is used in advanced {{renal cell carcinoma}} and refractory {{mantle cell lymphoma}}.

front: Azathioprine: how is it activated, and what are its main immunosuppressive uses?
back: It is a prodrug converted non-enzymatically to 6-mercaptopurine, taken up preferentially by immune cells. It blocks purine synthesis and DNA function, mainly suppressing cell-mediated immunity. Uses: transplant rejection (less effective than cyclosporine, so usually combined with it), low doses in rheumatoid arthritis, maintenance in inflammatory bowel disease, autoimmune hepatitis, vitiligo, and as a steroid-sparing drug in other autoimmune diseases. Key interaction: allopurinol blocks its breakdown by xanthine oxidase, so the dose must be cut to about one-quarter to one-third.

front: What is the role of TPMT in azathioprine and thiopurine therapy, and what happens in TPMT deficiency?
back: Thiopurine methyltransferase methylates the thiopurines as an alternative metabolic route.
