Genetic deficiency raises the risk of severe myelosuppression, mucositis and gut damage with mercaptopurine and azathioprine; NUDT15 variants (common in Asians, including Indians) have the same effect. TPMT (and where available NUDT15) status is checked before starting, and the dose is reduced or the drug avoided. Overexpression of TPMT is a cause of thiopurine resistance in leukaemic cells.

front: Mycophenolate mofetil: which enzyme does it inhibit, and why do lymphocytes depend on it?
back: It is a prodrug of mycophenolic acid, which inhibits inosine monophosphate dehydrogenase, the key enzyme of de novo guanine nucleotide synthesis. T and B cells lack an effective purine salvage pathway, so they are selectively affected. Used with a calcineurin inhibitor and steroid in kidney transplant, where it is at least as good as azathioprine and should not be combined with it; also in lupus nephritis. Adverse effects: vomiting, diarrhoea, leucopenia, CMV infection and GI bleeding. It is teratogenic, so effective contraception is needed.

front: Methotrexate in autoimmune disease: what does it do at low dose, and in which conditions is it first-line?
back: It markedly depresses cytokine production and cell-mediated immunity and has anti-inflammatory action. First-line in rapidly progressive rheumatoid arthritis, severe psoriasis, pemphigus, myasthenia gravis, uveitis and chronic active hepatitis. Low-dose maintenance is relatively well tolerated.

front: How do glucocorticoids act as immunosuppressants, and which arm of immunity do they mainly affect?
back: They reduce MHC class II expression, cytokine gene expression (IL-1, IL-2, IL-6) and adhesion molecule production, so helper T-cell activation falls. Their rapid lymphopenia reflects lymphocyte sequestration in tissue. They act mainly on cell-mediated immunity. They are the mainstay for graft-versus-host disease and acute rejection pulses, but long-term toxicity limits use.

front: Etanercept, infliximab and adalimumab: what do they target, and how do they differ?
back: All block TNF-alpha. Etanercept is a fusion protein of the TNF receptor and an IgG1 Fc fragment that neutralises TNF, given s.c. Infliximab is a chimeric monoclonal antibody given i.v. every 4 to 8 weeks. Adalimumab is fully human, given s.c., and less antigenic. They are used in rheumatoid arthritis (often with methotrexate), Crohn disease including fistulae, ulcerative colitis, psoriasis and ankylosing spondylitis. Screen for latent tuberculosis and hepatitis B before starting, because reactivation is a major risk.

front: Complete: anakinra.
text: Anakinra, a recombinant {{IL-1 receptor antagonist}}, is used in refractory rheumatoid arthritis; it is less effective as {{monotherapy}} and is usually given together with {{methotrexate}}.

front: Basiliximab and daclizumab: target, mechanism and use in transplantation.
back: Monoclonal antibodies against CD25, the alpha chain of the high-affinity IL-2 receptor on activated T cells, blocking IL-2-driven proliferation. Basiliximab (half-life about 1 week) is used for induction with steroid, a calcineurin inhibitor and mycophenolate or azathioprine to prevent kidney rejection. Daclizumab (half-life about 3 weeks) appears in KDT but has been withdrawn from the market. Risks include anaphylaxis, opportunistic infection, oedema and fever.

front: Anti-D immunoglobulin: what does it prevent, and when is it given?
back: A human IgG preparation with high titre against the Rh(D) antigen. It is given to Rh(D)-negative women within 72 hours of delivering or aborting an Rh(D)-positive baby, to stop them forming anti-D antibodies that would cause haemolytic disease in later pregnancies. It is also given around the 28th week of pregnancy. Higher doses are needed after accidental transfusion of Rh-positive blood. It is never given to Rh-positive people or to the infant.

front: What are the two general adverse effects of immunosuppressive therapy?
back: Increased risk of bacterial, fungal and viral (especially cytomegalovirus) and other opportunistic infections; and development of lymphoma and other malignancies after a long latency, because immune surveillance is weakened.

front: Complete: protective (rescue) agents paired with the drug whose toxicity they prevent.
text: Mesna protects the bladder from {{ifosfamide and cyclophosphamide}}; leucovorin rescues normal cells after high-dose {{methotrexate}}; dexrazoxane reduces cardiotoxicity of {{doxorubicin}}; amifostine reduces renal toxicity of {{cisplatin}}; rasburicase lowers uric acid in {{tumour lysis syndrome}}; uridine triacetate is the antidote for {{fluorouracil}} overdose.

front: Which anticancer drugs have cumulative-dose limits, and what toxicity does each limit prevent?
back: Doxorubicin (about 450 to 550 mg/m2 lifetime) and other anthracyclines: cardiomyopathy. Bleomycin (total about 400 units; KDT advises under 250 mg): pulmonary fibrosis, worse with age, renal impairment and high inspired oxygen. Cisplatin: cumulative nephrotoxicity and ototoxicity. Mitomycin C: haemolytic-uraemic syndrome and lung toxicity at high cumulative doses. Busulfan: pulmonary fibrosis with long-term use.

front: How does growth hormone act, and why do its growth effects depend on IGF-1?
back: GH binds a JAK-STAT-linked cytokine-type receptor on most cells, which alters gene transcription. Its growth-promoting and nitrogen-retaining effects are mostly indirect, carried by IGF-1 (somatomedin), made mainly in the liver. GH itself promotes lipolysis and gluconeogenesis and reduces glucose uptake, so it raises blood glucose.

front: List the main therapeutic uses of somatropin (recombinant GH).
back: GH deficiency in children (pituitary dwarfism), Turner syndrome (with timed oestrogen and androgen), growth failure from chronic renal insufficiency in children, adult GH deficiency and AIDS-related wasting. Use in idiopathic short stature is debated, and its use by athletes is banned.

front: What adverse effects limit somatropin therapy?
back: Injection-site pain and lipodystrophy, glucose intolerance, hypothyroidism (by unmasking central TSH deficiency), salt and water retention, myalgia, hand stiffness and headache. Intracranial pressure can rise in a few patients. Immunogenicity is low, so allergy and resistance are uncommon.

front: Why is native somatostatin unsuitable as a drug for acromegaly?
back: Its half-life is only 2 to 3 minutes. It is not selective: it also suppresses insulin, glucagon, TSH, gastrin and gut secretions. Stopping it causes GH rebound. Long-acting analogues (octreotide, lanreotide) are used instead.

front: How does octreotide differ from somatostatin, and what are its uses?
back: A synthetic octapeptide about 40 times more potent than somatostatin at suppressing GH, with a half-life of about 90 minutes. It is only a weak inhibitor of insulin. Uses: acromegaly, secretory diarrhoea (carcinoid, AIDS, chemotherapy or diabetes related) and IV control of variceal bleeding. Adverse effects: gallstones, steatorrhoea and abdominal pain.

front: How does pegvisomant work, and when is it used?
back: It is a pegylated mutant GH that binds the GH receptor without triggering signalling, so it acts as a GH antagonist. It is approved for acromegaly, mainly when the pituitary adenoma is small.

front: What controls prolactin secretion, and which drugs raise prolactin levels?
back: Dopamine (prolactin-inhibiting factor) keeps prolactin low by acting on D2 receptors of lactotrope cells. Dopamine blockers (chlorpromazine, haloperidol, metoclopramide) and the dopamine-depleting drug reserpine raise prolactin. Suckling keeps levels high after delivery, and prolactinomas are a common cause of hyperprolactinaemia.

front: Outline the steps in thyroid hormone synthesis and where TSH acts.
back: Iodide is trapped by the Na+/iodide symporter, a step TSH increases. Thyroid peroxidase oxidises it (using H2O2) and attaches it to tyrosyl residues of thyroglobulin as MIT and DIT. Coupling of two DIT gives T4; MIT plus DIT gives T3. Stored colloid is re-endocytosed and proteolysed, releasing T4 and T3; MIT and DIT are deiodinated and the iodide reused. TSH stimulates trapping, organification, coupling and release.

front: Why is T4 called a prohormone of T3?
back: T4 is secreted in larger amounts and is bound much more tightly to plasma proteins, so it acts as a circulating reserve. About a third of T4 is converted to T3 by deiodinases in the liver, kidney and target tissues. T3 is the active form: it binds the nuclear receptor more strongly, acts faster and is about five times more potent.

front: Which deiodinase is inhibited by propylthiouracil, and which antiarrhythmic inhibits both D1 and D2?
back: Propylthiouracil inhibits type 1 deiodinase (D1), found mainly in liver, kidney and thyroid, but not D2. Amiodarone inhibits both D1 and D2. Carbimazole does not. High-dose propranolol and glucocorticoids also reduce T4 to T3 conversion, except in brain and pituitary.

front: How do thyroid hormones increase heart rate and contractility?
back: They act directly on the heart by increasing the myosin isoform with higher Ca2+-ATPase activity. They also raise beta-adrenergic receptor numbers and coupling, so catecholamines have a greater effect. The result is tachycardia, a bounding pulse, higher systolic pressure and atrial fibrillation. Thyroid hormones can also precipitate heart failure or angina.

front: Why is levothyroxine preferred over liothyronine?
back: Liothyronine (T3) acts faster, but its action is short and it carries a higher risk of arrhythmia and angina. Levothyroxine gives a more sustained and uniform effect, and its oral bioavailability is about 75 percent. Liothyronine is not freely available in India and is used IV with T4 only in selected cases such as myxoedema coma.

front: How is myxoedema coma treated?
back: It is an emergency. Give IV levothyroxine as a loading dose (about 200 to 500 µg), then about 100 µg IV daily until oral therapy is possible; some add low-dose IV T3 in younger patients without arrhythmia or ischaemia. Also warm the patient, give IV hydrocortisone to cover possible adrenal insufficiency, support breathing and circulation, and correct hyponatraemia and hypoglycaemia.

front: Which drugs reduce levothyroxine absorption, and which speed its clearance?
back: Absorption is reduced by sucralfate, iron, calcium and proton pump inhibitors, and by food, so levothyroxine is taken on an empty stomach. Enzyme inducers (rifampicin, phenytoin, carbamazepine) speed T4 metabolism and may need a higher dose. Severe hypothyroidism itself reduces absorption.

front: When is subclinical hypothyroidism treated with thyroxine?
back: In a euthyroid patient with normal free T4 but raised TSH. Treat when TSH is above 10 mU/L. For TSH between 6 and 10 mU/L, treatment is optional and is preferred when cardiovascular risk factors are present.

front: Name drugs that cause hypothyroidism or goitre, and the mechanism of each.
back: Lithium inhibits hormone release. Amiodarone blocks peripheral T4 to T3 conversion and interferes with hormone action. Sulfonamides and para-aminosalicylic acid impair iodination and coupling. Phenobarbitone, phenytoin, carbamazepine and rifampicin speed T4 breakdown. Iodides and radioiodine can also cause hypothyroidism.

front: What is the pathogenesis of Graves' disease, and why is TSH low in it?
back: An IgG thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulin binds the TSH receptor and drives long-lasting thyroid stimulation. The excess hormone suppresses TSH through negative feedback. Stimulation of TSH receptors in periorbital tissue appears to cause exophthalmos. Toxic nodular goitre is TSH-independent, is more common in older people and usually lacks eye signs.

front: How do type 1 and type 2 diabetes differ in cause and insulin levels?
back: Type 1 results from loss of beta cells, usually autoimmune, so circulating insulin is low or absent and ketosis is common. Type 2 involves insulin resistance with impaired beta-cell secretion; insulin levels are normal or high and genetic predisposition is strong. Type 2 accounts for over 90 percent of cases.

front: How does glucose trigger insulin release from beta cells?
back: Glucose is phosphorylated by glucokinase and metabolised, which raises ATP. ATP closes ATP-sensitive K+ channels, depolarising the cell. Calcium enters and insulin granules undergo exocytosis. Oral glucose gives a stronger response than IV glucose because gut incretins (GLP-1, GIP) amplify secretion.

front: What is the mechanism of metformin's glucose-lowering effect?
back: Metformin does not stimulate insulin release, but it needs insulin to act. Its main effect is suppression of hepatic gluconeogenesis and glucose output, through AMPK activation that follows changes in cellular energy status. It also improves insulin-mediated glucose uptake in muscle and fat, and slightly reduces intestinal glucose absorption.

front: How do sulfonylureas lower blood glucose, and why is hypoglycaemia their main risk?
back: They bind the SUR1 subunit of the beta-cell KATP channel and close it. Depolarisation and calcium influx increase insulin release, mainly the second phase, and this happens even at low glucose. Because insulin is released regardless of meals, they can cause severe, unpredictable hypoglycaemia. They need functioning beta cells, so they do not work in type 1 diabetes.

front: Why must insulin be injected, and what is its plasma half-life?
back: Insulin is a peptide that is broken down in the gut, so it is ineffective orally. It is distributed only in extracellular fluid, and its plasma half-life is about 5 to 9 minutes. Nearly half of pancreatic insulin is cleared by the liver on first pass.

front: What are the onset, peak and duration of regular insulin, and how should it be timed?
back: Onset 30 to 60 minutes, peak 2 to 3 hours, duration 6 to 8 hours. Inject about 1 hour before a meal, because absorption is slow. It is unsuitable for basal cover, and it is the only insulin given IV, where its action is prompt.

front: Name the rapid-acting insulin analogues and how they are timed.
back: Insulin lispro (B28 and B29 residues reversed), insulin aspart (B28 proline replaced by aspartate) and insulin glulisine. They act within about 15 minutes, peak at 1 to 2 hours and last 3 to 5 hours. Lispro is given 0 to 20 minutes before a meal, giving better meal-time control and fewer late hypoglycaemic episodes than regular insulin.

front: What is insulin glargine, and how is it given?
back: A long-acting analogue that forms a depot after injection and releases a steady, peakless level for up to 24 hours. It is given once daily, often at bedtime, for basal cover; it does not control meal-time glucose. It is acidic and cannot be mixed with other insulins. It causes fewer night-time hypoglycaemic episodes than NPH.

front: How do DPP-4 inhibitors lower blood glucose?
back: They block DPP-4, the enzyme that breaks down GLP-1 and GIP, so incretin levels rise. This increases glucose-dependent insulin release and reduces glucagon, so hypoglycaemia risk is low and the drugs are weight neutral. Vildagliptin and saxagliptin bind DPP-4 covalently; sitagliptin binds without a covalent bond.

front: How do GLP-1 receptor agonists lower glucose, and what are their main adverse effects?
back: Exenatide and liraglutide are GLP-1 analogues that resist DPP-4 breakdown and act on GLP-1 receptors. They stimulate glucose-dependent insulin release, suppress glucagon, slow gastric emptying and reduce appetite, which lowers weight. They are given by subcutaneous injection. Nausea and vomiting are common, and acute pancreatitis is a risk.

front: How do SGLT-2 inhibitors act, and what are their main safety concerns?
back: They block SGLT-2 in the proximal tubule, which reduces glucose reabsorption and causes glycosuria. This lowers glucose and body weight with little hypoglycaemia. Risks include urinary and genital infections, volume depletion, electrolyte imbalance, frequent urination and ketoacidosis. They are contraindicated in renal insufficiency.

front: How does pioglitazone work, and what limits its use?
back: It is a PPAR-gamma agonist acting mainly in fat and muscle, where it enhances insulin-responsive gene expression and GLUT4 translocation. It improves insulin sensitivity without raising insulin levels, and it lowers triglycerides and raises HDL. Limitations: fluid retention, weight gain, heart failure, fractures and the need for liver monitoring. It is contraindicated in heart failure and liver disease.

front: How do you treat an episode of insulin-induced hypoglycaemia?
back: Give 15 to 20 g of oral glucose or sugar, and repeat after 15 to 20 minutes if there is no improvement. In severe cases give 30 to 50 mL of 50 percent glucose IV over about 10 minutes. If IV access is not available, glucagon 0.5 to 1 mg IV or IM, or subcutaneous adrenaline, can be given as a stopgap. Continue oral carbohydrate because hypoglycaemia may recur.

front: How is insulin started in diabetic ketoacidosis?
back: Give an IV bolus of regular insulin of 0.1 to 0.2 U/kg, then infuse 0.1 U/kg/hr. Double the infusion rate if glucose has not fallen significantly after 2 hours. When glucose reaches about 300 mg/dL, reduce the infusion to 2 to 3 U/hr until the patient is conscious, then switch to subcutaneous insulin.

front: Classify: antidiabetic choices in pregnancy
text: {{Insulin}} is the drug of choice for diabetes in pregnancy, including gestational diabetes. {{Pioglitazone}} should not be used in pregnancy. Safety of {{sulfonylureas}} is not established, so switch to insulin.

front: Which receptor does histamine use to switch on acid secretion by the parietal cell, and what does it do?
back: H2 receptors on the basolateral membrane. Activation raises cAMP, which switches on the H+/K+ ATPase proton pump, the final step of acid secretion. Histamine is the dominant physiological stimulus; gastrin and acetylcholine act partly by releasing histamine from ECL cells.

front: Why do H2 blockers also reduce acid responses to gastrin and acetylcholine?
back: Histamine plays a permissive role. The cAMP made by H2 activation is needed for a full secretory response to gastrin and cholinergic agonists, so H2 blockade weakens the response to almost every secretagogue.

front: Compare cimetidine, ranitidine and famotidine on potency and antiandrogen effects.
back: Ranitidine is about 5 times more potent than cimetidine, and famotidine is about 5 to 8 times more potent than ranitidine. Only cimetidine has antiandrogen effects (gynaecomastia, loss of libido), raises prolactin and slows hepatic breakdown of oestradiol.

front: Mechanism: omeprazole
text: Omeprazole irreversibly inhibits the {{H+/K+ ATPase}} proton pump, and it is converted to its reactive form only in the acidic {{canaliculus}} of the parietal cell.

front: Why are PPIs swallowed whole and taken before a meal?
back: They are acid labile, so they are given as enteric-coated forms that must not be crushed or chewed. Taken on an empty stomach, the drug is in the blood when a meal switches the pumps on, and food lowers bioavailability.

front: Why does a PPI take 3 to 4 days to reach full acid suppression?
back: Each dose blocks only the pumps that are actively secreting, and the drug is cleared within 1 to 2 hours. Repeated dosing blocks more pumps until a plateau is reached at about 3 to 4 days, with 80 to 98 percent of 24-hour acid output suppressed. Secretion takes 3 to 4 days to return after stopping.

front: What are the main concerns with long-term high-dose PPI therapy?
back: Compensatory hypergastrinaemia, with a theoretical tumour risk (no clear rise in humans), atrophic gastritis, more enteric and respiratory infections from loss of the acid barrier, and accelerated osteoporosis in the elderly, possibly from reduced calcium absorption. Gynaecomastia and erectile dysfunction have been reported with omeprazole.

front: Why does omeprazole matter with clopidogrel, and which PPI has the fewest interactions?
back: Omeprazole inhibits CYP2C19, the enzyme that activates clopidogrel, which can blunt its antiplatelet effect. Omeprazole also raises levels of warfarin, diazepam and phenytoin. Pantoprazole has the lowest affinity for cytochrome P450 and the least interaction risk.

front: Why is misoprostol seldom used for ulcers now?
back: It is a synthetic PGE1 analogue that lowers acid output, but the effect lasts only about 3 hours, it relieves ulcer pain poorly, and it needs four times daily dosing. Diarrhoea, cramps and uterine bleeding are common, and it can cause abortion. Its main remaining role is preventing NSAID-induced ulcers.

front: How does sucralfate protect an ulcer without neutralising acid?
back: Below pH 4 it polymerises into a sticky gel that binds to the ulcer base and forms a physical shield against acid, pepsin and bile. It has no acid-neutralising action and is barely absorbed. Antacids must not be given with it, because they stop it polymerising.

front: What is colloidal bismuth subcitrate, and why is it not an antacid?
back: A colloidal bismuth compound that heals ulcers without raising gastric pH. It precipitates below pH 5. Its benefit may come from protecting the ulcer base, raising mucosal prostaglandin, mucus and bicarbonate, and acting directly on H. pylori. It causes black tongue and stools, and milk or antacids must be avoided with it.

front: Why should every H. pylori-positive ulcer patient be offered eradication?
back: Eradication with PPI-based therapy heals ulcers faster and largely prevents relapse. H. pylori also drives chronic gastritis and contributes to gastric carcinoma and gastric lymphoma. Where testing is unavailable, patients with failed or relapsing ulcer therapy should still get eradication therapy.

front: What is the US-FDA approved H. pylori regimen, and its eradication rate?
back: Lansoprazole 30 mg with amoxicillin 1 g and clarithromycin 500 mg, all twice daily for 2 weeks. It achieves about 86 to 92 percent eradication.

front: Classify: antacid salts
text: Magnesium hydroxide is {{fast-acting}} and laxative, aluminium hydroxide is {{slow-acting}} and {{constipating}}, so combining them balances the effect on the bowel.

front: Where is the chemoreceptor trigger zone, and why can blood-borne drugs act on it?
back: In the area postrema, which lies outside the blood-brain barrier, so circulating drugs, toxins and hormones can act on it directly. It relays signals to the nucleus tractus solitarius, which drives the vomiting centre in the medulla.

front: How do cytotoxic drugs and radiation trigger vomiting through serotonin?
back: Gut cell damage releases 5-HT from enterochromaffin cells. It activates 5-HT3 receptors on vagal afferents, which carry the signal to the nucleus tractus solitarius and the chemoreceptor trigger zone. Substance P acting on NK1 receptors adds to the signal.

front: What is an effective IV ondansetron schedule for highly emetogenic cisplatin?
back: 8 mg IV given slowly over about 15 minutes, starting about 30 minutes before the infusion, then two more 8 mg doses 4 hours apart. Oral 8 mg twice daily for 3 to 5 days covers delayed vomiting.

front: Why is palonosetron preferred for delayed chemotherapy-induced vomiting?
back: It has the highest 5-HT3 affinity and the longest half-life (about 40 hours), so it covers days 2 to 5 better than ondansetron and keeps its effect in repeat cycles. Dose is 250 microgram IV before chemotherapy, not repeated within 7 days.

front: What does aprepitant add to a standard antiemetic regimen, and what are its key interactions?
back: It is a selective NK1 antagonist that blocks substance P in the brain. Added to ondansetron and dexamethasone for cisplatin, it mainly improves protection against delayed vomiting. It is metabolised by CYP3A4, so it can raise dexamethasone levels and alter warfarin effect, and those doses need adjusting.

front: Which receptors does metoclopramide use in the gut to speed gastric emptying?
back: It is a 5-HT4 agonist on myenteric neurones, which increases acetylcholine release and so improves propulsive contraction and lower oesophageal sphincter tone. Its D2 blockade in the gut and weak 5-HT3 block add to this at higher doses. Atropine blocks the 5-HT4 effect.

front: What are the adverse effects of metoclopramide, and which are most important in children?
back: Sedation, dizziness, loose stools and acute dystonic reactions, which are commonest in children. Long-term use can cause parkinsonism, and hyperprolactinaemia with galactorrhoea and gynaecomastia. Dystonia can occur after a single dose.

front: How does domperidone differ from metoclopramide?
back: Domperidone is a peripheral D2 antagonist that barely enters the brain, so extrapyramidal effects are rare and it does not block levodopa in Parkinson's disease. Its prokinetic action is not reversed by atropine. Its antiemetic action works through the chemoreceptor trigger zone, which lies outside the blood-brain barrier. Main drawbacks: hyperprolactinaemia, and arrhythmia after rapid IV injection.

front: Why was cisapride withdrawn from most markets?
back: It blocks cardiac delayed-rectifier potassium channels, which prolongs the QT interval and risks torsades de pointes. The risk rises with CYP3A4 inhibitors such as azole antifungals and macrolides. It was banned in India in 2011.

front: Which antiemetic class is first choice for motion sickness, and when should it be taken?
back: Antihistamines with anticholinergic action, such as hyoscine, promethazine, dimenhydrinate and meclozine. They block the cholinergic and histamine signals on the route from the vestibular apparatus to the vomiting centre. They work best about 1 hour before travel. Dopamine blockers and 5-HT3 antagonists are less effective.

text: Phenothiazines such as {{prochlorperazine}} and butyrophenones such as {{haloperidol}} block {{D2}} receptors in the chemoreceptor trigger zone.

front: Classify: CINV drugs
text: The NK1 antagonist {{aprepitant}} blocks the action of {{substance P}}, while the 5-HT3 antagonist {{ondansetron}} blocks {{5-HT}} signals on vagal afferents.

front: Ursodiol and gallstones
text: Ursodiol dissolves small cholesterol gallstones by {{lowering}} the cholesterol content of bile; its plasma half-life is about {{4 days}} because of enterohepatic cycling.

front: Why must bulk-forming laxatives be taken with plenty of water, and what do they not do?
back: They swell by absorbing water, which softens stool and speeds transit. Without enough fluid they can cause impaction, and ispaghula must never be swallowed dry. They take several days for full effect and do not soften stool already in the rectum, so they prevent constipation rather than treat it.

front: Why are stimulant laxatives such as bisacodyl and senna contraindicated in pregnancy and in bowel obstruction?
back: They can stimulate the gravid uterus reflexly, and they increase propulsion and fluid secretion, which is dangerous with an obstruction. Regular use causes hypokalaemia and colonic atony, and senna can cause melanosis of the colon.

front: How does lactulose lower blood ammonia in hepatic encephalopathy?
back: Colonic bacteria break lactulose down into acidic, osmotically active products. The lower stool pH turns ammonia into the ionised, non-absorbable ammonium form, and the laxative effect clears it. Blood ammonia can fall by 25 to 50 percent. Lactitol works similarly.

front: What are prucalopride and lubiprostone, and what is the key safety point for each?
back: Prucalopride is a 5-HT4 agonist that boosts colonic propulsion. It is used for chronic constipation in women when other laxatives fail, and appears to lack the cardiovascular risk that ended tegaserod. Lubiprostone is a prostaglandin analogue that opens chloride channels to draw fluid into the gut; nausea is its commonest side effect, and it is reserved for patients who have failed at least two other laxative classes.

front: What are the components and total osmolarity of the WHO low-osmolarity oral rehydration solution?
back: Sodium 75 mmol/L, glucose 75 mmol/L, potassium 20 mmol/L, chloride 65 mmol/L and citrate 10 mmol/L, with a total osmolarity of 245 mOsm/L. The older standard formula (310 mOsm/L, higher sodium) caused periorbital oedema in children and produced more stool and vomiting.

front: What is the role of zinc in acute childhood diarrhoea, and how is it given?
back: Given with low-osmolarity ORS, zinc shortens and reduces the severity of the episode and lowers recurrence for 2 to 3 months. It is given for 10 to 14 days: 20 mg per day for children aged 6 to 60 months and 10 mg per day under 6 months.

front: Why does loperamide cause few central effects, and when must it be avoided?
back: It is an opioid agonist that acts mainly on gut opioid receptors. It is poorly soluble and barely enters the brain, so it has no analgesic or abuse liability. Avoid it in invasive diarrhoea (fever, blood or mucus, risk of toxic megacolon and systemic spread) and in children under 4 years.

front: How does racecadotril reduce diarrhoea without slowing the gut?
back: It is a prodrug converted to thiorphan, an enkephalinase inhibitor. By protecting natural enkephalins it lowers mucosal cAMP and cuts intestinal secretion, but leaves motility alone. It is not contraindicated in children; the usual dose is 100 mg three times daily for up to 7 days.

front: In acute diarrhoea, which features suggest an invasive cause that needs an antibiotic?
back: Blood and mucus in the stool, fever, urgency and cramps, with only mild dehydration, point to colonic invasion (for example Shigella, EPEC, Campylobacter or Salmonella typhimurium). Watery diarrhoea with vomiting and little fever points to a noninvasive cause, where oral rehydration is the mainstay.

Prucalopride (5-HT4 agonist), lubiprostone (chloride channel activator)

front: Sulfasalazine: how it works
text: Colonic bacteria split the {{azo}} bond of sulfasalazine to release {{5-aminosalicylic acid}}, the active anti-inflammatory part, and {{sulfapyridine}}, which causes most side effects.

front: Azathioprine: a dangerous genetic interaction
text: Azathioprine is converted to {{6-mercaptopurine}}; patients deficient in the enzyme {{TPMT}} are at high risk of severe bone marrow toxicity.

front: Diphenoxylate: classification and limits
text: Diphenoxylate is a synthetic {{opioid}} given with {{atropine}} to discourage abuse, and it is contraindicated below {{6}} years of age.

front: Isotretinoin: why is it restricted in women of reproductive age?
back: It is highly teratogenic. Up to about a quarter of exposed fetuses have birth defects, mainly craniofacial, cardiac and CNS abnormalities. It is contraindicated in women who may become pregnant during treatment and for one month after stopping.

front: Isotretinoin: where is it used and what is the usual course?
back: Oral 13-cis retinoic acid for severe cystic acne that has not responded to other treatment. The usual dose is 0.5 to 1 mg/kg daily for about 20 weeks, and relapses can be treated by repeating the course. Half-life is about 18 hours, and unlike acitretin it does not accumulate in fat.

front: Acitretin: indications and its pregnancy and alcohol precautions.
back: Oral synthetic retinoid for severe psoriasis, lichen planus and severe ichthyosis. It is highly teratogenic and accumulates in body fat, so elimination takes months. Avoid conception during treatment and for 3 years after stopping, and avoid alcohol during treatment and for 3 months after.

front: Benzoyl peroxide in acne: how does it act and what are its limits?
back: In the presence of water it releases oxygen, which kills P. acnes and other anaerobic or microaerophilic bacteria. It also has keratolytic and comedolytic action, and bacteria do not develop resistance. It causes irritation and dryness, bleaches hair and fabric, and must not be applied together with tretinoin because it breaks the tretinoin down.

front: Calcipotriol: mechanism and place in psoriasis.
back: A synthetic vitamin D analogue that has little systemic effect on calcium when used topically. It binds the vitamin D receptor in keratinocytes, reducing proliferation and promoting differentiation. Response takes 4 to 8 weeks, efficacy is comparable to a moderate-potency steroid, and combining it with a steroid works better than either alone.

front: Keratolytics: salicylic acid and urea, concentrations and uses.
back: Salicylic acid at 10 to 20% (in alcohol or propylene glycol) dissolves corns and works better under an occlusive dressing; 3 to 5% is used in other conditions. Urea at 5 to 20% acts as a humectant that softens keratin in ichthyosis and hyperkeratotic lesions, and it enhances penetration of a topical steroid applied with it.

front: Short note: Isotretinoin in acne vulgaris

points: Reduces sebum output and corrects abnormal follicular keratinisation
Bacterial numbers fall secondarily
Severe cystic acne that has not responded to other therapy
About 20 weeks at 0.5 to 1 mg/kg daily
Cheilitis, dry skin, eyes, nose and mouth, epistaxis
Raised serum lipids, raised intracranial pressure, musculoskeletal pain
Highly teratogenic; contraindicated in women who may conceive during therapy
Also avoid pregnancy for one month after stopping

front: Short note: Drugs for psoriasis

points: Corticosteroids: start high potency, then step down; occlusion speeds response
Calcipotriol (vitamin D analogue) and tazarotene (retinoid prodrug)
PUVA: oral methoxsalen, then UVA exposure 1 to 2 hours later
Risks include skin cancer, cataract and premature skin ageing
Oral acitretin; systemic steroids or immunosuppressants
TNF inhibitors (etanercept, infliximab) reserved for severe disease
Controls lesions but does not cure; relapse is common on stopping

front: Essay: Acne vulgaris: pathogenesis and drug management

points: Androgen-driven sebum excess in follicles
P. acnes colonisation; bacterial lipases release irritant free fatty acids
Comedones form and may rupture into inflammation and pustules
Benzoyl peroxide: first line, antibacterial and comedolytic
Retinoids: tretinoin, adapalene (stable with benzoyl peroxide), tazarotene
Topical antibiotics for inflamed papules; azelaic acid 10 to 20%
Only for cysts and pustules likely to scar
Short courses of oral antibiotics such as tetracyclines or erythromycin
Isotretinoin for severe disease, with strict teratogenicity precautions
Tretinoin: start at a low strength; response takes 6 to 10 weeks
Long-term tetracyclines can cause raised intracranial pressure

front: Classify: sunscreens and sun protection
text: Chemical sunscreens such as {{PABA}} absorb UVB, {{benzophenones}} block UVA, and physical sunscreens such as {{zinc oxide}} and {{titanium dioxide}} scatter UV and visible light. SPF is the UVB dose causing minimal erythema on protected skin divided by the dose on unprotected skin.

front: Classify: topical corticosteroid potency
text: Very potent: {{clobetasol propionate}}; moderately potent: {{mometasone}}; mild: {{hydrocortisone acetate}}. Potency depends mainly on the lipophilicity of the compound, which governs how far it penetrates the skin.

front: Complete: demelanising agents
text: {{Hydroquinone}} is a weak agent that inhibits {{tyrosinase}} and needs months of use in melasma; {{monobenzone}} destroys melanocytes and can cause {{permanent depigmentation}}.

front: Define disinfection and sterilisation, and state the difference.
back: Sterilisation kills all microbes, including spores. Disinfection reduces pathogenic microbes to a level that does not endanger a person with normal defences, so it does not necessarily kill everything. Antiseptics are used on living tissue and disinfectants on inanimate objects.

front: Hexachlorophene: why was its use restricted?
back: A chlorinated phenol that is odourless, non-staining and persists on skin, but it is narrow spectrum: it kills gram-positive bacteria, not gram-negative bacteria or spores. A 3% bath for infants cut staphylococcal infection but caused brain damage in premature neonates, and preparations above 2% have been banned.

front: Chlorhexidine: class, mechanism and main uses.
back: A cationic biguanide that disrupts bacterial membranes and denatures proteins. It is more active against gram-positive bacteria and persists on skin. Used for surgical scrub, neonatal bath, obstetric and general skin antisepsis, and as a 0.12 to 0.2% mouthwash for gingivitis; repeated use can stain teeth brown.

front: Ethanol as an antiseptic: effective concentration and limits.
back: Effective at 40 to 90%, fastest near 70%, because it precipitates bacterial proteins. It does not kill spores and promotes rusting of instruments. It irritates mucosa, the scrotum and open wounds, where it forms a coagulum that can shelter bacteria. Alcohol-based rubs are used for hand hygiene.

front: Povidone-iodine: what is it, and how does it differ from tincture iodine?
back: An iodophore: iodine bound to polyvinylpyrrolidone that releases free iodine slowly. It is non-irritant, non-staining and long-acting, and it does not blister when covered with a dressing. Tincture iodine (2% in alcohol) stings on abrasions. Povidone-iodine is used on boils, burns, ulcers, tinea, vaginitis, surgical scrubs and endoscope disinfection.

front: Permethrin: why is it the first-choice drug for scabies?
back: A pyrethroid that paralyses the insect nervous system. Human toxicity is very low, systemic absorption is minimal and resistance is rare. A single application cures most scabies and lice, including cases that did not respond to lindane. For scabies, 5% cream is applied over the body except face and scalp and washed off after 8 to 12 hours.

front: Short note: Lindane

points: Broad-spectrum insecticide that enters the chitinous cover and affects the nervous system
Effective against lice and scabies after one treatment
Lice: applied to scalp for 12 to 24 hours; repeat after one week if needed
Scabies: applied below the neck, scrub bath 12 to 24 hours later
Lipid soluble, so absorbed through skin, especially from oily vehicles and in children
Resistance reported; less effective than permethrin
CNS stimulation, convulsions and cardiac arrhythmias
Avoid in infants, young children and pregnancy

front: Short note: Ivermectin in scabies and lice

points: Anthelmintic that is also effective against ectoparasites
The only oral drug used for ectoparasitosis; used less often because good topicals exist
Single oral dose of 0.2 mg/kg (about 12 mg in adults)
Cures roughly 91 to 100% of scabies cases, including patients with AIDS
Not for children under 5 years, pregnant women or breastfeeding women
Very few side effects

front: Essay: Scabies: drugs and control

points: Contagious mite infestation that burrows through the epidermis and causes intense itch
Finger webs are the usual entry site; spreads to forearms, trunk, genitals and legs
Permethrin 5% cream: single application, first choice
Benzyl benzoate: second-line; contraindicated in children due to neurological effects
Lindane: effective but systemic toxicity risk; avoid in children and pregnancy
Crotamiton: lower cure rate; a 5-day course is used in children
Sulfur: cheap but messy and malodorous; largely superseded
Oral ivermectin when topical drugs are unsuitable
Treat family contacts together; wash garments and bed linen in hot water

front: Classify: scabicides and pediculicides
text: First choice: {{permethrin}}; second line: {{benzyl benzoate}} and {{crotamiton}}; older agents: {{sulfur}} and {{DDT}}; oral option: {{ivermectin}}.

front: Classify: oxidising agents, aldehydes and halogens
text: {{Potassium permanganate}} and {{hydrogen peroxide}} are oxidising agents; {{glutaraldehyde}} is less irritant than {{formalin}}, which is a 37% solution of {{formaldehyde}}.

front: Complete: silver compounds
text: {{Silver nitrate}} 1% is used for {{ophthalmia neonatorum}} because it is highly active against {{gonococci}}; {{silver sulfadiazine}} is used on burns because it is highly active against {{Pseudomonas}}.

front: What features make a chelating agent clinically useful?
back: It must form a stable ring with the metal, ideally a 5 to 7 membered ring with two or more ligand groups. It should bind the toxic metal more strongly than calcium and the body's own ligands, distribute into the same compartments as the metal, and be water soluble. Its efficacy falls as the gap between exposure and treatment increases.

front: Dimercaprol: which metals does it treat, and what is the main contraindication?
back: It treats arsenic, mercury, gold, bismuth, nickel and antimony poisoning, and is an adjuvant with calcium EDTA in lead poisoning and with penicillamine in copper poisoning. It is contraindicated in iron and cadmium poisoning, because its complexes with these metals are themselves toxic.

front: Calcium disodium EDTA: main use, route and key toxicity.
back: Given intravenously because it is not absorbed orally and does not enter the brain. It is the mainstay for lead poisoning and also treats iron, zinc, copper, manganese and some radioactive metals, but not mercury. Its main toxicity is proximal tubular necrosis, which is reduced by keeping urine flow high.

front: Disodium EDTA: why must it be infused slowly?
back: It is a potent calcium chelator, so rapid intravenous injection causes tetany. A slow infusion avoids this because calcium is drawn from bone. For emergency hypercalcaemia bisphosphonates are preferred.

front: Penicillamine: which isomer is used, and what are its main indications?
back: The D-isomer, because the L-isomer and the racemate cause optic neuritis. Indications are Wilson's disease (0.5 to 1 g daily, taken 1 hour before or 2 hours after meals), copper or mercury poisoning, cystinuria and cystine stones, and scleroderma. Prolonged use causes skin, renal, haematological and collagen toxicity.

front: Desferrioxamine: what is it used for and what is its chelating capacity?
back: An iron chelator derived from an actinomycete. One gram binds about 85 mg of elemental iron. It removes loosely bound iron and iron from ferritin and haemosiderin, but not iron in haemoglobin or cytochromes. Used in acute iron poisoning (mainly children) and transfusion siderosis; it is given parenterally because little is absorbed orally.

front: Short note: Dimercaprol (BAL)

points: Oily compound developed as an antidote to the arsenical war gas lewisite
Two SH groups bind metals that inactivate sulfhydryl enzymes; 2:1 complexes are most stable
Arsenic, mercury, gold, bismuth, nickel and antimony poisoning
Adjuvant with calcium EDTA in lead poisoning and with penicillamine in copper poisoning
Intramuscular 5 mg/kg stat, then 2 to 3 mg/kg every 4 to 8 hours for 2 days
Then once or twice daily for 10 days; start early and alkalinise urine
Dose-related rise in BP, tachycardia, vomiting, burning, sweating and headache
An antihistamine given 30 minutes before reduces the reactions

front: Short note: Iron chelators

points: Acute iron poisoning, mainly in children
Transfusion siderosis in thalassaemia and other chronic iron overload
Parenteral; histamine release causes flushing, hypotension and urticaria
Repeated use can cause lens and retinal changes
Oral; somewhat less effective than desferrioxamine but cheaper and more convenient
Anorexia, vomiting, joint pain and reversible neutropenia; agranulocytosis rare
Oral once daily on an empty stomach; iron complex excreted in bile
High affinity for iron, low for copper and zinc; GI bleeding and renal failure reported

front: Essay: Chelation therapy in heavy metal poisoning

points: Chelators form stable ring complexes that the body excretes
Early treatment matters: efficacy falls as the delay increases
Ideal agent: high affinity for the toxic metal, water soluble, matching distribution
Arsenic and mercury: dimercaprol or succimer; penicillamine as an alternative for mercury
Lead: calcium disodium EDTA, with succimer preferred for chronic lead
Copper: penicillamine; iron: desferrioxamine, deferiprone or deferasirox
Dimercaprol intramuscular; calcium EDTA intravenous only; succimer and deferasirox oral
Calcium EDTA stays extracellular and does not reach the brain
Dimercaprol: dose-related hypertension and pain; antihistamine pre-treatment helps
Calcium EDTA: proximal tubular necrosis and febrile reactions
Penicillamine: skin, renal and haematological toxicity on long-term use

front: Classify: chelators by target metal
text: Dimercaprol and {{succimer}} treat arsenic and mercury; {{calcium disodium edetate}} treats lead; {{penicillamine}} treats copper in Wilson's disease; {{desferrioxamine}} treats iron overload.

front: Complete: adverse effects of chelators
text: Rapid intravenous {{disodium edetate}} causes {{tetany}} by chelating calcium; {{calcium disodium edetate}} can cause {{proximal tubular necrosis}}, which is reduced by high {{urine flow}}.

front: Complete: oral iron chelators
text: {{Deferiprone}} is an oral option that can cause reversible {{neutropenia}}; {{deferasirox}} is given once daily on an empty stomach and is excreted in {{bile}}.

front: Fat-soluble and water-soluble vitamins: how do they differ in storage and toxicity?
back: Fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K) are stored for long periods, so regular large doses can accumulate to toxic levels. Water-soluble vitamins (B complex and C) are poorly stored and excess is excreted, so toxicity is rare. Water-soluble vitamins mostly act as cofactors for enzymes.

front: Vitamin A: features of deficiency.
back: Xerophthalmia, Bitot's spots, corneal softening (keratomalacia) and night blindness progressing to total blindness. Also dry rough skin with follicular papules, increased infection, diarrhoea, urinary stone formation, impaired spermatogenesis and growth retardation. Common in infants and children in developing countries.

front: Vitamin A: chronic and acute toxicity.
back: Chronic: about 100,000 IU daily for months causes nausea, dermatitis, hair loss, bone pain, raised intracranial pressure and liver disease; it is also teratogenic, so daily intake should stay under about 20,000 IU. Acute: over 1 million IU gives headache, drowsiness, vomiting and skin shedding; treat by stopping intake and giving vitamin E. Excess carotenoids do not cause toxicity.

front: Vitamin E: why is antioxidant use for heart disease and cancer not justified?
back: Large observational studies and meta-analyses have not shown fewer cardiovascular events or cancers in well-nourished people, and high doses (over 400 mg/day of tocopherol) have been linked to heart failure. No clear human deficiency syndrome exists. Its recognised uses are narrow: supplementation for at-risk patients, G6PD deficiency and acanthocytosis.

front: Isoniazid and vitamin B6: what is the interaction and how is it handled?
back: Isoniazid combines with pyridoxal and increases renal loss of pyridoxine, which can cause deficiency and peripheral neuropathy. Pyridoxine at 10 to 100 mg/day prevents or treats these effects and is routinely given with anti-MDR-TB regimens. Hydralazine, cycloserine and penicillamine also interfere with pyridoxine.

front: Pellagra: classic features and which niacin form is preferred for treatment?
back: The three Ds: dermatitis (a sunburn-like rash that darkens and peels), diarrhoea with glossitis and stomatitis, and dementia. Treatment is 200 to 500 mg/day in divided doses. Nicotinamide is preferred, especially by injection, because nicotinic acid causes flushing and other side effects.

front: Short note: Thiamine (vitamin B1) deficiency

points: Converted to thiamine pyrophosphate, a coenzyme in decarboxylation and the hexose monophosphate shunt
Requirement rises with carbohydrate intake (about 0.3 mg per 1000 kcal)
Mainly polyneuritis: numbness, weakness, wrist drop or foot drop
Mental changes, poor memory and constipation
Cardiovascular: palpitation, high-output heart failure and ECG changes
Oedema from heart failure, worsened by protein deficiency
Wernicke's encephalopathy and Korsakoff's psychosis: high-dose parenteral thiamine (about 100 mg/day)
Beriberi: 100 mg/day intramuscular or intravenous, then oral maintenance; prophylaxis 2 to 10 mg/day

front: Short note: Vitamin C (ascorbic acid)

points: Needed for hydroxylation of proline and lysine in collagen
Also needed for carnitine, catecholamine and steroid synthesis, and for folate conversion
Scurvy: capillary fragility, bleeding gums, petechiae, brittle bones, poor wound healing
Seen in malnourished infants, the elderly, alcoholics and drug users
Scurvy: 0.5 to 1.5 g/day; prevention 50 to 100 mg/day
Improves iron absorption; acidifies urine in urinary tract infection
Rebound scurvy after stopping long-term mega-doses
Urinary oxalate stones; cytotoxic if added to iron preparations

front: Essay: Vitamins: rational use, deficiency and toxicity

points: Organic, non-energy-yielding compounds needed in small amounts
Main drug role is preventing and treating deficiency
Poor intake, malabsorption, raised need, increased loss, genetic defects and drug interactions
Stored in the body, so toxicity is cumulative
Vitamin A: teratogenic; keep daily intake under about 20,000 IU
Generally low toxicity; excess is excreted
Pyridoxine: sensory neuropathy at 0.2 to 2 g/day; ascorbic acid: rebound scurvy
Vitamins are over-prescribed; many popular claims lack evidence
Antioxidant supplements have no proven benefit in well-nourished people

front: Classify: vitamins and their coenzyme forms
text: Thiamine forms {{thiamine pyrophosphate}}; riboflavin forms {{FAD}} and {{FMN}}; niacin forms {{NAD}} and {{NADP}}; pyridoxine forms {{pyridoxal phosphate}}.

front: Classify: signs of vitamin deficiency
text: Scurvy reflects a {{connective tissue}} defect; {{angular stomatitis}} and corneal vascularisation point to riboflavin deficiency; {{seborrhoeic dermatitis}} and glossitis suggest pyridoxine deficiency.

front: Fill: vitamin C and iron
text: Vitamin C improves {{iron}} absorption by keeping it in the {{ferrous}} state; abrupt stopping of large doses can cause {{rebound scurvy}}.

front: Active versus passive immunity: which products give each, and which gives immediate protection?
back: Vaccines give active immunity by stimulating the recipient's own antibody or cell-mediated response, which takes weeks. Antisera and immunoglobulins give passive immunity with ready-made antibodies, so protection is immediate but short-lived. Only antisera are also curative for an established infection.

front: Live attenuated vaccines: who must not receive them?
back: People with impaired defences: leukaemia or other malignancy on cytotoxic chemotherapy, systemic lupus, those on corticosteroids, and those with AIDS or other immunodeficiency. Two live vaccines not given together should be separated by about one month. Vaccines are also deferred during pregnancy and acute infection.

front: Sabin (OPV) versus Salk (IPV) polio vaccine: which is preferred for children and for adults?
back: OPV is the live vaccine of choice for children: easy to give, induces intestinal as well as systemic immunity, and reduces carriage, which supports pulse immunisation. IPV, which is inactivated, is preferred for adults (lower risk of vaccine-associated paralysis) and for immunocompromised people.

front: Rabies post-exposure prophylaxis: intradermal (Thai) regimen for tissue-culture vaccines.
back: 0.1 ml of PCEV or PVRV, or 0.2 ml of HDCV, injected intradermally at two sites on days 0, 3 and 7, then one site on day 28 and one on day 90, with no dose on day 14. Rabies immunoglobulin is added for category III bites, because the vaccine takes 10 to 14 days to produce antibodies.

front: Human versus equine antisera: which is preferred for rabies and tetanus?
back: Human immunoglobulin is preferred. Human rabies immunoglobulin (20 IU/kg on day 0, infiltrated around the bite) and human tetanus immunoglobulin (250 to 500 IU prophylaxis) have longer half-lives and rare serum sickness. Equine rabies serum (40 IU/kg) and tetanus antitoxin (1500 to 3000 IU) are used only when the human product is unavailable.

front: Polyvalent antisnake venom: which venoms does it neutralise, and how is it given?
back: Each ml neutralises standard venom of Indian cobra, Russell's viper, saw-scaled viper and common krait. Give 20 ml intravenously at about 1 ml/min, repeated every 1 to 6 hours until signs of envenomation stop. Viper bites may need up to about 300 ml; some serum is also infiltrated around the bite to limit local gangrene.

front: Short note: Typhoid vaccines

points: S. typhi plus S. paratyphi A and B; 0.5 ml subcutaneously in 2 to 3 doses
About 70% effective for one year; more local and systemic reactions
Single 0.5 ml dose; about 72% protection at 18 months
Fewer reactions; no paratyphoid protection; not for children under 2 years or in pregnancy
Attenuated strain lacking Vi; enteric-coated capsules on alternate days (3 doses)
Protection for about 3 years; not for children under 5 years or in pregnancy
Vi and Ty21a give better and longer protection with fewer adverse effects than TAB

front: Short note: Hypersensitivity and serum sickness with antisera

points: Urticaria, angioedema, respiratory distress and anaphylaxis
Keep adrenaline 1:1000 ready and ask about any past reaction to serum
Intradermal or scratch test before equine serum
A positive test contraindicates use; a negative test does not rule out systemic sensitivity
Serum sickness 7 to 12 days later: fever, rash, arthralgia, lymphadenopathy
More common with large or repeated doses; overall about 5 to 10%
Arthus-type local reaction after intramuscular injection
Human immunoglobulins do not cause serum sickness

front: Essay: Vaccines: types, examples and contraindications

points: Killed or inactivated: organism inactivated by heat or chemicals; several doses, shorter immunity
Live attenuated: avirulent but still replicates; usually long-lasting immunity
Toxoids: detoxified exotoxins that keep their antigenicity
Killed: cholera, pertussis, influenza, inactivated polio, hepatitis A, rabies (HDCV, PCEV)
Live: BCG, oral polio, MMR, varicella, oral Ty21a typhoid
Toxoid or subunit: tetanus, diphtheria, Vi polysaccharide, recombinant hepatitis B
Defer during acute (especially respiratory) infection and pregnancy
Poor response during steroid or immunosuppressant therapy; keep adrenaline available
Live vaccines in immunocompromised people; MMR and varicella in pregnancy
Pertussis: not after a severe reaction or with a history of convulsions

front: Classify: vaccines by type
text: Killed vaccines include {{cholera}}, {{pertussis}} and {{influenza}}; live attenuated vaccines include {{BCG}}, {{MMR}} and {{varicella}}; toxoids include {{tetanus}} and {{diphtheria}}.

front: Fill: hepatitis B vaccine
text: The hepatitis B vaccine is a {{recombinant}} surface antigen made in {{yeast}} cells, given as three doses at {{0, 1 and 6}} months, with protective antibody in about 99% of recipients.

front: Fill: passive immunity products
text: Hepatitis B immune globulin should be given within {{7 days}} of exposure to HBsAg-positive blood; normal human gamma globulin is used for prophylaxis of {{hepatitis A}}, {{measles}} and {{chickenpox}}.

front: How do glucocorticoids produce their slow, gene-mediated effects?
back: The steroid enters the cell and binds a high-affinity cytoplasmic glucocorticoid receptor. The activated complex moves into the nucleus, binds glucocorticoid response elements and alters transcription, so protein synthesis changes. This takes roughly 30 to 60 minutes, and the effects last longer than the drug because the proteins it switches on persist. A few fast actions, such as suppression of ACTH release, may work through membrane receptors instead.

front: Compare hydrocortisone with prednisolone for duration and glucocorticoid potency.
back: Hydrocortisone is short acting and has glucocorticoid and mineralocorticoid activity of roughly equal strength, so it is also the replacement drug in adrenal insufficiency. Prednisolone is about four times as potent as a glucocorticoid and has an intermediate duration, which makes it suitable for alternate-day or single-morning dosing.

front: Which oral doses are roughly equal in anti-inflammatory effect to 20 mg of hydrocortisone?
back: Prednisolone 5 mg, methylprednisolone 4 mg, triamcinolone 4 mg, deflazacort 6 mg, and dexamethasone or betamethasone 0.75 mg. So dexamethasone is roughly 25 to 30 times as potent as hydrocortisone as a glucocorticoid, with practically no salt-retaining action.

front: Why is DOCA not given by mouth, and what is it used for?
back: DOCA is almost purely mineralocorticoid, but it is not effective when swallowed, so it is given sublingually or by intramuscular injection. It is used occasionally for replacement in Addison's disease.

front: What is fludrocortisone used for?
back: It is an orally active, potent mineralocorticoid with some glucocorticoid action. Uses: replacement in Addison's disease when sodium is still being lost, salt-wasting congenital adrenal hyperplasia, and idiopathic postural hypotension.

front: What is the first-line emergency treatment for acute adrenal insufficiency?
back: Intravenous hydrocortisone 100 mg as a bolus, then about 200 mg per 24 hours (as a continuous infusion or 50 mg every 6 hours); older texts give 100 mg every 8 hours. Rapid IV isotonic saline with glucose, guided by haemodynamic monitoring because water excretion is impaired, and a vasopressor if needed. Dexamethasone (KDT lists it as an alternative) does not interfere with the cortisol assay but lacks mineralocorticoid action, so hydrocortisone is preferred once blood has been drawn. Treat the precipitating cause.

front: Why are dexamethasone or betamethasone preferred over prednisolone in cerebral oedema?
back: They have little sodium-retaining activity, so they do not worsen fluid retention when brain swelling must be controlled. Corticosteroids are also useful in oedema from tumours and in tubercular meningitis.

front: What antenatal steroid regimen is used when preterm delivery is expected, and why?
back: Betamethasone 12 mg IM, two doses 24 hours apart, or dexamethasone 6 mg IM every 12 hours for four doses, given between about 24 and 34 weeks when preterm birth is expected within 7 days. It speeds fetal lung maturation and surfactant production, reducing respiratory distress, intraventricular haemorrhage and neonatal death. These two are chosen because they cross the placenta well. (KDT gives 12 mg x 2 for either drug; the dexamethasone schedule above is the standard one.)

front: What is the current role of corticosteroids in septic shock?
back: High-dose steroids were abandoned because they worsen outcome. Current Surviving Sepsis guidance: IV hydrocortisone 200 mg/day (50 mg every 6 hours or as an infusion) for adults with septic shock who still need vasopressors (for example noradrenaline 0.25 microgram/kg/min or more for at least 4 hours); adrenal function testing is not needed first. Older texts (KDT) describe 100 mg every 8 hours for 5 to 7 days in patients with "relative adrenal insufficiency" unresponsive to fluids and vasopressors. Steroids shorten shock duration; any mortality benefit is modest.

front: How does metyrapone work, and how is it used diagnostically?
back: Metyrapone blocks 11-beta-hydroxylase in the adrenal cortex, so cortisol synthesis falls. Pituitary ACTH output rises, and 11-deoxycortisol accumulates and is excreted in urine. The response is used to test whether the pituitary can mount an ACTH response. Related enzyme inhibitors such as ketoconazole are also tried in Cushing's disease when surgery is not an option.

front: What distinguishes deflazacort from prednisolone?
back: Deflazacort is a slightly less potent glucocorticoid than prednisolone (6 mg is roughly 5 mg prednisolone) and lacks mineralocorticoid activity. Some trials found less growth retardation in children, so it is often chosen for paediatric patients, though its milder side-effect profile may simply reflect lower potency. It is used for inflammatory and immune disorders and is approved for Duchenne muscular dystrophy.

front: Short note: Anti-inflammatory and immunosuppressant actions of glucocorticoids

points: Suppress inflammation whatever the cause
Palliative: the underlying disease keeps progressing
Induce annexins, which block phospholipase A2 and so reduce prostaglandins, leukotrienes and PAF
Suppress COX-2 and genes for cytokines such as IL-1, IL-2 and TNF
Reduce adhesion molecules, leukocyte recruitment and capillary leak
Cell-mediated immunity (T cells) is suppressed more than antibody production
Basis for use in autoimmune disease and transplantation
Impair defence against infection
Delay wound healing and can mask a perforating peptic ulcer

front: Short note: Adverse effects of prolonged systemic corticosteroid therapy

points: Rounded face, dorsocervical fat pad, central obesity with thin limbs
Thin skin, purple striae, easy bruising, hirsutism
Hyperglycaemia; can unmask or worsen diabetes
Protein catabolism; high-protein, high-potassium diet advised beyond 2 weeks
Osteoporosis of vertebrae; avascular necrosis of femoral head
Proximal myopathy; growth retardation in children
Posterior subcapsular cataract and glaucoma
Peptic ulcer, infections, latent TB flaring, mood change or psychosis

front: Short note: HPA axis suppression and steroid withdrawal

points: Exogenous steroid suppresses the hypothalamo-pituitary-adrenal axis
Adrenal cortex atrophies with time; depends on dose and duration
More than about 20 to 25 mg/day hydrocortisone, or 5 mg/day prednisolone, for over 2 to 3 weeks
Malaise, fever, anorexia, nausea, postural hypotension, electrolyte upset, myalgia
Original disease may flare; stress can precipitate adrenal crisis and collapse
Taper gradually in weekly steps, with smaller steps near physiological dose
Cover stressful events for up to a year after stopping
ACTH does not hasten recovery

front: Short note: Relative contraindications and precautions with corticosteroids

points: Peptic ulcer, diabetes, hypertension, heart failure, renal failure
Viral and fungal infections, tuberculosis, herpes simplex keratitis
Osteoporosis, psychosis, epilepsy
Use only when the benefit justifies the risk, as they may be life-saving
Do not stop abruptly after 2 to 3 weeks
Increase the dose during infection, trauma or surgery
Use local routes (topical, inhaled, intranasal, intra-articular) where possible
Enzyme inducers such as phenytoin and phenobarbitone increase steroid clearance

front: Short note: Replacement therapy in chronic adrenal insufficiency and congenital adrenal hyperplasia

points: Oral hydrocortisone is the mainstay, typically about 20 mg in the morning and 10 mg in the afternoon
Add fludrocortisone if the patient still loses sodium
Adequate salt and water intake
Intravenous hydrocortisone with saline and glucose
Vasopressor if needed
Most often a 21-hydroxylase deficiency
Hydrocortisone suppresses ACTH drive and the excess androgens
Fludrocortisone added for salt wasting

front: Essay: Systemic corticosteroids in non-endocrine disease

points: Empirical and largely palliative, but can be life-saving
Aim for the lowest effective dose and shortest course
A single high dose is usually harmless
Start high in severe disease, then taper once symptoms settle
Give extra cover during stress
Rheumatoid arthritis: low-dose, short-term bridging while DMARDs take effect; not long-term monotherapy
SLE, vasculitis such as polyarteritis nodosa, dermatomyositis, nephrotic syndrome and some glomerulonephritides often need steroids
Short courses in urticaria and serum sickness; adrenaline remains the first drug in anaphylaxis
Autoimmune haemolytic anaemia and idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura respond
Asthma: inhaled steroids first; systemic courses for acute severe asthma or exacerbations
Under antimicrobial cover: severe TB (meningeal, miliary), severe lepra reaction, bacterial meningitis, Pneumocystis pneumonia with hypoxia
COVID-19 needing oxygen: dexamethasone 6 mg/day for up to 10 days (RECOVERY trial)
Cerebral oedema, Bell's palsy, MS relapse, neurocysticercosis
Lymphoid leukaemias and lymphomas; transplant rejection with other immunosuppressants

front: Essay: Adverse effects of long-term glucocorticoid therapy and how to limit them

front: Classify the systemic glucocorticoids by biological duration.
text: Short-acting: {{hydrocortisone}}. Intermediate-acting: {{prednisolone}}, {{methylprednisolone}}, {{triamcinolone}} and {{deflazacort}}. Long-acting: {{dexamethasone}} and {{betamethasone}}.

front: Classify the mineralocorticoids.
text: {{Fludrocortisone}} is orally active and has some glucocorticoid action; {{DOCA}} is an almost pure mineralocorticoid given parenterally or sublingually; {{aldosterone}} is the most potent natural one but is not used clinically because of poor oral bioavailability.

front: Complete the list of adverse effects of prolonged glucocorticoid use.
text: Glucocorticoids cause {{hyperglycaemia}}, {{osteoporosis of the vertebrae}}, {{avascular necrosis of the femoral head}}, {{posterior subcapsular cataract}} and {{delayed wound healing}}.

front: Complete the list of relative contraindications to systemic corticosteroids.
text: Relative contraindications include {{peptic ulcer}}, {{diabetes mellitus}}, {{hypertension}}, {{viral and fungal infections}}, {{osteoporosis}}, {{herpes simplex keratitis}}, {{psychosis}}, {{epilepsy}}, {{heart failure}} and {{renal failure}}.

front: Which enzyme converts testosterone to dihydrotestosterone, and why does DHT matter?
back: 5-alpha reductase converts testosterone to DHT, which binds the androgen receptor more tightly and drives androgen action in the prostate, external genitalia, genital skin and hair follicles. Testosterone itself mediates feedback inhibition of LH, effects on skeletal muscle, erythropoiesis and spermatogenesis. Type 2 5-alpha reductase predominates in the urogenital tract and genital skin, which is why finasteride (type 2 selective) shrinks the prostate.

front: Why is free testosterone not given orally or as a simple injection?
back: Oral testosterone is inactivated by first-pass hepatic metabolism, and a plain intramuscular dose lasts only minutes to hours. Slowly released esters given intramuscularly last weeks, and oral testosterone undecanoate is absorbed through lymphatics, bypassing the liver.

front: Which androgens cause cholestatic jaundice, and why are injectable esters preferred?
back: The 17-alkyl derivatives such as methyltestosterone, fluoxymesterone, oxymetholone and stanozolol cause dose-related cholestatic jaundice, which reverses when the drug is stopped. Parenteral testosterone esters do not cause this, so they are preferred for long-term replacement.

front: How does cyproterone acetate reduce androgen action, and what is it used for?
back: It is a weak androgen receptor blocker related to progesterone. Its progestational action suppresses LH, which lowers testosterone and adds to the direct antiandrogen effect. Uses include precocious puberty, inappropriate sexual behaviour in men, and acne or hirsutism in women, given with an estrogen. Hepatotoxicity limits its use.

front: Why is flutamide given together with a GnRH agonist in metastatic prostate cancer?
back: Flutamide is a nonsteroidal androgen receptor blocker, but blocking feedback raises LH and testosterone, which partly offsets it, so monotherapy is poor. It is therefore used with a GnRH agonist or after orchidectomy (combined androgen blockade). KDT advises starting it about 3 days before the agonist to block the initial testosterone flare. Its main toxicity is hepatic; gynaecomastia and breast tenderness are common, while libido and potency are largely preserved. Bicalutamide is now preferred: once daily and less hepatotoxic.

front: What does finasteride do, and how is it used?
back: It is a competitive inhibitor of 5-alpha reductase, mainly type 2, which lowers DHT in the prostate. It shrinks the prostate and improves urinary flow in benign prostatic hyperplasia, but benefit takes about 6 months. It works best in large glands, and 1 mg daily can help male-pattern baldness. Typical side effects are reduced libido, impotence and lower ejaculate volume.

Hepatic tumours with long-term oral use
Carcinoma of prostate or male breast, pregnancy, liver or kidney disease
Coronary artery disease, heart failure, men over 65
Can worsen sleep apnoea, migraine and epilepsy

front: Complete the note on anabolic steroids.
text: Anabolic steroids include {{nandrolone}}, {{oxymetholone}}, {{stanozolol}} and {{methandienone}}. Their anabolic selectivity is only modest, and the 17-alkyl ones, such as oxymetholone and stanozolol, can cause {{cholestatic jaundice}} and adverse lipid changes.

front: Complete the note on PDE-5 inhibitors.
text: The PDE-5 inhibitors used for erectile dysfunction are {{sildenafil}}, {{tadalafil}} and {{vardenafil}}. Of these, {{tadalafil}} has the longest action (half-life about 18 hours), so nitrates must be avoided for {{48 hours}} after it, and {{vardenafil}} can prolong the QT interval.

front: Classify the antiandrogens and related agents.
text: {{Cyproterone acetate}} is a progesterone-related steroid antagonist; {{flutamide}} and {{bicalutamide}} are nonsteroidal androgen receptor blockers; {{finasteride}} inhibits 5-alpha reductase type 2; {{GnRH agonists}} suppress gonadal androgen output.

front: How do estrogens act at the cell level?
back: Estradiol binds nuclear estrogen receptors, ERalpha and ERbeta. The receptor dimerises, binds estrogen response elements and changes gene transcription with the help of coactivators or corepressors. ERalpha predominates in uterus, breast, bone and blood vessels, while ERbeta predominates in the prostate and ovary. Some rapid membrane-initiated effects also exist.

front: Why is ethinylestradiol used by mouth when natural estradiol is not?
back: Natural estrogens are inactivated by rapid first-pass metabolism in the liver, so oral estradiol is weak and short acting. Ethinylestradiol is metabolised slowly, so it is orally active and more potent, which is why it is used in oral contraceptives and oral hormone therapy.

front: What is the usual cyclical oral HRT regimen for a woman with an intact uterus?
back: Conjugated estrogens 0.625 mg daily for 3 weeks, then 1 week off. A progestin is added for the last 10 to 12 days of each cycle to protect the endometrium from hyperplasia and carcinoma. Lower estrogen doses of about 0.3 to 0.45 mg are also used now. In women without a uterus, estrogen is given alone.

front: What effects do estrogens have on clotting and lipids?
back: They increase synthesis of clotting factors II, VII, IX and X and lower PAI-1, which raises the thrombotic tendency despite increased fibrinolysis. They lower LDL and raise HDL and triglycerides. They also raise SHBG, TBG and CBG levels in the liver.

front: How does clomiphene induce ovulation, and what are its main adverse effects?
back: It blocks estrogen negative feedback at the hypothalamus and pituitary, so more LH and FSH are released with each pulse, driving follicle growth and ovulation. Usual course: 50 mg daily for 5 days from cycle day 5, increased if there is no ovulation, for no more than about 6 cycles. Adverse effects: multiple pregnancy, ovarian enlargement or hyperstimulation, hot flushes and visual disturbance. Current international PCOS guidelines prefer letrozole as first-line for ovulation induction (higher live-birth rate); KDT notes that India banned letrozole for this use in 2011.

front: Why is tamoxifen called a SERM, and where does it act as an agonist?
back: It is an estrogen antagonist in breast tissue (and centrally, causing hot flushes), but a partial agonist in endometrium, bone, liver and pituitary. So it treats and prevents ER-positive breast cancer, preserves bone density and lowers LDL, while its endometrial agonism can cause hyperplasia and endometrial cancer and its hepatic action raises venous thromboembolism risk 2 to 3 fold.

front: What is the tissue profile of raloxifene, and what is it used for?
back: It is an estrogen agonist in bone and lipid metabolism, but an antagonist in breast and endometrium. It prevents postmenopausal bone loss and vertebral fracture and reduces the risk of ER-positive breast cancer. It does not relieve hot flushes, and it raises the risk of venous thrombosis.

front: Why are aromatase inhibitors not used in premenopausal women with functioning ovaries?
back: They block estrogen synthesis from androgens, but functioning ovaries keep making estrogen, so the block is incomplete. They are used in premenopausal women only after ovarian removal or with GnRH suppression. In postmenopausal women, extraglandular aromatisation is the main estrogen source, so they nearly abolish estrogen.

front: What is the medical abortion regimen with mifepristone and misoprostol for early pregnancy?
back: Current WHO and Indian MTP practice: mifepristone 200 mg orally, then 24 to 48 hours later misoprostol 800 microgram buccally, sublingually or vaginally, up to 9 weeks (63 days) of gestation; success is over 95 percent. Older texts (KDT): mifepristone 600 mg followed after 48 hours by misoprostol 400 microgram orally, up to 7 weeks (49 days). Common effects are cramping, nausea, diarrhoea and bleeding; prolonged heavy bleeding and incomplete abortion are the main complications, so follow-up is needed.

front: What is the dose and time window for ulipristal as emergency contraception?
back: Ulipristal 30 mg as a single oral dose, taken within 120 hours of unprotected intercourse. It is as effective as levonorgestrel when taken within 72 hours and more effective than levonorgestrel from 72 to 120 hours. It is a selective progesterone receptor modulator.

front: What is the mechanism of danazol?
back: Danazol is an orally active ethisterone derivative with weak androgenic, anabolic, progestational and glucocorticoid activity. Its main action is suppression of the mid-cycle gonadotropin surge, so ovarian or testicular function falls; it also directly inhibits steroidogenic enzymes (not aromatase). As a 17-alkylated steroid it raises C1 esterase inhibitor levels, so it prevents hereditary angioedema attacks. Other uses: endometriosis (now second line because of androgenic and hepatic adverse effects), menorrhagia and fibrocystic breast disease.

front: Why are desogestrel and gestodene preferred in some combined pills?
back: They are potent gonane progestins with strong antiovulatory action and little or no androgenic activity. Because of their potency, the ethinylestradiol dose can be lowered, and they do not blunt estrogen's favourable effect on lipids, so they suit women with acne or hyperandrogenism. The trade-off: pills containing desogestrel or gestodene carry about twice the venous thromboembolism risk of levonorgestrel pills, so a levonorgestrel combination remains the usual first choice.

Reduces uterine motility and oxytocin sensitivity; supports pregnancy
Lowers the frequency of GnRH pulses
Blunts the mid-cycle LH surge when given early in the cycle
Dysfunctional uterine bleeding: high dose stops bleeding, then cyclic low dose
Endometriosis: suppresses menstruation and ectopic implants
Endometrial carcinoma: palliative in advanced disease
Breast tenderness, bloating, mood change, weight gain
Androgenic 19-nortestosterone types lower HDL
Early pregnancy exposure is best avoided

points: Nausea, headache, breast discomfort, spotting, mostly in the first cycles
Chloasma, acne or weight gain with older androgenic progestins
Venous thromboembolism and arterial events, greater with age, smoking and older high-dose pills
Blood pressure rise, usually reversing after stopping
Thrombosis or stroke, coronary disease, moderate to severe hypertension
Liver disease, genital or breast cancer, porphyria

Diabetes, obesity, smoking, age over 35, migraine, mild hypertension, gallbladder disease
