text: A single-base substitution is a {{single-nucleotide variant (SNV)}}; deletion or duplication of a whole gene or a large DNA segment is a {{copy number variant (CNV)}}; variants that are inherited together on a chromosome are in {{linkage disequilibrium}}.

front: Name the three situations in which a single pharmacogene produces a large effect on drug response.
back: 1) The drug's key metabolic or transport step depends on one enzyme or transporter with variable function (e.g. codeine and CYP2D6). 2) The drug acts on a target, or an off-target protein, that varies (e.g. aminoglycosides and MT-RNR1). 3) The drug's effect depends on the wider biological setting (e.g. antimalarials and rasburicase in G6PD deficiency).

front: What is the two-sided risk of codeine with CYP2D6 variation?
back: Codeine is a prodrug that CYP2D6 converts to morphine. Poor metabolisers make little morphine, so analgesia is absent. Ultrarapid metabolisers make excess morphine, which can cause respiratory depression and death.

front: Which enzyme's variants affect tamoxifen efficacy, and why?
back: CYP2D6. Tamoxifen is a prodrug that CYP2D6 converts to its most active metabolite, endoxifen. Poor metabolisers (and patients on strong CYP2D6 inhibitors such as paroxetine or fluoxetine) form less endoxifen, and have been linked to higher breast cancer recurrence. Current guidance (CPIC) suggests considering an aromatase inhibitor in postmenopausal poor metabolisers; the clinical evidence remains mixed.

front: Clopidogrel: how does CYP2C19 status change the antiplatelet plan?
back: Clopidogrel is a prodrug that CYP2C19 must activate. Poor metabolisers (two no-function alleles) get weak platelet inhibition and more stent thrombosis, and raising the dose does not reliably overcome this (US boxed warning). Current CPIC guidance (2022) for ACS or PCI: in both poor and intermediate metabolisers, avoid clopidogrel and use prasugrel or ticagrelor if not contraindicated. Older texts suggested a higher clopidogrel dose for intermediate metabolisers. Frequency: poor metabolisers about 2 to 3% of Europeans and over 10% of East Asians; intermediate about 25% of Europeans and over 45% of East Asians; South Asians also have high no-function allele frequencies.

front: Classify: CYP2C19 and proton pump inhibitors
text: Omeprazole and lansoprazole are inactivated by {{CYP2C19}}. CYP2C19 poor metabolisers have higher {{parent drug}} exposure, stronger acid suppression and a higher chance of {{ulcer cure}} than rapid or ultrarapid metabolisers.

front: Which transporter variant is linked to simvastatin myopathy, and how was it found?
back: SLCO1B1, which encodes OATP1B1, the transporter that takes statins up into the liver. The reduced-function variant (c.521T>C, Val174Ala) lowers hepatic uptake, so plasma simvastatin acid rises and myopathy risk increases, especially at 80 mg. It was found by a genome-wide association study of a small simvastatin myopathy group (85 cases, 90 controls), showing that GWAS works with few subjects when the effect is large. Guidance: use a lower simvastatin dose or another statin in carriers.

front: Essay: Loss-of-function and gain-of-function metabolic variants and their effect on drug action

points: Drugs with a narrow margin, cleared by a single enzyme, are the highest-risk group
Outcome depends on whether the parent drug or a metabolite is the active species
Parent drug and upstream metabolites rise, so toxicity or overdose-like effects follow
Downstream metabolites fall
If the active species is a metabolite formed by the enzyme, efficacy is lost
Parent drug falls, so efficacy can be lost
Downstream active metabolites rise, which can cause adverse effects
Loss of activation gives inefficacy (clopidogrel, codeine analgesia)
Gain of activation can give excess active drug (codeine and morphine)
Codeine and CYP2D6
Clopidogrel and CYP2C19
Tacrolimus and CYP3A5: functional alleles lower exposure, so higher doses are needed
Omeprazole and CYP2C19: poor metabolisers get a stronger acid-suppressing effect
Genotype the enzyme before using a narrow-margin drug that depends on it
Interpret results with ancestry in mind, since allele frequencies vary between populations

front: Short note: Pharmacogenetics of warfarin

points: CYP2C9 metabolises the more active S-enantiomer
CYP2C9 poor and intermediate metabolisers need lower steady-state doses and have more bleeding
Target VKORC1 is needed to recycle vitamin K to its active reduced form
Promoter variants that lower VKORC1 expression need lower doses (more common in Asian ancestry)
Rare coding variants cause partial or complete resistance and higher dose needs
CYP4F2 inactivates vitamin K by hydroxylation
CYP2C9, VKORC1 and CYP4F2 together explain over 50% of the dose variability

front: How do MT-RNR1 variants raise the risk of aminoglycoside hearing loss?
back: Aminoglycosides bind bacterial 16S rRNA, but in the inner ear they also bind human mitochondrial ribosomes (off-target). MT-RNR1 variants make human mitochondrial rRNA resemble bacterial rRNA, increasing binding affinity. Hearing loss can then occur even when serum levels are judged non-toxic.

front: Why must tumour genotype be checked before some targeted anticancer drugs?
back: Response depends on somatic (tumour) mutations as well as germline DNA. EGFR activating mutations predict response to gefitinib, and BRAF V600E predicts response to vemurafenib. Trastuzumab helps only HER2-expressing breast cancers, yet it can cause cardiomyopathy, and HER2-negative patients carry that risk without benefit.

front: Classify: drug targets and variant-specific drug action
text: Warfarin's target is {{VKORC1}}; ivacaftor partly corrects the gating defect of the CFTR {{G551D}} variant; lumacaftor improves surface expression of the CFTR {{F508del}} variant; vemurafenib inhibits {{BRAF V600E}} kinase.

front: Why is NUDT15 testing relevant to thiopurine toxicity in East Asian patients?
back: TPMT and NUDT15 variants both alter the levels of active thiopurine metabolites and the risk of bone marrow toxicity. TPMT poor metabolisers are rare in East Asian populations, but NUDT15 poor and intermediate metabolisers are more frequent there. Thiopurine toxicity is more common in Asian patients, and NUDT15 was found by GWAS, so TPMT testing alone can miss risk.

front: What does the UGT1A1*28 allele do, and which drugs does it affect?
back: UGT1A1*28 has seven TA repeats in the promoter instead of the common six, which lowers UGT1A1 expression. The allele frequency can reach about 30%, with up to 10% of people homozygous depending on ancestry. Reduced activity raises SN-38, the active metabolite of irinotecan, and so raises the risk of serious toxicity. It also causes Gilbert syndrome and atazanavir-related hyperbilirubinaemia.

front: Acetylator (NAT2) polymorphism: what are the consequences of slow and fast acetylation?
back: NAT2 variants give slow and fast acetylators; about 60 to 70% of Indians are slow acetylators (isoniazid half-life about 3 h versus 1 h in fast). Slow acetylators: isoniazid peripheral neuropathy (pyridoxine deficiency; give pyridoxine); higher risk of isoniazid hepatotoxicity on current evidence; hydralazine- and procainamide-induced lupus; sulfonamide hypersensitivity. Fast acetylators: poorer response to once- or twice-weekly isoniazid (daily dosing is unaffected) and need higher hydralazine doses. Older texts said fast acetylators had more isoniazid hepatotoxicity (via acetylhydrazine); current studies point to slow acetylators, and the toxic metabolite is formed from acetylhydrazine by CYP2E1.

front: Short note: G6PD deficiency and drug response

points: G6PD makes NADPH in the pentose phosphate pathway, which keeps glutathione reduced in red cells
Deficient red cells cannot cope with oxidant drugs, so haemolysis follows
X-linked; common in Mediterranean, African and Asian (including Indian) populations; severity depends on the variant
Primaquine and tafenoquine: test G6PD before use (tafenoquine needs a quantitative test)
Dapsone (haemolysis and methaemoglobinaemia)
Rasburicase; methylene blue; nitrofurantoin; sulfonamides and cotrimoxazole
Quinine, chloroquine and high-dose aspirin carry lower risk
Its action produces hydrogen peroxide, which G6PD-deficient cells cannot handle
Haemolytic anaemia and methaemoglobinaemia can follow
Contraindicated in G6PD deficiency; screen high-risk patients first
G6PD is neither the drug's metabolic enzyme nor its target; it is a pharmacodynamic background factor
Methylene blue does not work, and may worsen haemolysis, for methaemoglobinaemia in G6PD deficiency

front: Classify: pharmacogene, drug and consequence
text: TPMT and NUDT15: {{azathioprine}} and mercaptopurine cause marrow toxicity; DPYD (dihydropyrimidine dehydrogenase): {{capecitabine}} and {{fluorouracil}} cause toxicity; UGT1A1: {{irinotecan}} causes neutropenia and diarrhoea; NAT2: {{isoniazid}} causes neuropathy in slow acetylators; G6PD: {{rasburicase}} causes haemolysis and methaemoglobinaemia.

front: Essay: Pharmacogenetic approach to severe toxicity from antimetabolite and cytotoxic drugs

points: Many of these drugs have a narrow therapeutic margin, and toxicity can be life-threatening
Germline variants affect the host; somatic variants affect the tumour
TPMT and NUDT15 variants raise marrow toxicity risk
The same variants alter the risk of second cancers
NUDT15 matters more in Asian ancestry, where TPMT variants are less common
DPYD variants predict toxicity with fluorouracil and capecitabine
Reduced UGT1A1 activity raises SN-38 exposure
Higher SN-38 is linked to serious toxicity
TYMS enhancer repeat: two copies rather than three raises host toxicity and tumour susceptibility to TYMS inhibitors
Somatic markers such as EGFR and BRAF V600E select patients for targeted drugs
Genotype before prescribing where a validated test exists
Ancestry determines which variants are informative for a given patient

front: How does HLA-B*57:01 testing change abacavir treatment?
back: Carriers of HLA-B*57:01 are at high risk of abacavir hypersensitivity syndrome: a multi-system reaction with fever, rash, gastrointestinal and respiratory symptoms, usually within 6 weeks, which can be fatal on rechallenge. It is not typically Stevens-Johnson syndrome. A randomised trial (PREDICT-1) showed that screening before treatment eliminated immunologically confirmed hypersensitivity. Screening is now standard; carriers must not receive abacavir. The drug binds within the HLA-B*57:01 peptide groove and alters the self-peptides presented to T cells.

front: Which HLA allele predicts carbamazepine skin reactions in East Asian and in European-ancestry patients?
back: HLA-B*15:02 in Han Chinese and Southeast Asian patients (SJS/TEN); the US label advises testing patients of Asian ancestry before starting carbamazepine. In European-ancestry and Japanese patients, HLA-A*31:01 is the risk allele; it was found by a GWAS of 65 cases and 3987 controls, and is linked to a wider range of reactions including DRESS.

front: Why check both CYP2C9 and HLA-B genotype before starting phenytoin?
back: Two separate risks. CYP2C9 poor and intermediate metabolisers clear phenytoin slowly, so exposure and dose-related toxicity rise; they need lower maintenance doses. HLA-B*15:02 carriers are at risk of SJS/TEN with phenytoin, as with carbamazepine, so phenytoin (and fosphenytoin) should be avoided in phenytoin-naive carriers. CYP2C9 reduced-function alleles (e.g. *3) have also been linked to severe skin reactions, so CPIC guidance reads both genotypes together.

front: Classify: HLA alleles and drug hypersensitivity
text: HLA-B*57:01 with {{abacavir}}; HLA-B*58:01 with {{allopurinol}} SJS/TEN and DRESS; HLA-B*15:02 with {{carbamazepine}}, oxcarbazepine and {{phenytoin}} (Asian ancestry); HLA-A*31:01 with {{carbamazepine}} (European and Japanese ancestry).

front: Short note: HLA testing for drug hypersensitivity and its limits

points: HLA-A, -B and -C encode MHC class I proteins that present peptides to T cells
HLA-B is among the most polymorphic genes in the genome
HLA-B*15:02 is common in Han Chinese and Southeast Asian groups (about 10 to 15% in some), and present at lower and variable frequency in South Asians, including Indians
It is absent or very rare in European and sub-Saharan African populations
Other regional risk alleles include HLA-B*15:21, B*15:11, B*15:08 (Asian) and B*56:02 (Aboriginal Australian)
A negative result is reassuring only if the correct allele panel for the patient's population was tested
Low positive predictive value: most carriers never react
The immune mechanism is incompletely understood

front: Why has the candidate-gene approach worked well in pharmacogenetics when it often fails elsewhere?
back: Pharmacogenetic candidate genes were chosen from known drug disposition or action pathways, and the variants found often have large effects that replicate. Elsewhere, candidate-gene findings frequently failed to replicate. GWAS is now used without a prior hypothesis and can give clear signals even with small samples when the effect is large (e.g. carbamazepine and HLA-A*31:01).

front: Why are the results of warfarin genotyping trials mixed?
back: Large RCTs disagreed. COAG (US) found no improvement in time in therapeutic range (TTR) over the first 4 weeks, with worse results in African-American patients because their key variants were not tested. EU-PACT found a modest improvement in TTR. GIFT, in hip and knee arthroplasty, used a composite clinical endpoint (major bleeding, INR of 4 or more, venous thromboembolism, death) and showed a significant benefit of genotype-guided dosing. EHR-based studies link CYP2C9 and CYP4F2 variants to bleeding.

front: Short note: Clinical implementation of pharmacogenomic testing

points: Point-of-care: genotype when the drug is prescribed; each drug needs its own assay
Multi-gene panel stored in the EHR, with clinical decision support when a relevant drug is prescribed
Strongest: RCTs comparing a genotype-guided strategy with standard care
HLA-B*57:01 with abacavir: genotyping eliminated severe skin reactions
Clopidogrel: genotype-guided care gave fewer bleeding events without more stent thrombosis
Warfarin: mixed results overall
Non-randomised data are weaker, and RCTs for rare variants may be impractical
The variant must link to a clinically important outcome, and the test must lead to actionable advice (change drug or dose)
Evidence strength varies by drug-gene pair
CPIC publishes peer-reviewed, genotype-based prescribing guidance across drugs
Allele panels must suit the target population

front: Essay: Role of human genomics in new drug discovery and development

points: Genetic pathways in physiology and disease point to new drug targets
Drugs with human genetic support are about two to three times more likely to reach the market
Work on familial hypercholesterolaemia and the LDL receptor validated the cholesterol pathway that statins target
PCSK9 gain-of-function variants cause familial hypercholesterolaemia; loss-of-function variants lower LDL cholesterol and coronary risk; PCSK9 antibodies and inclisiran followed
Loss-of-function variants in APOC3, SLC30A8 and HSD17B13 reduce risk of common diseases
SCN9A loss of function causes insensitivity to pain, suggesting an analgesic target
Genetic variants may identify likely responders, as proposed for dalcetrapib and an ADCY9 variant (the confirmatory trial was negative)
Polygenic risk scores may pick patients most likely to benefit from costly LDL-lowering drugs
Phenome-wide association studies link variants to phenotypes, suggesting new indications
Such studies can also predict adverse effects of drugs
Variants are often population specific, so diverse cohorts are needed (e.g. PCSK9 variants in African American subjects)
Ancestry diversity drives discovery in all populations

front: Classify: genomic evidence in drug development
text: Loss-of-function variants in {{PCSK9}} lower LDL cholesterol and point to it as a target; a GWAS suggested that an {{ADCY9}} variant predicts response to {{dalcetrapib}}; PheWAS can suggest {{repurposing}} of existing drugs; drugs with human genetic support are about {{two- to three-fold}} more likely to be marketed.

front: Atypical plasma cholinesterase: what happens with succinylcholine, and how is it detected?
back: Variants of the BCHE gene produce atypical or deficient butyrylcholinesterase (pseudocholinesterase), which cannot hydrolyse succinylcholine (or mivacurium) normally. Neuromuscular block that should last about 5 to 10 minutes can persist for hours (succinylcholine apnoea). Management is continued ventilation and sedation until recovery. Detected by the dibucaine number: dibucaine inhibits normal enzyme about 80% but the atypical homozygous enzyme only about 20%; heterozygotes are intermediate.

front: What is the genetic basis of malignant hyperthermia, and which drugs trigger it?
back: Autosomal dominant variants in RYR1 (the skeletal muscle ryanodine receptor calcium-release channel), or less often CACNA1S. Volatile anaesthetics (halothane, sevoflurane, desflurane, isoflurane) and succinylcholine trigger uncontrolled calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum, causing rigidity, hypercarbia, hyperthermia, rhabdomyolysis and hyperkalaemia. Treatment: stop the trigger, give dantrolene (blocks RYR1), cool and correct acidosis and hyperkalaemia. Known carriers should receive a non-triggering anaesthetic.

front: DPYD testing before fluoropyrimidines: why, and how is the dose changed?
back: Dihydropyrimidine dehydrogenase (DPD, gene DPYD) inactivates over 80% of fluorouracil. Reduced-function variants (e.g. DPYD*2A, c.2846A>T) cause severe or fatal neutropenia, mucositis, diarrhoea and hand-foot syndrome with fluorouracil and capecitabine. Current guidance (CPIC; EMA recommends testing before treatment): intermediate metabolisers start at about 50% of the dose and titrate by tolerance; complete DPD deficiency means avoid fluoropyrimidines. Uridine triacetate is the antidote for overdose or early-onset severe toxicity.

front: What does the WHO mean by rational use of medicines?
back: Patients receive medicines suited to their clinical needs, in doses that match their own requirements, for an adequate period, and at the lowest cost to them and their community. It covers the whole supply-use chain, though prescribing is the clinical core.

front: Which criteria show that a prescription is appropriate?
back: A sound indication; a drug that suits the patient for efficacy, tolerability, safety and cost; a dose, route and duration fitted to the patient; no contraindication, the drug acceptable to the patient, and expected benefit greater than likely harm; correct dispensing with instructions; and follow-up of adherence, benefit and adverse effects.

front: Short note: Irrational prescribing

points: Prescriber habits, copied from teachers or popular doctors
Heavy patient load leading to routine symptom-based prescribing
Imprecise diagnosis, so several drugs are given to cover every possibility
Industry promotion, unrealistic claims and inducements
Patient demand for a 'pill for every ill'; knowledge alone does not fix this
Drug given when none is needed (antibiotic for a viral fever)
Drug unrelated to the diagnosis (PPI for any abdominal symptom)
Wrong dose, route or duration (stopping TB treatment early; prolonged post-operative antibiotics)
Unnecessary combinations and polypharmacy with interaction risk
Unsafe use (corticosteroid for fever)
Costly new drug used where a cheaper equivalent works
Delayed relief or cure; more adverse effects
Emergence of microbial resistance
Financial loss to patient and community; loss of trust in the doctor
Follow a stepwise prescribing process
Use essential medicines and formularies
Audit prescribing and give feedback

front: Classify: examples of irrational prescribing
text: Antibiotic for a viral fever is {{use when no drug is needed}}; tetracycline for pharyngitis is {{wrong drug selection}}; corticosteroid for fever is {{unsafe use}}; ciprofloxacin plus tinidazole for any diarrhoea is {{unnecessary combination}}; an injection where tablets would do is {{incorrect route}}.

front: Why should a drug be prescribed by its generic (non-proprietary) name, and when is a brand name better?
back: A generic name is uniform, shorter and easier to remember than many brand names, and it lets the pharmacist supply any manufacturer's product, which is usually cheaper because no brand promotion is paid for. A brand name is safer when product consistency in quality and bioavailability matters and official quality control is weak.

front: Classify: the three names of a drug
text: A {{chemical}} name describes the molecule and is too cumbersome for prescribing; a {{non-proprietary}} name is the accepted generic name, and the WHO recommends {{rINN}} names for new drugs; a {{brand}} name is the manufacturer's trademark and can differ between countries.

front: What are the steps of rational prescribing?
back: 1) Establish at least a provisional diagnosis. 2) Define the therapeutic problem and goals (symptom relief, cure, prevention of complications). 3) Select the drug class for each goal. 4) Choose the drug on efficacy, safety, suitability for this patient and cost. 5) Decide route, dose and duration for this patient. 6) Give information and instructions. 7) Monitor adherence, goal achievement and adverse effects, and change therapy as needed.

front: What information must a patient receive when a drug is prescribed?
back: What effect to expect and when; whether the disease is cured or only controlled; what happens if doses are missed; common side effects, told without alarming the patient; how and how long to take it, and which tests are needed; precautions such as not driving after sedating antihistamines or not drinking alcohol with metronidazole. The patient should repeat the instructions back to confirm understanding.

front: Short note: Prescription writing

points: Name, age, sex, date
Body weight for paediatric and dose-critical drugs
Known allergies and relevant contraindications
Generic name preferred; strength and dosage form
Dose, route, frequency, duration and quantity written unambiguously
Name, registration number and signature
Legible handwriting or printed text
Avoid error-prone abbreviations (e.g. 'U' for units, trailing zeros)
Include simple written instructions for the patient

front: Essay: Drug-use studies and prescribing audit

points: Find out how drugs are actually prescribed and compare this with agreed standards
Use the findings to improve prescribing
Descriptive studies show what is used and how much
Data come from prescriptions, dispensing records and case notes
Average number of drugs per encounter
Percentage of drugs prescribed by generic name
Percentage of encounters with an antibiotic or an injection
Percentage of drugs taken from the essential medicines list
Average consultation and dispensing times
Set explicit standards, for example from guidelines
Collect data, compare with standards, feed back to prescribers
Change practice and repeat the audit
Indicators show patterns, not whether each prescription was appropriate
Sampling and recording bias can distort results; pair with clinical review

front: Classify: WHO prescribing indicators
text: Average number of drugs per {{encounter}}; percentage of drugs prescribed by {{generic name}}; percentage of encounters with an {{antibiotic}}; percentage of encounters with an {{injection}}; percentage of drugs taken from the {{essential medicines list}}.

front: How does the WHO define essential medicines?
back: Medicines that satisfy the priority health care needs of a population. They are chosen for public health relevance, evidence of efficacy and safety, and comparative cost-effectiveness. They should be available at all times in working health systems, in adequate amounts and suitable dosage forms, with assured quality, adequate information and a price the individual and community can afford.

front: Essay: Selection criteria for essential medicines

points: Only a small set of medicines meets most health needs
Cheaper, well-tested drugs are often as good as newer, costlier ones
Concentrating resources on this set gives better value
Adequate efficacy and safety data from clinical studies
Quality, including bioavailability, and stability on storage must be assured
Pattern of prevalent diseases
Facilities and trained personnel; financial resources
Genetic, demographic and environmental factors
Compare efficacy, safety, quality, price and availability
Cost-benefit ratio is a major consideration
Pharmacokinetic properties and local manufacturing capacity also count
Mostly single compounds; fixed-ratio combinations only with proven advantage
List is reviewed continuously as disease patterns, evidence and drugs change
Selection should follow rationally developed treatment guidelines

front: Short note: WHO and National List of Essential Medicines

points: First model list in 1977; revised periodically
20th list (2017): about 433 medicines, including 25 FDCs
Member countries adapt it to local needs
First list 1996; revised in 2011, then 2015 as the National List of Essential Medicines (NLEM)
2015 NLEM: 376 medicines, of which 20 are FDCs
Medicines are grouped for primary, secondary and tertiary care
Basis for public procurement and supply
Improves availability, saves money and promotes rational use
Later editions of both lists have been issued; check the current versions

front: What is the P-drug concept in rational prescribing?
back: A P-drug list is a short, evidence-based list of preferred drugs for common conditions, chosen for efficacy, safety, cost and suitability. It is used as a guide for first-line choice in a hospital, department or region, and it narrows the range of drugs used for each condition.

front: What is an orphan drug, and why do governments support it?
back: A drug for a rare disease, or for a common disease that is endemic only in resource-poor areas, where the cost of development is unlikely to be recovered from sales. Under the US Orphan Drug Act (1983), a rare disease affects fewer than 0.2 million people in the USA. Governments give tax benefits and other incentives to encourage development.

front: What are over-the-counter (OTC) drugs, and how is prescription status regulated in India?
back: OTC drugs can be bought without a prescription because they are relatively harmless, e.g. paracetamol, aspirin, antacids, senna, lactulose, vitamins and ferrous salts. Most drugs, including all antibiotics, are prescription-only; in India they are placed in Schedule H of the Drugs and Cosmetics Rules.

front: When is a fixed-dose combination (FDC) rational? Give the main advantages.
back: When every component is needed at the stated doses. Advantages: better adherence and convenience; synergy (sulfamethoxazole plus trimethoprim, levodopa plus carbidopa); components with different mechanisms add their effect while side effects differ (amlodipine plus atenolol); one component offsets another's side effect (thiazide plus a potassium-sparing diuretic); a single drug cannot be given alone in TB, HIV or falciparum malaria; sometimes cheaper than separate tablets.

front: Complete: disadvantages of fixed-dose combinations
text: The patient may receive {{unneeded}} components; one ingredient's dose cannot be changed without altering the other; components may have different {{time courses}} and renal or hepatic handling; an adverse effect is hard to {{attribute}} to one drug; a {{contraindication}} to one part bars the whole product; and a false sense of {{superiority}} may follow.

front: Classify: examples of rational fixed-dose combinations
text: Sulfamethoxazole + {{trimethoprim}} (synergy); levodopa + {{carbidopa}} (synergy); {{isoniazid}} + rifampin (single-drug use avoided in TB); amlodipine + {{atenolol}} (different mechanisms, antihypertensive); thiazide + {{potassium-sparing diuretic}} (side effect offset).

front: Short note: Irrational fixed-dose combinations

points: Contains an ingredient the patient does not need
Fixed ratio prevents individual dose adjustment
Components with different pharmacokinetics given at one interval
No proven advantage over the single agents
Antimicrobial combinations used without need, adding toxicity and resistance risk
Tonic or vitamin add-ons with no clear benefit
Products containing doubtful-efficacy ingredients
Use a combination only if every component is needed at that dose
Prescribe separate drugs when individual dosing matters
Know the exact composition of any FDC used
Banned combinations are listed in an appendix of the reference book
Several hundred irrational FDCs have been banned in India in recent years
WHO and NLEM lists include only a small number of FDCs

front: Which drug class must not be given as a fixed-dose combination with other drugs for internal use?
back: Corticosteroids. The reference states they should never be combined with any other drug meant for internal use, because the steroid dose can then not be adjusted on its own.

front: Short note: Therapeutic drug monitoring (TDM)

points: Narrow safety margin: digoxin, anticonvulsants, antiarrhythmics, theophylline, aminoglycosides, lithium, tricyclic antidepressants
Large individual variation: antidepressants, lithium
Toxic drugs in renal failure: aminoglycosides, vancomycin
Poisoning, to confirm it and track clearance
Unexplained treatment failure (antimicrobials); checking compliance (psychotropics)
Response is easily measured: antihypertensives, hypoglycaemics, diuretics, oral anticoagulants, inhalational anaesthetics
Drug is a prodrug needing activation (levodopa)
Effect outlasts plasma level ('hit and run'): reserpine, MAO inhibitors, omeprazole
Action is irreversible: organophosphates, phenoxybenzamine
Dose adjustment of long-acting drugs: trough level just before the next dose
Short-acting intermittent drugs (ampicillin, gentamicin): sample about 1-2 hours after dosing
Poisoning: sample early and repeat to judge clearance

front: Classify: types of pharmacoeconomic analysis
text: Cost-{{minimisation}} analysis compares only the costs of options with equal outcomes; cost-{{effectiveness}} analysis gives cost per outcome in natural units, such as cases cured; cost-{{benefit}} analysis converts outcomes into money; cost-{{utility}} analysis gives cost per {{QALY}} gained.

front: What is a QALY and how is it used?
back: Quality-adjusted life year. One year lived in perfect health counts as 1; time in a poorer health state is weighted between 0 and 1 by quality of life; death counts as 0. Cost per QALY gained lets treatments for different diseases be compared, which is why it is used in policy and resource allocation.

front: When is cost-utility analysis preferred to cost-effectiveness analysis?
back: Cost-effectiveness uses a disease-specific unit (e.g. cost per case cured or per life-year), so it cannot compare treatments for different diseases. Cost-utility uses a common unit, the QALY, which includes quality of life, so it allows comparison across diseases. Its quality weights are partly subjective.

front: What is antimicrobial stewardship?
back: A coordinated set of actions that makes antimicrobial use correct in choice of drug, dose, route and duration, so patients benefit most while resistance, toxicity and cost are kept down. It applies rational prescribing principles to anti-infectives, including narrowing or stopping therapy once the pathogen is known.

front: What principles guide empirical antimicrobial therapy before culture results are known?
back: Make at least a tentative clinical diagnosis; guess the likely organism from the clinical features and local experience; start a specific drug. Use broad cover only when the infection is severe or diagnostic services are unavailable. Review the response and narrow or change treatment on bacteriological findings, avoiding hasty, arbitrary switches.

front: Why are antimicrobial combinations discouraged outside specific indications?
back: They encourage a casual approach to diagnosis; they increase adverse effects (e.g. vancomycin with an aminoglycoside causes excess nephrotoxicity); they raise the risk of superinfection; underdosed non-synergistic drugs can select resistance; and they cost more. Combinations are justified for mixed infections, for empirical cover in severe infection until cultures are known, and for topical use.

front: Essay: Antimicrobial stewardship as rational use

points: Rational antimicrobial use means the right drug, dose, route and duration
Goal: best outcome with least harm, resistance and cost
Confirm a clinical diagnosis; obtain cultures before treatment where feasible
Use local resistance data for empirical choice
No antibiotics for viral illnesses or non-specific diarrhoea
Narrowest effective agent, given in full therapeutic dose
Adjust doses for renal or hepatic impairment
Never a single drug where combined therapy is standard (e.g. TB)
Combinations only for mixed infections or temporary empirical cover
Avoid routine prophylaxis beyond established indications
Stop prolonged post-operative courses
Review once culture results return; de-escalate or stop
Audit antibiotic use and give prescriber feedback
Infection control reduces the need for antibiotics

front: SGLT2 inhibitors beyond glucose lowering: main indications and key adverse effect?
back: They block Na+-glucose reabsorption in the proximal tubule. They reduce heart failure hospitalisation and cardiovascular death in heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, a benefit seen without diabetes too, and slow kidney function decline in chronic kidney disease. Key adverse effect: genital mycotic infections; euglycaemic ketoacidosis and volume depletion are also important.

front: Finerenone: class, key use and key adverse effect?
back: A non-steroidal mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist that competitively blocks aldosterone binding. Used to reduce kidney decline and cardiovascular events in chronic kidney disease with type 2 diabetes. Key adverse effect: hyperkalaemia, so it is contraindicated in existing hyperkalaemia and needs caution with strong CYP3A4 inhibitors.

front: Sacubitril-valsartan: what does each component do, and what is the key safety rule?
back: Valsartan is an AT1 receptor blocker. Sacubitril inhibits neprilysin, so natriuretic peptides (ANP, BNP) and other vasoactive peptides are broken down more slowly, giving natriuresis and vasodilation. Used in chronic heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, where it was superior to enalapril. Never combine with an ACE inhibitor (36-hour gap is required); the main serious adverse effect is angioedema.

front: Tirzepatide: mechanism, key use and key adverse effect?
back: A single peptide that activates both GIP and GLP-1 receptors (dual incretin agonist). Used in type 2 diabetes and for weight reduction in obesity. Key adverse effects are gastrointestinal (nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea). It carries a thyroid C-cell tumour warning and should be avoided in MEN 2 or a personal or family history of medullary thyroid cancer.

front: Semaglutide: why is it used in obesity, and what is its key adverse effect?
back: A long-acting GLP-1 receptor agonist that resists DPP-4 breakdown and is given once weekly. It reduces appetite and body weight and is approved for obesity as well as type 2 diabetes. Key adverse effects are dose-related nausea, vomiting and diarrhoea; pancreatitis and gallbladder disease are also reported. Avoid in MEN 2 or medullary thyroid cancer.

front: Inclisiran: how does it lower LDL-cholesterol, and how is it given?
back: A small interfering RNA that binds PCSK9 messenger RNA in the liver and blocks synthesis of the PCSK9 protein. Fewer LDL receptors are degraded, so LDL-cholesterol falls. Given as a subcutaneous injection after two initial doses, then about twice a year. Common adverse effects: injection-site reactions and bronchitis.

front: Bempedoic acid: where does it act, and what adverse effects follow?
back: An oral prodrug, activated in the liver, that inhibits ATP-citrate lyase, an enzyme upstream of HMG-CoA reductase. Cholesterol synthesis falls and LDL receptors increase. Used in heterozygous familial hypercholesterolaemia or established ASCVD needing extra LDL lowering, and can be combined with statins. Watch for hyperuricaemia with gout and tendon rupture.

front: Romosozumab: target, effect on bone, and key warning?
back: A monoclonal antibody against sclerostin, a Wnt-pathway inhibitor made by osteocytes. Blocking it increases bone formation and, unlike most antiresorptives, also reduces resorption. Used in severe postmenopausal osteoporosis. Key warning: increased risk of myocardial infarction, stroke and cardiovascular death, so it is avoided after a recent MI or stroke.

front: Gepants: mechanism and why they suit migraine patients who cannot take triptans?
back: Small-molecule CGRP receptor antagonists (rimegepant, ubrogepant, atogepant). CGRP released from trigeminal nerves drives migraine pain and is a potent vasodilator. Blocking its receptor treats or prevents attacks without vasoconstriction, so they suit patients with cardiovascular disease, in whom triptans are avoided. Ubrogepant and rimegepant treat acute attacks; rimegepant and atogepant are used for prevention.

front: Lecanemab: target, use and main safety issue?
back: A monoclonal antibody that binds soluble amyloid-beta protofibrils and aggregated forms, clearing plaque and slowing decline in early Alzheimer disease. Key adverse effect: amyloid-related imaging abnormalities (ARIA), with oedema and microhaemorrhages. Risk is higher in APOE e4 homozygotes, so MRI monitoring is required.

front: Bedaquiline: mechanism, use and key adverse effect?
back: A diarylquinoline that inhibits the c-subunit of mycobacterial ATP synthase, stopping energy production. Used for multidrug-resistant tuberculosis as part of a combination regimen. Key adverse effect: QT prolongation, driven by its M2 metabolite, so ECG monitoring is needed with other QT-prolonging drugs. Nausea and diarrhoea are common but rarely stop treatment.

front: Pretomanid: how is it activated, what is its spectrum, and what is a key interaction?
back: A nitroimidazole prodrug activated inside Mycobacterium tuberculosis by an F420-dependent nitroreductase, which releases reactive nitrogen species. Active against M. tuberculosis only, not other mycobacteria. Used in XDR-TB with bedaquiline and linezolid. Avoid strong CYP3A inducers such as rifampicin, which lower its levels.

front: Cefiderocol: how does it enter bacteria, and when is it reserved?
back: A parenteral cephalosporin carrying a siderophore side chain, so it is taken up through bacterial iron-transport channels. Active against Pseudomonas and ESBL- and KPC-producing Enterobacterales. Reserve it for resistant Gram-negative infections to protect stewardship. Adverse effects are those typical of cephalosporins, such as diarrhoea and rash.

front: Baloxavir marboxil: target, dosing principle and key adverse effect?
back: A prodrug converted to baloxavir acid, which inhibits the cap-dependent endonuclease of influenza polymerase (PA subunit), blocking viral mRNA synthesis. Given as a single oral dose for uncomplicated influenza within about 2 days of symptoms, and for post-exposure prophylaxis. Active against influenza A and B. Key adverse effect: diarrhoea. Resistance can arise through a PA I38T substitution.

front: Classify the oral COVID-19 antiviral nirmatrelvir.

front: Molnupiravir: mechanism and key restriction?
back: An oral prodrug of the ribonucleoside beta-D-N4-hydroxycytidine. Its triphosphate is incorporated into viral RNA by the viral RNA-dependent RNA polymerase, causing lethal mutagenesis. Used early in mild-to-moderate COVID-19 in people at risk of progression, under emergency authorisation. Contraindicated in pregnancy because of developmental toxicity seen in animals.

front: CTLA-4 and PD-1 checkpoint inhibitors: where do they act, and which agents block each?
back: CTLA-4 competes with CD28 for B7 ligands on antigen-presenting cells, damping T-cell priming. Anti-CTLA-4 antibodies (ipilimumab, tremelimumab) release this brake early, in lymphoid tissue. PD-1 on activated T cells binds PD-L1 and PD-L2, exhausting T cells within tumours. Anti-PD-1 (nivolumab, pembrolizumab, cemiplimab) and anti-PD-L1 (atezolizumab, durvalumab, avelumab) restore antitumour activity.

front: Sotorasib: which mutation does it target, how does it bind, and what are its key adverse effects?
back: An oral covalent inhibitor of KRAS G12C. It binds a cysteine present only in the mutant protein and locks KRAS in the inactive state. Approved for previously treated KRAS G12C-mutant NSCLC. Key adverse effects: diarrhoea, nausea and low-grade hepatotoxicity; pneumonitis is rare.

front: Source of late (phalloidin-type) mushroom toxins

front: Organs damaged in late mushroom poisoning

front: Toxin from A. phalloides that binds actin (phalloidin type)

front: Atropine value in delayed-onset mushroom poisoning

front: Plant family of atropinic natural alkaloids

front: Natural atropinic alkaloids: list all

front: Which isomers are more active among atropinic alkaloids

front: Atropine CNS effect at low doses

front: Medullary centres stimulated by atropine

front: Atropine effect on vestibular excitation

front: Atropine action in parkinsonism
back: Suppresses tremor and rigidity by blocking basal ganglia cholinergic overactivity

front: High-dose atropine CNS effects

front: Atropine effect on AV node

front: Atropine effect on blood pressure

front: Vasodepressor action blocked by atropine
back: Cholinergic agonists

front: Topical atropine effects on the eye

front: Eye risk with atropine

front: Atropine effect on gut motility

front: Atropine effect on airways

front: Atropine effect on ureter and bladder

front: Secretions most reduced by atropine

front: Pancreatic and intestinal secretion with atropine
back: Not significantly reduced

front: Atropine blocks exogenous agonists vs nerve-released ACh

front: Chief sources of atropine

front: Hyoscine CNS effect at low dose

front: Hyoscine vs atropine: duration

front: Hyoscine vs atropine: potency on eye and secretory glands

front: Hyoscine vs atropine: anti-motion sickness

front: Atropine metabolism and excretion

front: Half-life of atropine

front: Hyoscine metabolism and brain penetration vs atropine

front: Atropine sulfate dose (adult i.m. or i.v.)

front: Hyoscine hydrobromide oral dose

front: Oral absorption of quaternary atropine substitutes

back: Peptic ulcer and GI hypermotility

front: Flavoxate use

front: Solifenacin compared with darifenacin

front: Vasicoselective anticholinergics: list all
